Indonesia’s US$1.5 trillion economy is still nearly triple that of Vietnam, whose marginal per capita lead may not last
Gross domestic product per capita, which provides a snapshot of a country’s standard of living, is projected to rise 8.9 per cent to US$5,259 in Vietnam this year – nearly double the figure a decade earlier and overtaking Indonesia’s US$5,153.

articles.title: Draft import-export strategy: How can Vietnamese businesses avoid remaining perpetually behind FDI? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Draft import-export strategy: How can Vietnamese businesses avoid remaining perpetually behind FDI?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(NB&CL) The draft Strategy for Import and Export of Goods until 2030, with a vision to 2045, aims for an average annual export growth of 15-16%, while increasing the proportion of domestic enterprises to 28-30% by 2030.
In recent years, import and export trade has consistently maintained double-digit growth, forming a crucial driving force for Vietnam's economy . In 2024, total import and export turnover reached US$786.29 billion, an increase of 15.4% compared to the previous year. In 2025, this figure is projected to exceed US$930 billion, an increase of over 18%.
According to the latest report from the General Statistics Office of the Ministry of Finance , in the first 10 months of 2026, Vietnam's total import and export turnover reached US$1,010.55 billion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year.
The General Statistics Office emphasized that this is the first time Vietnam's merchandise trade has exceeded the $1 trillion mark, setting an all-time high. This result reflects the ever-expanding scale of international trade and demonstrates the growing role of import and export in the economy.
Speaking with a reporter from the Newspaper of Journalists and Public Opinion, Dr. Huynh Thanh Dien, an economic expert, said that the fact that import and export turnover will exceed the 1,000 billion USD mark in 2026 has been predicted beforehand.
According to him, the impressive growth in import and export activities in recent times has been largely contributed by the foreign direct investment (FDI) sector.
Data for the first 10 months of 2026 shows that, on the export side, total turnover reached nearly 500 billion USD. Of this, FDI accounted for 81.2% of the total turnover, while domestic enterprises accounted for only 18.8%.
This disparity is also reflected in imports. Of the total import value of $511.31 billion, the FDI sector accounted for 74.2%, while domestic enterprises accounted for approximately 25.8%.
Dr. Huynh Thanh Dien explained that, thanks to a stable investment environment, skillful policies, and an increasingly expanding network of free trade agreements (FTAs), Vietnam is becoming an attractive destination for international investment capital.
Furthermore, strategic competition between the US and China is leading some businesses to expand or relocate their production facilities to neighboring countries in order to optimize costs.
“ Vietnam is one of the preferred destinations thanks to its advantageous geographical location, investment environment, and connectivity with international markets ,” said Dr. Huynh Thanh Dien.
Therefore, many FDI enterprises choose Vietnam as a production base for export goods, thereby creating an important impetus for Vietnam's international trade growth.
An ambitious goal
You may also like
Building on its achievements, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is developing a draft strategy for goods import and export until 2030, with a vision to 2045. The draft aims for an average annual growth rate of 15-16% in goods export turnover and 12-13% in imports during the 2026-2030 period.
According to many experts, this is considered an ambitious goal, but it is not without a basis for achievement.
According to Mr. Nguyen Tuan Viet, General Director of VIETGO and an expert in the import-export field, total import-export turnover is a very important indicator reflecting the strength of the economy.
" To become a superpower and build a strong nation, Vietnam first needs strong growth in total import and export turnover ," he said.
According to Mr. Viet, Vietnam already has many favorable foundations to achieve the target of an average annual growth rate of 15-16% in merchandise exports.
First and foremost are the strategic steps taken by the Government over the past 20 years, particularly the expansion of the network of free trade agreements (FTAs) and the implementation of an effective foreign policy.
Furthermore, Resolution 68, issued in 2025, marked a significant milestone by affirming the role and position of entrepreneurs and businesses in the economy, while identifying the private sector as one of the most important driving forces of the national economy.
" Accordingly, ministries, sectors, and agencies need to focus on supporting the development of businesses. I believe this is a strategically significant step by the Government ," he said.
The next driving force comes from the agility and adaptability of the business community. Vietnamese businesses have been actively learning from the experience of FDI enterprises, while also improving in both production and sales.
In particular, over the last three to four years, we have gradually formed the sales force of the economy, which are trading companies.
"These are businesses that don't directly own manufacturing facilities but purchase goods from domestic production facilities for export. The development of this group is very positive, helping Vietnam become more proactive in sales and access to international markets," Mr. Viet shared.
Creating room for domestic businesses to thrive.
Besides the goal of maintaining growth momentum, the Draft Strategy for Goods Import and Export until 2030, with a vision to 2045, also aims to enhance the role of domestic enterprises and increase the processing and technological content in exported goods.
The draft aims for the proportion of export turnover from domestic enterprises in the total national export turnover to reach approximately 28% - 30% by 2030, increasing to 38% - 40% by 2045.
Dr. Huynh Thanh Dien assessed that Vietnam needs to directly address the issue of FDI enterprises' export value significantly surpassing that of domestic businesses, and then find a "solution" to this goal.
You may also like
He analyzed that currently, the FDI business sector has a trade surplus, meaning the value of exports is greater than imports. Meanwhile, the domestic business sector has a trade deficit, importing not only machinery, equipment, and components but also consumer goods, including items that the country is capable of producing domestically.
"If a portion of imported goods are replaced by products made by domestic businesses, we will create more opportunities for investment, technological innovation, and jobs. Workers will have better incomes, purchasing power will increase, and this will contribute back to growth," he said.
Therefore, Dr. Huynh Thanh Dien believes that Vietnam has been successful in attracting foreign investment, but the next step is to build a sufficiently strong domestic production base. Only when domestic businesses develop will the economy have a foundation for sustainable long-term growth.
Regarding solutions, this expert suggested that Vietnam should use public investment as a tool to activate domestic production capacity.
Currently, Vietnam is implementing numerous infrastructure projects in transportation, energy, and information technology. When developing these projects, it is necessary to clearly identify which domestic enterprises can participate, which enterprises can play a leading role, and which small and medium-sized enterprises can supply products and services.
For products that Vietnamese businesses can produce, opportunities should be created for them to participate. For example, suitable bidding packages could be designed, joint ventures with domestic businesses could be encouraged, and a certain percentage of public procurement could be allocated to small and medium-sized enterprises, based on compliance with relevant regulations.
“ Many products that we currently import to serve public works projects, in my opinion, domestic businesses could absolutely produce. The problem is that the opportunities haven't been clearly presented. If we keep importing inputs to expedite project implementation, domestic businesses will lose opportunities to invest, master technology, and grow, ” he said.

articles.title: Fintech associations from 12 countries, the EBA, and ASEAN regulators build a new financial corridor in Kuala Lumpur - Singapore Business Review
articles.summary: Fintech associations from 12 countries, the EBA, and ASEAN regulators build a new financial corridor in Kuala Lumpur  Singapore Business Review
articles.full_text:
Finweek Kuala Lumpur is where European capital meets ASEAN velocity.
The global financial axis is shifting. Whilst Europe has built the world’s most comprehensive regulatory architecture with MiCA and digital finance frameworks, ASEAN is driving the world’s fastest-growing digital economy. On Wednesday, 11 November 2026, the two regions will stop talking about cooperation in theory and start building shared market infrastructure in practice.
At the Founding Edition of Finweek Kuala Lumpur 2026, the premier EU–ASEAN institutional fintech summit, the national fintech associations of twelve countries will take the main stage to sign the Founding Memorandum of the EU–ASEAN Investment Gateway.
Convened by Finweek Global, the organiser, together with Fintech Valley Europe as co-organiser and in partnership with the International Digital Economies Association (IDEA)—which spans 100 countries—endorsed by the European Digital Finance Association (EDFA) as the European network, and joined by the Global FinTech Alliance (GFA), the coalition unites national associations from Slovakia (FINAS), Czechia, Hungary, Ukraine, Moldova (Fintech Moldova) and Armenia (FinTech Armenia, together with FinTech EurAsia) with their counterparts across Indonesia (AFSI, Asosiasi Blockchain Indonesia), Myanmar (MDEA, FinTech Alliance Myanmar), Cambodia (CAFT), Vietnam (APAC DAO / Vietnam Fintech Summit), the Philippines and Malaysia, the host nation. Together, they represent thousands of financial technology innovators across Europe, ASEAN, and Eurasia.
A sovereign gateway for capital and regulation
Finweek Kuala Lumpur is not a conventional commercial event—it is a B2G and B2B diplomatic platform designed to turn regulatory alignment into cross-border deal flow.
At the heart of the summit is the Regulators’ Table, chaired by Kati Ferry (CEO, EUROCHAM Malaysia). Inside one room, senior policymakers and supervisors from the European Banking Authority (EBA — Rūta Merkevičiūtė, Head of the Digital Finance Unit), the Ministry of Finance of the Slovak Republic (Martin Peter, Director of the Banking Department), Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (OJK) of Indonesia (R. Rinto, Director, Digital Services and Cybersecurity Specialist Group), the Labuan Financial Services Authority (Labuan FSA — Doreen Fadli, Acting Director, Market Development & Innovations), the Trust Regulator of Cambodia (Sakal Ney, Deputy Director General) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) of the Philippines will address the hard operational realities of cross-border finance: real-world asset (RWA) tokenisation, the practical lessons of Europe’s MiCA framework, cross-border settlement, and stablecoin supervision.
Diplomatic momentum carries onto the main stage as the Ambassadors of the Czech Republic (H.E. Juraj Koudelka), Hungary (H.E. Dr Sándor Sipos), and Ukraine (H.E. Dr Hennadii Nadolenko), alongside senior diplomatic representatives of the Embassy of Indonesia and the Embassy of the Slovak Republic, officially open the afternoon Corridor block.
“Fintech no longer needs just founders; it needs diplomats,” said Davy Čajko, Founder of Finweek, President of FINAS (Fintech & Insurtech Association of Slovakia), and architect of the EU–ASEAN corridor. “Europe brings deep institutional capital and regulatory clarity through MiCA. ASEAN brings unmatched demographic energy, rapid adoption, and scale. Yet until today, a founder or investor crossing between our regions had to navigate fragmented rules alone. On 11 November, we are putting European and ASEAN regulators, ambassadors, and the associations of twelve countries into one room—not to exchange business cards, but to sign a joint commitment, announce the Malaysia Fintech Radar partnership, and open a Sovereign Gateway for capital and talent.”
The Malaysia Fintech Radar: A research partnership announced
To move capital across borders, institutional investors need verified data, not just stage panels. A flagship milestone of the Founding Edition (16:40 MYT) is the announcement of the research partnership behind the Malaysia Fintech Radar, presented by Dr Masrina Nadia Mohd Salleh of Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM).
Five pillars of the main stage (11 November 2026)
Instead of generic keynotes, the summit’s confirmed leaders focus on what actually runs in production:
Cyber Sovereignty & The ASEAN Investment Thesis (09:30–10:25): Following opening remarks by Davy Čajko and Kati Ferry (EUROCHAM Malaysia), YBhg. Dato’ Ts. Dr Haji Amirudin Abdul Wahab (Special Advisor on Cybersecurity & Digital Technology to HH The Crown Prince of Selangor; former CEO, CyberSecurity Malaysia) delivers the opening keynote on digital sovereignty and cyber resilience. The investment fireside follows with Farah Jaafar (Straits Investment Bank), Nicholas Kew (Crewstone International), and Dr Bilal İlhan (Presidency of the Republic of Türkiye Investment and Finance Office).
AI in Financial Operations — From Pilots to Accountability (10:45): Moderated by Firuz Alimov (The AI Collective), bringing together policy architects and front-line operators: Sam Majid (Former CEO, National AI Office Malaysia), Dr Aini Suzana Ariffin (Industrial Institute of Responsible AI), Dr Sekar Jaganathan (Kenanga Investment Bank), Lolitta Suffian (Bank Simpanan Nasional), Nate Wentzlaff (FinanTEXT, USA), and Eddy Wong Kok Hoe (VSure).
Islamic Digital Finance at Scale & The ASEAN–GCC–EU Nexus (11:35): Chaired by Aida Lim Abdullah (MFPC), examining sukuk tokenisation and Shariah-compliant digital assets with Vikra Ijas (AFSI Indonesia), Prof Irfan Syauqi Beik (IPB University), Effendy Zulkifly (YAPEIM Holdings), and Muttmaein Zairul (Masryef Advisory).
Tokenisation, RWA & Cross-Border Stablecoins (14:10–16:25): Featuring an opening industry case by Tran Hung (CEO, Uquid), a regulatory keynote on the MiCA gateway by Martin Peter (Ministry of Finance of the Slovak Republic), and the flagship Tokenisation panel with Michael Heaney (EY Malaysia), Krishnavenee Krishnan (KLDX), Jason Ding (MHub / Malaysia Proptech Association), and Shinoy Varghese (S&P Global Ratings). At 15:35, Gerard M. Pillai (PIKOM) leads the cross-border payments and stablecoin debate with Razin Nizar (Pragmax Consulting), Muhammad Yusuf Musa (Nanovest / Asosiasi Blockchain Indonesia), Edison Tan (EMAS ESTATE) and Harpreet Singh (Access Blockchain).
The Founding Circle, Corridor Showcase & Startup Pitch (12:30 & 16:50–18:10): High-growth startups including GORO, Koha Digital, and GoBarakah pitch to an international investor jury (Vatsala Arunachalam, Karen S Puah, Ben Stubbings, Audra Pakalnytė, Dr Alexander Titov). In the afternoon, Cristina Amor Maclang (IDEA / Global FinTech Alliance) chairs the Founding Circle townhall with association presidents and a message from Alessandra Guion, Chair of the Board of the European Digital Finance Association (EDFA), followed by Tan Sri Michael Yeoh (President, KSI Strategic Institute for Asia Pacific) chairing the Corridor Showcase with Dr Zsolt Polereczki (Neuron Labs) and Matthew Barsing (ASEAN Rising), culminating in the 17:50 Signing Ceremony and the Founding Dinner.
Landing Day in TRX (Thursday, 12 November 2026)
Because market entry happens on the ground, Landing Day takes visiting European delegations, regulators, and investors out of the ballroom and directly into Tun Razak Exchange (TRX), Malaysia’s international financial district—starting at INFINITY8 Reserve TRX (The Mastermind Mansion, Level 23)—to connect directly with licensing authorities, innovation hubs, and financial institutions where European companies establish their ASEAN headquarters.
Building on European momentum
The Kuala Lumpur Founding Edition follows the milestone 10th anniversary edition of Finweek Bratislava (13–14 October 2026), which welcomed 81 speakers from 15 countries, more than 400 registrations from 26 countries, and six public authorities—where H.E. Dato’ Fenny Nuli, Ambassador of Malaysia in Vienna, inaugurated the Europe–Asia corridor dialogue.
Registration, partnerships, and media accreditation
Finweek Kuala Lumpur 2026 is organised by Finweek Global and co-organised by Fintech Valley Europe, in partnership with the International Digital Economies Association (IDEA), with the support of the Embassy of the Slovak Republic in Kuala Lumpur, Charlton Media Group as Official Media Partner, IFN (REDmoney Group) as Official Islamic Finance Media Partner, and AlHuda CIBE as media partner.

Founding Dinner Seat (11 November, 19:30, by invitation / limited paid allocation): MYR 1,476 · EUR 300 · USD 326
Venue: PARKROYAL COLLECTION Kuala Lumpur (COLLECTION Ballroom)
Registration & Programme: www.finweek.my
For institutional partnerships, hosted dinner tables, pre-booked bilateral meetings, or press accreditation (including press positions for the 17:50 Memorandum Signing Ceremony), please contact: Davy Čajko, CEO & Founder, Finweek Kuala Lumpur 2026 (ceo@finweek.my / +421 903 429 190), Slávka Mikulášiková, Event Manager (eventmanager@finweek.my), or Peter Bielčík, media relations (peter.bielcik@beead.sk)

articles.title: Malaysia steps up military readiness amid South China Sea tensions - NST Online
articles.summary: Malaysia steps up military readiness amid South China Sea tensions  NST Online
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia is strengthening its military preparedness and pursuing bilateral and multilateral cooperation to address growing security challenges in the Asia-Pacific region, particularly in the South China Sea.
Defence Minister Datuk Seri Khaled Nordin said the government maintained its position of not interfering in other countries' defence and security policies, while respecting the right of every sovereign nation to determine its own defence policies.
"However, this does not mean that we are not paying serious attention to the situation or making the necessary preparations, particularly as efforts to maintain stability and security in the South China Sea have become increasingly challenging and complex.
"For Malaysia, the measures we are undertaking are carried out at 3 levels, namely unilateral, bilateral and multilateral," he said in reply to William Leong (PH-Selayang) in the Dewan Rakyat.
Leong had asked about the government's position on rising tensions and military escalation in the Asia-Pacific region, as well as measures to safeguard national security and Asean stability.
At the unilateral level, Khaled said the government was strengthening the readiness of the armed forces through four main approaches.
"First is the continuous modernisation of military assets and development of the armed forces' capabilities.
"Second involves strengthening training and capacity-building for armed forces personnel to ensure they remain prepared and capable of facing various contemporary challenges.
"Third is demonstrating and strengthening the country's presence through continuous patrols and surveillance in Malaysian waters, including standalone and joint operations involving the navy, air force and Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency.
"Fourth is developing the people's resilience and resistance," he said.
Khaled stressed, however, that no country could address the challenges in the Asia-Pacific, particularly in the South China Sea, on its own.
"Therefore, defence cooperation and diplomacy at the Asean regional level and on the global stage are crucial, particularly in managing the challenges in the South China Sea," he said.
He identified two major challenges in the South China Sea.
The first involves overlapping claims among Asean member states, including Malaysia and Vietnam, as well as Malaysia and the Philippines, alongside China's claims over waters involving several Asean countries, including Malaysia.
The second concerns strategic competition among major powers seeking greater presence and influence in the region, particularly the United States and China. This increases the risk of miscalculation that could escalate into a wider conflict.
To address these challenges, Khaled said Malaysia was strengthening defence diplomacy through bilateral cooperation with trusted partners, including Japan, Thailand, Australia and Germany.
The cooperation focuses on information-sharing, expertise transfer, capacity-building, as well as scheduled exercises and operations to enhance maritime domain awareness.
At the multilateral level, Malaysia is strengthening defence cooperation through platforms such as the Asean Defence Ministers' Meeting (ADMM), which brings together all Asean defence ministers, and the ADMM-Plus, involving Asean member states and eight other countries, including the United States, China, South Korea, New Zealand and Russia.
It also includes the Five Power Defence Arrangements, involving Malaysia, the United Kingdom, Singapore, Australia and New Zealand.
Khaled said Malaysia had consistently maintained that peace and stability in the Asia-Pacific could only be preserved through a peaceful, stable and united Asean.

articles.title: Imports and exports surpass $1 trillion: Impressive growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Imports and exports surpass $1 trillion: Impressive growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Exports continue to grow.
 According to estimates from the Ministry of Industry and Trade , Vietnam's total import and export turnover in the first 10 months of 2026 reached US$1,010.6 billion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year. Notably, in October alone, the economy's exports reached approximately US$499 billion, an increase of 27.4% compared to the same period. This growth rate creates a favorable basis for Vietnam to strive to achieve, or even surpass, its export growth target of 15-16% in 2026.
 This import-export achievement is remarkable considering the volatile global economic and trade environment. Geopolitical conflicts, instability on international shipping routes, energy prices, inflation, and interest rates continue to put pressure on production costs, logistics, and purchasing power in many markets. Furthermore, increasingly stringent environmental standards, traceability requirements, and trade protection measures present export businesses with numerous new challenges.
 Under these circumstances, maintaining a high export growth rate demonstrates the adaptability of the economy , from production activities to market organization and the utilization of free trade agreements (FTAs).
 Export growth was recorded in both the domestic and foreign direct investment (FDI) sectors. Many major markets such as China, the United States , the EU, South Korea, and ASEAN continued to record positive growth.
 Mr. Nguyen Anh Son, Director of the Import-Export Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade), noted that in recent years, Vietnam's export structure has shifted positively towards increasing the proportion of processed and manufactured industrial goods, gradually reducing dependence on exports heavily reliant on resources and unskilled labor. This is the result of attracting investment, developing production, and participating more deeply in the global supply chain.
 However, despite the achievements, Vietnam's export activities still have some limitations that need to be addressed. One of the important issues is that the added value created domestically is not commensurate with the scale of export turnover, especially in some high-value sectors such as electronics, machinery and equipment, textiles, and footwear.
 In reality, surpassing the $1 trillion mark is not simply an increase in trade volume. Behind this figure lies the effort of millions of businesses, production facilities, and workers in maintaining orders, ensuring supply, seeking markets, and meeting the increasingly high standards of international partners.
 Take advantage of FTAs.
 Increasingly deep participation in the network of FTAs helps Vietnamese goods expand their market space, gain more competitive advantages in terms of tariffs, and have opportunities to participate in global supply chains.
 However, the benefits of integration lie not only in expanding markets or taking advantage of tariff preferences, but more importantly in the ability to improve production capacity, increase domestic value, and participate more deeply in the supply chain.
 Mr. Truong Van Cam, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Textile and Garment Association, believes that FTAs are creating a change in how businesses approach integration. The benefits of these agreements are not only export opportunities but also encourage businesses to invest, reorganize production, and be more proactive in securing raw materials.
 For example, the rules of origin from yarn onward in the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) create incentives for businesses to invest in yarn and fabric production, gradually developing domestic supply sources. Meanwhile, the Vietnam-EU Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), with its requirement of origin from fabric onward, necessitates investment in fabric production, which remains one of the weaknesses of the textile and garment industry. The cumulation of origin mechanism for Korean fabrics also opens up opportunities for businesses to utilize raw materials that meet the conditions for preferential treatment.
 However, alongside the positive results, the fact that trade volume has exceeded $1 trillion also poses new demands for sustainable development. This requires not only growth in scale but also a continued improvement in the quality of growth, increasing the value created domestically, reducing dependence on external supply sources, and enhancing the position of Vietnamese businesses in the global value chain.
 In the fourth quarter of 2026, the Ministry of Industry and Trade identified key priorities to further boost exports, diversify markets, and enhance the compliance capacity of businesses. The focus will be on effectively utilizing signed FTAs, expanding into new markets, strengthening early warning systems for trade defense cases, tariff barriers, green standards, traceability, and rules of origin. Simultaneously, support will be provided to businesses to improve product quality, build brands, and ensure transparency in the supply chain.

articles.title: Vietnam in the wave of supply chain relocation in Southeast Asia. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam in the wave of supply chain relocation in Southeast Asia.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Amid geopolitical shifts, trade tensions, and global trends toward supply chain diversification, Southeast Asia is becoming an increasingly important destination for international investment.
Against this backdrop, Vietnam has the opportunity to attract high-tech projects, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, data centers, and logistics, while enhancing its position in the global value chain. These were the issues discussed by international leaders, experts, and business representatives at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit, organized by Fortune magazine in Ho Chi Minh City on November 3rd.
Supply chains are shifting significantly towards Southeast Asia.
Geopolitical tensions, protectionist trade policies, tariff changes, and technological competition are driving global businesses to adjust their production, sourcing, and investment strategies. The trend toward diversifying production locations, expanding supplier networks, and increasing resilience to external shocks is becoming increasingly evident.
Khám phá thêm
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch
Khám phá ĐNA
Thomas Knudsen, Executive Chairman of Toll Group, believes that supply chains are gradually shifting from traditional manufacturing hubs to Southeast Asia. This shift from China to ASEAN will continue, while intra-regional connectivity, infrastructure development, and investment demand in the region are increasing.
According to Thomas Knudsen, building a resilient supply chain requires businesses to be flexible in choosing and combining multiple transportation methods, developing transit warehouse systems, and strengthening connectivity between countries. Southeast Asia has many advantages due to its dynamism, rapidly developing real-time payment systems, and network of free trade agreements. However, to capitalize on these advantages, the region needs to improve its connectivity with global markets and build effective bridges between the public and private sectors.
Sharing the same view on the long-term nature of the shift, James Nesbitt, Managing Director and Head of Global Corporate Clients for ASEAN at Standard Chartered Bank, noted that businesses are proactively increasing the number of suppliers, raising inventory levels, adjusting production methods, and diversifying customer markets to reduce the risk of supply chain disruptions. Security and political factors are also increasingly impacting investment decisions and production organization.
You may also like
Meanwhile, Thammasak Sethaudom, Chairman and CEO of SCG Group, believes that competitive pressure from overcapacity in China is spreading throughout the region. To adapt, businesses need to expand production scale, leverage free trade agreements, reduce costs, and increase added value. In particular, automation not only saves labor costs but also improves accuracy, product quality, energy, and raw materials. This allows businesses to focus resources on product design, research, and development, gradually moving up to higher value-added stages in the production chain.
Vietnam is ready to welcome the wave of investment.
Amidst Southeast Asia's growing role in global production and trade networks, Vietnam is considered to have favorable conditions to attract a new wave of investment, especially in high-tech, semiconductor, electronics, AI , data center, clean energy, and logistics sectors.
According to Mr. Le Tan Can, Deputy Minister of Finance, Vietnam aims to become a regional hub for artificial intelligence and data centers, and a destination for multinational corporations, investment funds, and international financial institutions. To realize this goal, Vietnam is focusing on building a new generation investment ecosystem, connecting foreign-invested enterprises with domestic businesses; while also developing logistics infrastructure, data, clean energy, and high-quality human resources.
Vietnam hopes that foreign investors will not only invest, produce, and exploit the domestic market, but also become partners in research, technological innovation, product development, and market expansion at the regional and global levels. Priority areas of cooperation include research, development, and mastery of technology; investment in high technology, semiconductors, and electronics; development of self-reliant and sustainable value chains; training of high-quality human resources; and participation in the development of international financial centers.
From a local perspective, Mr. Nguyen Loc Ha, Permanent Vice Chairman of the People's Committee of Ho Chi Minh City, emphasized that Ho Chi Minh City currently possesses many advantages in finance, trade, services, industry, high-tech industrial parks, and the Cai Mep - Thi Vai deep-water port, creating conditions for connecting production, logistics, trade, and financial service chains.
You may also like
In the first nine months of 2026, the city's GRDP increased by 9.06%; registered foreign investment reached over US$19 billion, four times higher than the same period and accounting for more than 30% of the total registered foreign investment nationwide. These are positive signs, demonstrating the interest and confidence of investors in the business environment in Ho Chi Minh City.
"Besides its advantages in market and production systems, Ho Chi Minh City aims to strengthen connections between new investors and local businesses, suppliers, and partners; promote cooperation in the fields of automation, AI, energy management, and human resource training. The city also aims to develop an international financial center, a free trade zone, logistics, and a transportation-integrated urban area. However, to effectively capitalize on the investment relocation wave, Vietnam needs not only to attract more factories but also to enhance the capacity of domestic businesses, develop supporting industries, strengthen linkages with multinational corporations, and participate more deeply in high value-added stages," Mr. Nguyen Loc Ha further informed.
According to businesses, the opportunities arising from the reshaping of global supply chains lie not only in the ability to attract investment capital but also in the capacity to transform that capital into technology, knowledge, production capacity, and added value domestically. This will be a crucial factor for Vietnam to enhance its competitiveness and strengthen its position in regional and global production and trade networks.

articles.title: Imports and exports surpass $1 trillion, opening up new room for growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Imports and exports surpass $1 trillion, opening up new room for growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Vietnam's total import and export turnover of goods after 10 months of 2026 is estimated to exceed 1,000 billion USD, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year.
Speaking to the press on November 3rd, Mr. Nguyen Anh Son, Director of the Import-Export Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), said that this milestone marks the need to shift from focusing on scale growth to improving the quality of trade, increasing the localization rate, and enabling Vietnamese businesses to participate more deeply in the global value chain.
Sir, according to estimates, after 10 months of 2026, Vietnam's total import and export turnover of goods exceeded US$1 trillion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year. This is a particularly significant milestone for the economy . In your opinion, what are the driving forces behind this strong growth in import and export activities amidst the volatile global trade environment?
It can be affirmed that the fact that the total value of goods exports and imports has surpassed the 1,000 billion USD mark is an important milestone, demonstrating the scale and increasingly deep integration of the Vietnamese economy into international trade.
This result is a combination of many factors. First and foremost is the recovery and sustained growth of domestic production, especially in the processing and manufacturing industries – the key sectors in Vietnam's export activities. As production capacity expanded, coupled with businesses effectively capitalizing on opportunities from international market demand, export turnover continued to maintain positive growth.
Secondly, the foreign-invested enterprise sector continues to play a crucial role in key export industries such as electronics, machinery, equipment, textiles, and footwear, contributing to maintaining export growth and enabling Vietnam to participate more deeply in global supply chains.
Thirdly, the effective utilization of free trade agreements (FTAs), along with efforts to expand and diversify export markets, has created more opportunities for Vietnamese businesses to access larger markets. Besides traditional markets, businesses are increasingly interested in new, potentially lucrative markets in the Middle East, South Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
Furthermore, it is impossible to overlook the proactive and flexible approach of the business community in adapting to the fluctuations of global trade, from changing market demands and technical standards requirements to green transitions and adjustments in the trade policies of various countries.
However, alongside the positive results, the fact that trade volume has exceeded $1 trillion also poses new demands for sustainable development. This requires not only growth in scale but also a continued improvement in the quality of growth, increasing the value created domestically, reducing dependence on external supply sources, and enhancing the position of Vietnamese businesses in the global value chain.
Despite the impressive growth rate, Vietnam's export activities still have some limitations that need to be addressed, sir?
It can be seen that, over the years, Vietnam's export structure has shifted positively towards increasing the proportion of processed and manufactured industrial goods, gradually reducing dependence on exports that rely heavily on resources and simple labor. This is the result of attracting investment, developing production, and participating more deeply in global supply chains.
However, despite the achievements, Vietnam's export activities still have some limitations that need to be addressed. One of the important issues is that the added value created domestically is not commensurate with the scale of export turnover, especially in some high-value sectors such as electronics, machinery and equipment, textiles, and footwear.
The main reason is the limited capacity of domestic enterprises, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, to participate in global supply chains. Many businesses have not fully met the requirements regarding production scale, technical standards, quality management, technological innovation capabilities, and supply stability.
You may also like
Furthermore, the linkages between domestic and foreign-invested enterprises have not yet met expectations. Some export-oriented manufacturing sectors still rely significantly on imported raw materials and components, limiting the potential for spillover effects from export activities to the domestic business sector.
To address these issues, I believe we need to focus on several groups of solutions. First, we must continue to strongly develop supporting industries, especially in sectors with high potential for value-added creation such as electronics, semiconductors, precision mechanics, electrical equipment, and processing industries.
In addition, it is necessary to enhance the capacity of Vietnamese businesses through support for technological innovation, improved management capabilities, meeting international standards, and deeper participation in supply chains.
Promoting linkages between FDI enterprises and domestic enterprises will create conditions for Vietnamese enterprises to gradually become suppliers in global production chains, instead of only participating in low value-added stages.
In attracting foreign investment, it is necessary to continue orienting towards projects with high technological content, a commitment to developing the domestic supply chain ecosystem, and the potential to create spillover effects on the economy.
In the long term, the goal is not only to maintain the growth rate of export turnover, but more importantly to increase the Vietnamese value content in each exported product, thereby enhancing the competitiveness and position of Vietnamese businesses in international trade.
In the context of Vietnam's goal of double-digit economic growth, import and export are identified as crucial drivers. According to you, what breakthrough solutions should be focused on in the coming period to maintain the growth momentum of import and export, diversify markets, proactively secure raw material supplies, and enhance the competitiveness of Vietnamese goods?
In the context of a continuously volatile global economy, the target for import and export growth in the coming period needs to be set with higher requirements: rapid but sustainable development, growth in scale while simultaneously improving the quality and efficiency of trade activities.
In my opinion, we need to focus on several key solutions. Accordingly, we need to continue promoting the diversification of export markets. Vietnam needs to better exploit traditional markets while expanding into regions with significant potential such as the Middle East, South Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Diversifying markets will help businesses minimize risks when international markets fluctuate.
Furthermore, it is essential to enhance the effectiveness of utilizing free trade agreements. Following the expansion of the FTA network, the current requirement is to move towards in-depth exploitation, enabling businesses not only to take advantage of tariff preferences but also to better access supply chains, investment capital flows, and business cooperation opportunities from partner markets.
In particular, enhancing domestic production capacity, especially developing supporting industries and proactively securing input material supplies, is crucial for reducing dependence on imports, improving the economy's resilience to external fluctuations, and increasing the domestic value added in exports.
Simultaneously, it is crucial to support businesses in adapting to the new demands of international trade. Markets are increasingly focused on quality standards, sustainable development, green transformation, traceability, and responsibility in the supply chain. Vietnamese businesses need to proactively enhance their capacity to meet these requirements, instead of competing solely on cost.
For the Ministry of Industry and Trade, in the coming period, it will continue to coordinate with other ministries, sectors, localities, and the business community to implement comprehensive solutions to develop export markets, support businesses in taking advantage of opportunities from integration, enhance competitiveness, and promote the sustainable shift in the structure of import and export.
The ultimate goal is not only to continue increasing import and export turnover, but also to build a trade system that is better able to adapt to global fluctuations, in which Vietnamese businesses play an increasingly larger role and create increasingly higher domestic value.

articles.title: Indonesia 3Q GDP growth at 5.47%, beats expectations - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: Indonesia 3Q GDP growth at 5.47%, beats expectations  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
JAKARTA (Nov 5): Indonesia's economy expanded 5.47% in the third quarter from a year earlier, official data showed on Thursday, faster than the 5.18% forecast in a Reuters poll.
Indonesia's economic growth in the second quarter stood at 5.29%.
Southeast Asia's largest economy has contended with weaker investor sentiment this year amid heightened scrutiny of the government's fiscal plans and its broader policy directions, as well as lingering downgrade risks on its stock market.
Growth was supported by sectors such as manufacturing, including the processing of palm oil to produce fuel as Indonesia expanded its mandatory biodiesel programme, the statistics bureau said.
The 2026 state budget projects economic growth of 5.4%, although finance minister Suahasil Nazara has said it could slightly exceed that target and reach 5.5% this year.
The target falls within Bank Indonesia's GDP growth outlook range of 4.9% to 5.7%. At its meeting last month, the central bank said the domestic economy remained resilient but required further strengthening.
President Prabowo Subianto, who took office two years ago, aims to lift economic growth to 8% by 2029.

articles.title: TISEZA Investment Projects Hit 3,538 Worth USD 68.6 Billion in Five Years, Most in Manufacturing, China Leads FDI With USD 14.1 Billion - TanzaniaInvest
articles.summary: TISEZA Investment Projects Hit 3,538 Worth USD 68.6 Billion in Five Years, Most in Manufacturing, China Leads FDI With USD 14.1 Billion  TanzaniaInvest
articles.full_text:
The Tanzania Investment and Special Economic Zones Authority (TISEZA) registered 3,538 investment projects worth USD 68.6 billion in the five years from 2021 to 2026.
These are expected to create more than one million jobs, its Director General told editors in Dar es Salaam on 2 November 2026.
The Director General of TISEZA, Gilead Teri, presented the figures at a meeting with editors from various media organisations held in Dar es Salaam on 2 November 2026.
Manufacturing registered the largest number of projects at 1,061, equivalent to 30.0% of the 3,538 projects registered between 2021 and 2026.
Transport followed with 525 projects, ahead of tourism with 335 projects, agriculture with 308 projects, and commercial buildings with 301 projects.
Teri said the registered projects involve local investors, foreign investors, and joint ventures between the two groups.
China leads foreign capital with investments worth USD 14.1 billion, followed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) with USD 5.039 billion.
Mauritius ranked third with USD 2.1 billion, ahead of the United Kingdom with USD 1.6 billion and India with USD 1.5 billion, according to the figures Teri presented.
For 2027, TISEZA aims to enable small producers to reach international markets, develop the country’s special economic zones, and strengthen its registration systems to make investment activity easier.
TISEZA was launched on 1 July 2025 under the Tanzania Investment and Special Economic Zones Act No. 6 of 2025, which merged the Tanzania Investment Centre (TIC), established in 1997, with the Export Processing Zones Authority (EPZA), established in 2002.
President Samia Suluhu Hassan appointed Teri, previously Executive Director of TIC, as the first Director General of TISEZA on the same day the authority was launched.
The law requires all investors to register with TISEZA before starting operations in Tanzania, whether or not they apply for fiscal incentives, and makes the authority a one-stop centre for permits and approvals.
In its latest Quarterly Investment Bulletin, TISEZA reported 243 projects worth USD 1.88 billion registered between April and June 2026 under its general investment scheme.
In September 2026, TISEZA was named the Best Investment Promotion Agency in the Africa Region at the AIM Investment Awards held during the AIM Congress 2026 in Dubai.

articles.title: Enhancing domestic value in exports. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Enhancing domestic value in exports.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| The scale of imports and exports exceeded 1 trillion USD, but the FDI sector held nearly 785 billion USD. | 
 This was the statement made by Mr. Nguyen Anh Son, Director of the Import-Export Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), when assessing the milestone of Vietnam's foreign trade reaching and exceeding 1,000 billion USD.
 Foreign direct investment (FDI) enterprises contributed nearly $785 billion.
 According to the General Statistics Office, in the first 10 months of 2026, Vietnam's total import and export turnover of goods exceeded 1 trillion USD, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year. This is a particularly significant milestone for the economy , demonstrating the scale and increasingly deep integration of the Vietnamese economy into international trade.
 Trade surpassed $1 trillion with only two months left in the year, clearly demonstrating the recovery and sustained growth of domestic production, especially in the processing and manufacturing industries – the key export sectors.
 Over the past 10 months, many key export product groups have recorded high growth rates.
 Leading the way were electronics, computers, and components with a turnover of $149.4 billion, a 71% increase compared to the same period last year. Machinery, equipment, tools, and spare parts reached $63.268 billion, a 30.4% increase; telephones and components reached $57.6 billion, an 18.4% increase; and transportation vehicles and parts reached nearly $17 billion, a 17.1% increase. Wood and wood products also brought in over $15 billion, a 6.8% increase.
 This result demonstrates the continued expansion of production capacity and reflects the ability of businesses to capitalize on opportunities arising from international market demand. As a result, export turnover maintained positive growth momentum, making a significant contribution to the country's record trade volume.
 However, behind the impressive growth picture, the contribution of the domestic business sector remains "thin".
 Statistics show that the foreign direct investment (FDI) sector achieved a total import and export turnover of US$784.86 billion (including crude oil), accounting for 77.6% of the country's total import and export turnover. Meanwhile, the domestic enterprise sector only achieved US$225.69 billion, equivalent to 22.4%.
 Notably, the gap is even more pronounced in export activities. Exports from the domestic business sector reached $93.93 billion, an increase of 8.2%, accounting for only 18.8% of total export turnover. Conversely, the FDI sector reached $405.31 billion, an increase of 33%, accounting for as much as 81.2%.
 The FDI sector also holds an overwhelming share in the export turnover of many key industries, especially electronics, machinery, equipment, and spare parts. These three product groups alone brought in over $270 billion, accounting for approximately 54% of the country's total export turnover.
 Increase the Vietnamese value content in export goods.
 Commenting on the milestone of foreign trade exceeding 1 trillion USD, Mr. Nguyen Anh Son stated that the greater challenge is not only maintaining the scale of growth but also improving the quality of growth, increasing the value created domestically, reducing dependence on external supply sources, and enhancing the position of Vietnamese businesses in the global value chain.
 According to Mr. Son, the value added generated domestically is not commensurate with the scale of export turnover, especially in some high-value sectors such as electronics, machinery, equipment, textiles, and footwear. The capacity of domestic enterprises to participate in global supply chains remains limited.
 The main reason stems from production capacity and the ability to meet the requirements of international markets and corporations. Many Vietnamese businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, have not fully met the requirements regarding production scale, technical standards, quality management, technological innovation, and supply chain stability.
 Furthermore, the linkages between domestic businesses and FDI have not met expectations. Although FDI contributes a large portion of export turnover, the ability to connect, transfer technology, and develop a domestic supplier ecosystem is still not commensurate with the scale of operations of these businesses.
 Some export-oriented manufacturing sectors still rely heavily on imported raw materials and components, resulting in limited domestic value creation and a low spillover effect on the economy.
 This reality necessitates a shift in the export growth model. Instead of primarily relying on expanding production, processing, and assembly capacity, Vietnam needs to increase the localization rate, develop its capacity to supply raw materials and components, and gradually participate in higher value-added stages.
 To gradually address these shortcomings, the Ministry of Industry and Trade stated that it will continue to promote the development of supporting industries, focusing on sectors with high potential for value-added creation such as electronics, semiconductors, precision mechanics, electrical equipment, and processing industries.
 This is coupled with solutions to enhance the capacity of Vietnamese businesses through support for technological innovation, improved governance, meeting international standards, and increasing their ability to participate more deeply in global supply chains.
 Another important task is to promote linkages between FDI enterprises and domestic enterprises. Strengthening connections between the two sectors will create conditions for Vietnamese enterprises to gradually become suppliers of raw materials, components, services, and input products for multinational corporations, instead of only participating in low value-added stages.
 Regarding attracting FDI, according to Mr. Nguyen Anh Son, it is necessary to continue orienting projects with high technological content, committed to developing the domestic supply chain ecosystem, and capable of creating a spillover effect on the economy. Because the long-term goal is not simply to continue increasing export turnover, but more importantly, to enhance the Vietnamese value content in each product.

articles.title: What can we learn from the fact that Vietnam's import and export figures have surpassed $1 trillion for the first time? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: What can we learn from the fact that Vietnam's import and export figures have surpassed $1 trillion for the first time?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
In the first 10 months of 2026, Vietnam's total import and export turnover reached a record high. In this context, in addition to expanding the scale of trade, the need to enhance domestic value and the role of Vietnamese businesses in the global supply chain has become even more urgent.
Những động lực đưa xuất nhập khẩu Việt Nam lập đỉnh
Theo số liệu sơ bộ của Cục Thống kê (Bộ Tài chính), tổng kim ngạch xuất nhập khẩu hàng hóa của Việt Nam trong 10 tháng năm 2026 đạt 1.010,55 tỷ USD, tăng 32,3% so với cùng kỳ năm trước, chính thức vượt mốc 1.000 tỷ USD.
Trong đó, kim ngạch xuất khẩu đạt 499,24 tỷ USD, tăng 27,5%, động lực chính đến từ nhóm hàng công nghiệp chế biến với 452,74 tỷ USD, chiếm 90,7%. Cùng với đó, kim ngạch nhập khẩu đạt 511,31 tỷ USD, tăng 37,4%, chủ yếu đến từ nhóm hàng tư liệu sản xuất với 481,03 tỷ USD, chiếm 94,1%.
Đánh giá về dấu mốc này, ông Nguyễn Anh Sơn - Cục trưởng Cục Xuất nhập khẩu (Bộ Công Thương) cho rằng, việc tổng kim ngạch xuất nhập khẩu hàng hóa vượt 1.000 tỷ USD là kết quả có ý nghĩa quan trọng, thể hiện quy mô và mức độ hội nhập ngày càng sâu rộng của nền kinh tế Việt Nam vào thương mại quốc tế.
Theo ông Sơn, kết quả trên là sự tổng hòa của nhiều yếu tố, trước hết là sự phục hồi và duy trì đà tăng trưởng của sản xuất trong nước, đặc biệt ở các ngành công nghiệp chế biến, chế tạo - nhóm ngành giữ vai trò chủ lực trong hoạt động xuất khẩu.
Bên cạnh đó, khu vực doanh nghiệp có vốn đầu tư nước ngoài (FDI) tiếp tục đóng vai trò quan trọng trong các ngành hàng xuất khẩu chủ lực như điện tử, máy móc, thiết bị, dệt may, da giày. Qua đó, góp phần duy trì tốc độ tăng trưởng xuất khẩu và đưa Việt Nam tham gia sâu hơn vào các chuỗi cung ứng toàn cầu.
Một động lực khác đến từ việc khai thác các hiệp định thương mại tự do (FTA), đồng thời mở rộng và đa dạng hóa thị trường. Ngoài những thị trường truyền thống, doanh nghiệp Việt Nam ngày càng quan tâm đến các khu vực còn nhiều tiềm năng như Trung Đông, Nam Á, châu Phi và Mỹ Latinh.
Cục trưởng Cục Xuất nhập khẩu cũng đề cao sự chủ động, linh hoạt của cộng đồng doanh nghiệp trong việc thích ứng với những biến động thương mại toàn cầu, từ thay đổi nhu cầu thị trường, tiêu chuẩn kỹ thuật đến yêu cầu chuyển đổi xanh và điều chỉnh chính sách thương mại của các nước.
Cũng theo ông Nguyễn Anh Sơn, những kết quả trên, bên cạnh nỗ lực của cộng đồng doanh nghiệp còn có sự đồng hành và triển khai đồng bộ các giải pháp của Chính phủ, bộ, ngành. Trong đó, Bộ Công Thương giữ vai trò nòng cốt trong việc phát triển thị trường, hỗ trợ doanh nghiệp và nâng cao năng lực cạnh tranh của hàng hóa Việt Nam.
Thời gian qua, một trong những nhiệm vụ trọng tâm của Bộ là hỗ trợ doanh nghiệp khai thác hiệu quả mạng lưới FTA mà Việt Nam đã ký kết. Cùng với đó, Bộ đã không ngừng đẩy mạnh công tác phát triển thị trường xuất khẩu theo hướng vừa duy trì các thị trường truyền thống, vừa mở rộng sang những khu vực có tiềm năng.
You may also like
"Các hoạt động xúc tiến thương mại, kết nối giao thương và hỗ trợ doanh nghiệp tham gia hệ thống phân phối quốc tế được triển khai có trọng tâm, phù hợp với đặc điểm từng ngành hàng và thị trường", ông Sơn nhận định.
Doanh nghiệp Việt cần tiến sâu hơn vào chuỗi cung ứng toàn cầu
Không thể phủ nhận rằng, trong những năm qua, cơ cấu xuất khẩu của Việt Nam đã có sự chuyển dịch tích cực theo hướng tăng tỷ trọng nhóm hàng công nghiệp chế biến, chế tạo, giảm dần phụ thuộc vào các mặt hàng xuất khẩu dựa nhiều vào tài nguyên, lao động giản đơn.
Tuy nhiên, theo đánh giá từ Cục trưởng Cục Xuất nhập khẩu, giá trị gia tăng tạo ra trong nước vẫn chưa tương xứng với quy mô kim ngạch xuất khẩu, đặc biệt ở một số ngành có kim ngạch lớn như điện tử, máy móc, thiết bị, dệt may, da giày.
"Nguyên nhân chủ yếu nằm ở năng lực tham gia chuỗi cung ứng toàn cầu của doanh nghiệp trong nước, đặc biệt là doanh nghiệp nhỏ và vừa, còn hạn chế", ông Sơn cho biết.
Theo đó, nhiều doanh nghiệp chưa đáp ứng đầy đủ yêu cầu về quy mô sản xuất, tiêu chuẩn kỹ thuật, quản trị chất lượng, đổi mới công nghệ cũng như khả năng duy trì nguồn cung ổn định.
Đáng chú ý, trong 10 tháng qua, dù kim ngạch xuất khẩu tăng trưởng tích cực, khu vực kinh tế trong nước chỉ đạt 93,93 tỷ USD, chiếm 18,8%. Trong khi đó, khu vực có vốn đầu tư nước ngoài lại đạt 405,31 tỷ USD, chiếm tới 81,2%.
Bên cạnh đó, mối liên kết giữa doanh nghiệp trong nước và khu vực FDI chưa đạt kỳ vọng. Một số ngành sản xuất vẫn phụ thuộc lớn vào nguồn nguyên liệu, linh kiện nhập khẩu, biểu hiện rõ rệt qua số liệu nhập khẩu tư liệu sản xuất trong 10 tháng. Điều này khiến khả năng lan tỏa từ hoạt động xuất khẩu sang khu vực doanh nghiệp nội địa còn hạn chế.
Để tháo gỡ những điểm nghẽn này, ông Nguyễn Anh Sơn cho rằng cần phát triển mạnh công nghiệp hỗ trợ, nhất là trong các ngành có tiềm năng tạo giá trị gia tăng lớn như điện tử, bán dẫn, cơ khí chính xác, thiết bị điện và công nghiệp chế biến.
Cùng với đó, doanh nghiệp Việt Nam cần được hỗ trợ đổi mới công nghệ, nâng cao năng lực quản trị và đáp ứng các tiêu chuẩn quốc tế. Việc thúc đẩy liên kết giữa doanh nghiệp FDI với doanh nghiệp trong nước cần được chú trọng để tạo điều kiện cho doanh nghiệp Việt từng bước trở thành nhà cung cấp trong chuỗi sản xuất toàn cầu, thay vì chỉ tham gia ở những công đoạn có giá trị gia tăng thấp.

Trong bối cảnh Việt Nam đặt mục tiêu tăng trưởng kinh tế hai con số, xuất nhập khẩu tiếp tục được xác định là một trong những động lực quan trọng. Tuy nhiên, theo ông Sơn, phát triển nhanh nhưng phải bền vững, tăng trưởng về quy mô phải đi đôi với nâng cao chất lượng và hiệu quả của hoạt động thương mại.
Ông Sơn cho rằng thời gian tới cần tiếp tục đẩy mạnh đa dạng hóa thị trường xuất khẩu, khai thác sâu hơn các FTA, tập trung phát triển công nghiệp hỗ trợ và chủ động nguồn cung nguyên liệu đầu vào.
Cùng với đó, doanh nghiệp cần nâng cao năng lực cạnh tranh để đáp ứng những yêu cầu ngày càng cao về chất lượng, truy xuất nguồn gốc, chuyển đổi xanh và trách nhiệm trong chuỗi cung ứng quốc tế.

“Mục tiêu cuối cùng không chỉ là đưa kim ngạch xuất nhập khẩu tiếp tục tăng trưởng, mà là xây dựng một nền thương mại có khả năng thích ứng tốt hơn với biến động toàn cầu, trong đó doanh nghiệp Việt Nam giữ vai trò ngày càng lớn hơn và giá trị tạo ra trong nước ngày càng cao hơn”, ông Nguyễn Anh Sơn nhấn mạnh.

Investing.com-- Indonesia's economy grew faster than expected in the September quarter, aided by robust manufacturing activity that helped ease some concerns over the country's fiscal health.
Gross domestic product grew 5.47% year-on-year in the third quarter, government data showed onThursday. The print surpassed expectations of 5.2% and accelerated from the 5.29% growth recorded in the second quarter.
GDP grew 1.6% quarter-on-quarter, beating expectations of 1.3% but slowing sharply from the 3.7% rise in the prior quarter.
Southeast Asia's largest economy has faced weaker investor sentiment this year due to increased scrutiny of the government's fiscal plans and broader policy directions, along with ongoing downgrade risks on its stock market.
The statistics bureau said growth was supported by sectors including manufacturing, particularly the processing of palm oil to produce fuel as Indonesia expanded its mandatory biodiesel program.

articles.title: Improving FDI quality to strengthen growth momentum - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Improving FDI quality to strengthen growth momentum  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Hanoi (VNA) – Vietnam has recorded positive developments in attracting foreign direct investment (FDI), with major commitments highlighting the country’s growing appeal to international investors. 
At the recent Autumn Economic Forum 2026, Ho Chi Minh City announced 12 projects with combined registered capital of 13 billion USD. They included a 2.29-billion-USD smart complex in Functional Zone 2A of Thu Thiem New Urban Area, developed by a joint venture between Lotte Properties HCMC Co. Ltd. and Phat Dat Real Estate Development Corporation. 
Other major projects include the 770-million-USD Gemalink Port project by Cai Mep Gemadept-Terminal Link and the Swift Logistics project by Singapore’s Tokgistic Pte. Ltd., with registered capital of about 987.4 million USD. 
The Vietnam International Financial Centre in Ho Chi Minh City also announced its first 10 members, including foreign investors like VinaCapital International Partners Co. Ltd. 
Reporting to the National Assembly, Prime Minister Le Minh Hung said Vietnam attracted more than 50.36 billion USD in FDI in the first nine months of 2026, up 76.4% year-on-year. Investment was concentrated in processing and manufacturing, high technology, electronics and semiconductors. 
Major investors include Samsung, with more than 24 billion USD in investment; LG, 10.6 billion USD; Foxconn, 5 billion USD; Intel, 4.1 billion USD; and Amkor, 1.6 billion USD. Other technology groups, including NVIDIA, Qualcomm, Marvell, Synopsys and Bosch, have also established or expanded operations in Vietnam. 
The Ministry of Finance reported that disbursed capital totalled nearly 21.2 billion USD during the period, while full-year disbursement is estimated at around 31 billion USD. 
Focusing on investment quality 
Strong inflows reaffirm Vietnam’s attractiveness to international investors. However, beyond record figures, a key question is how effectively the FDI sector contributes to the domestic economy. 
FDI plays an important role in expanding production capacity, developing infrastructure and generating more than 70% of Vietnam's export turnover. As the country targets annual growth of at least 10% during 2026-2030, Minister of Finance Ngo Van Tuan stressed that FDI attraction should not be measured solely by capital volumes. 
Investment, he said, must generate greater domestic value added, facilitate technology transfer and enable Vietnamese enterprises to participate more deeply in global supply chains. 
National Assembly deputies have also called for a shift from growth driven by scale to a model based on productivity, technology and domestic value creation. 
Deputy Le Huu Tri of Khanh Hoa said greater attention should be paid to strengthening domestic enterprises, developing supporting industries, improving localisation rates, promoting technology transfer and upgrading the workforce. Investment performance, he argued, should not be assessed solely on registered or disbursed capital. 
Deputy Tran Thi Hong Thanh of Ninh Binh noted that localisation rates in several key industries remain at around 40%, urging the Government to link FDI incentives with measurable commitments in technology transfer, workforce training, the use of Vietnamese suppliers and higher domestic value added. 
The Ministry of Finance has also pointed to limited spillover effects from the FDI sector. Links between foreign-invested and domestic enterprises remain weak, while Vietnamese firms have yet to participate deeply in FDI supply chains. Localisation rates in FDI production chains stand at only 20-25%, and technology transfer remains limited. 
The extent to which registered capital is translated into actual investment and new production capacity also warrants closer scrutiny. 
Rapid growth in registered capital is encouraging, but unless these commitments are promptly converted into implemented projects and productive capacity, their contribution to economic growth will remain constrained. 
In its latest report, the Foreign Investment Agency under the Ministry of Finance noted that registered FDI is growing considerably faster than disbursed capital. This highlights the need to accelerate the implementation of licensed projects, particularly large-scale investments, to ensure that FDI delivers a stronger contribution to Vietnam's ambition of achieving double-digit economic growth./.

articles.title: US Democratic win unlikely to ease firms’ cost, tariff woes in near term, executives say - The Straits Times
articles.summary: US Democratic win unlikely to ease firms’ cost, tariff woes in near term, executives say  The Straits Times
articles.full_text:
FRANKFURT/TOKYO/GDANSK – Global companies said on Nov 4 that Democrats’ capture of the United States Congress is unlikely to change their near-term outlook, as businesses struggle with higher costs of energy and raw materials and a stretched US consumer.
Some, though, welcomed the prospect of political stability.
Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives, scoring sweeping victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to US President Donald Trump.
But it is too early to know what the results mean for the issues roiling companies worldwide, from tariffs and energy prices to inflation and consumer confidence.
Soaring costs related to the Iran war are the latest headache for companies making everything from food and drink to consumer electronics and cars, after contending in 2025 with Trump’s tariffs on imported goods.
High gas and grocery bills were big concerns among voters in the US midterm elections.
“What we need as a company in the US is political stability and a reliable economic framework. And everything which is embracing this is welcome,” said Roland Welzbacher, CFO of German car parts supplier Continental.

“What it really means for us and for the economy at large remains to be seen, but it brings stability, which is good.”
Global stocks and the dollar rose after the results, although chip stocks in Asia came under pressure, as investors expect the Democratic-controlled Congress to apply more scrutiny to AI.
The election outcome could also have broad implications for the US fiscal outlook as well as sectors such as defence, healthcare and banking.
White House could face greater pressure to avoid trade wars
While analysts said the White House may face greater pressure to avoid a return to the trade wars that have raised costs for American consumers, some European manufacturers expect little immediate material relief from Trump’s hefty import tariffs.
The administration largely pursued its tariff agenda through executive authorities that do not require congressional approval, and those powers remain in place, said Andrew Adair, trade policy adviser for North America at German machinery association VDMA.
Congress could seek to roll back existing tariffs, but such legislation would face major political hurdles and could ultimately be vetoed by the President, he said.
“We therefore do not anticipate national politics to directly impact business conditions over the short term,” he told Reuters.
Kenichi Hori, president and chief executive of Japanese trading house Mitsui, which generates significant revenue in the US, told the media that he will be closely watching US policy on tariffs, critical minerals trade and AI data centre build-outs, but he expects the business environment to remain “highly uncertain”.
Result could boost visitor numbers
The result could improve the United States’ image abroad, which has been hurt by Trump’s tougher stance on immigration and trade policies, with visitor numbers dropping sharply since he took office.
“There might be less tariff-related irritation and a greater willingness to travel, which should have a rather positive impact on the aviation sector,” Fraport chief executive Stefan Schulte said. “But I wouldn’t overestimate the significance of this.”
Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management, was among those to warn of gridlock in Washington, saying that federal funding runs out on Dec 11 and that Trump has promised to become “Mr Veto” against a Democratic Congress.
“Divided government means gridlock, and gridlock means noise: investigations, vetoes, funding deadlines, and very likely another government shutdown or two, or more,” he said. REUTERS

articles.title: Chinese Capital Pours 4.5 Billion Dollars into Vietnam Manufacturing - Retail News Asia
articles.summary: Chinese Capital Pours 4.5 Billion Dollars into Vietnam Manufacturing  Retail News Asia
articles.full_text:
In this article (9)
Chinese and Hong Kong investors registered 4.5 billion dollars in capital across 1,104 new Vietnamese projects in the first nine months of 2026, targeting industrial supply lines.
Bilateral trade between China and Vietnam expanded 37.6 per cent year on year to exceed 253 billion dollars during the same nine-month period, following a full-year total of more than 256 billion dollars in 2025.
Factory Lines Take the Bulk of Inbound Funds
Manufacturing absorbed 80.61 per cent of the registered capital committed by Chinese groups, placing China fourth among foreign direct investment sources in Vietnam. The figures, presented at the Autumn Economic Forum in Ho Chi Minh City, reveal an accelerating shift from basic merchandise exchange toward deep factory linkages.
Cross-border commerce now relies on coordinated production networks rather than simple container shipments. Electronics assemblers and industrial component vendors are shifting sub-tier operations directly into Vietnamese industrial parks to retain tariff efficiency while drawing technical oversight from mainland supply hubs.
Consulate Calls for Direct Process Integration
Xu Shou, acting consul general of China in Ho Chi Minh City, said the two economies hold complementary industrial structures that demand technical coordination.
Cooperation between Chinese and Vietnamese businesses has moved beyond traditional trade in goods into a new phase of supply chain coordination, technology exchange, and knowledge sharing
Xu urged suppliers and downstream manufacturers to align quality control, factory automation, and workforce training. He also pressed for joint ventures in urban rail systems, digital trade infrastructure, and cross-border settlement channels.
Sourcing Hubs Deepen Downstream Roots
For consumer brands and contract electronics manufacturers operating across Southeast Asia, these capital commitments reduce the friction of sourcing raw components. Moving intermediate fabrication closer to Vietnamese assembly plants cuts lead times for export-bound goods, but it ties regional factory schedules even tighter to Chinese industrial design and material supplies.
The operational risk sits squarely in logistics bottlenecks at overland crossing points. Factory operators face acute delays whenever northern border gates back up, which makes physical rail integration and unified technical customs standards the primary gating factor for factory productivity.
Transport Corridors Form the Next Test
Hanoi is pushing infrastructure projects to match the incoming industrial volume. Vietnamese Deputy Minister of Finance Nguyen Thi Bich Ngoc met with China’s State Council Research Office in late October, laying out five priority areas that feature the planned Lao Cai-Hanoi-Hai Phong railway line alongside smart border checkpoints.
Regional conglomerates are building commercial networks around the trade flow. Sunwah Group, through its Sunwah Innovations unit established in 2020, runs business hubs across Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, and Da Nang to link early-stage technology and factory partnerships between domestic firms and mainland investors.
Questions & Answers
Q.
Which sectors are attracting the majority of Chinese capital in Vietnam?
Manufacturing absorbed 80.61 per cent of the 4.5 billion dollars committed by Chinese and Hong Kong investors during the first nine months of 2026. Electronics assemblers and industrial component vendors are establishing operations in Vietnamese industrial parks to improve tariff efficiency.
Q.
What operational bottlenecks threaten these cross-border manufacturing networks?
Factory operators face acute delivery delays caused by logistics bottlenecks at overland northern border gates. Resolving these issues depends heavily on physical rail integration, streamlined customs standards, and the construction of priority transport projects like the Lao Cai-Hanoi-Hai Phong railway line.
Q.
How rapidly is bilateral trade between China and Vietnam expanding?
Bilateral trade grew by 37.6 per cent year on year to surpass 253 billion dollars during the first nine months of 2026. This places the two countries on track to comfortably exceed the full-year total of 256 billion dollars recorded in 2025.

articles.title: Indonesia Weighs Moratorium on Nickel Smelters Amid Global Oversupply - Jakarta Globe
articles.summary: Indonesia Weighs Moratorium on Nickel Smelters Amid Global Oversupply  Jakarta Globe
articles.full_text:
Jakarta. Indonesia is considering a moratorium on new mineral smelters that produce only semi-finished goods as the government seeks to push the downstream industry toward higher-value products and address a global nickel oversupply.
Bahlil Lahadalia, energy and mineral resources minister and coordinating minister for downstream industrialization and energy transition, said Indonesia's mineral processing industry remained heavily concentrated on intermediate products, with an estimated 50% to 60% of downstream output still at the semi-finished stage.
He said he had instructed the Energy and Mineral Resources Ministry's Directorate General of Minerals and Coal to study whether the government should continue issuing permits for smelters producing only intermediate goods or impose a moratorium.
"We need to conduct a study to determine whether it is still feasible to build smelters that produce only semi-finished products, or whether we should impose a moratorium," Bahlil said at the opening of the 2026 Mineral and Coal Convention and Exhibition (Minerba Convex) at JIExpo in Jakarta on Monday.
The proposed policy is intended to encourage investment in facilities that manufacture finished products rather than allowing semi-finished materials to be exported for further processing overseas.
"For semi-finished products intended for smelters, what we need to promote are finished goods. This is so that these semi-finished raw materials aren't all exported abroad, ensuring that Indonesia truly reaps the full benefits," he said.
Bahlil also pointed to a global nickel oversupply as a major factor behind falling prices. "Why are prices falling? Because our production is out of control. Global demand is only 3.5 million metric tons per year. Now there's an oversupply of nearly 800,000 metric tons. How could prices possibly remain high?" Bahlil said.
Nickel Export Value Climbs After Downstream Push
Despite concerns over oversupply, Bahlil said Indonesia's downstream processing policy had significantly increased the value of nickel exports.
According to Energy and Mineral Resources Ministry data, the value of Indonesia's nickel exports rose from around US$3.3 billion during the 2017–2019 period to US$33.9 billion in 2024.
He attributed the increase to the government's 2020 ban on nickel ore exports, which encouraged investment in domestic smelting and processing facilities.
"Back when I was still at the Investment Coordinating Board (BKPM), our nickel exports from 2017 to 2019 totaled only $3.3 billion. We halted nickel exports, then built up the industry and pursued downstream processing. What happened? By 2023 and 2024, our exports had climbed to around $33 billion to $34 billion," Bahlil said.
However, he said the increase in export value did not mean Indonesia had fully realized the economic potential of downstream processing, as most domestic production remained concentrated on intermediate goods rather than finished products.
The government is therefore seeking to move the industry further along the value chain, encouraging manufacturers to produce higher-value goods domestically rather than relying primarily on the export of processed raw materials.

articles.full_text:
JOHOR BAHRU, Nov 3 — A 19-year-old Singaporean man was among three individuals fined RM3,500 each under the newly amended law against illegal racing by the Magistrate's Court here today.
The three, Syajahan Alfian Abdullah, 19; Muhammad Daniel Hakim Mohamad Rashid, 24; and Gonzales Mckhovic anak George, 18, pleaded guilty to engaging in illegal racing and riding their motorcycles in a dangerous manner on the Second Link Expressway last month.
They entered their guilty pleas after the charges were read out to them individually before Magistrate Nur Fatin Mohamad Farid.
The court also ordered all three to serve four months in prison if they failed to pay their fines.
According to the charge sheet, Singaporean national serviceman Syajahan Alfian was accused of riding a motorcycle at high speed and participating in a speed contest at Kilometre 12.5 of the southbound section of the Second Link Expressway at 2.10am on October 18.
He was charged under Section 42A(2) of the Road Transport Act 1987, as amended in 2026, which carries a fine of between RM2,000 and RM10,000, imprisonment for up to two years, or both, upon conviction.
Meanwhile, Muhammad Daniel Hakim and Gonzales Mckhovic were each charged with racing their motorcycles on the northbound section of the Second Link Expressway between Kilometres 7.8 and 18.2 at 2.10am on October 18.
Both men were charged under Section 42A(1) of the same Act, which carries a fine of between RM2,000 and RM10,000, imprisonment for up to two years, or both.
The case was prosecuted by traffic police prosecuting officer Inspector S. Vikineswary, while all three accused were unrepresented.
The Road Transport (Amendment) Act 2026, which came into effect on October 16, introduced harsher penalties for illegal racing and reckless motorcycle riding through the inclusion of Section 42A.
The Transport Ministry said the amendments to the Road Transport Act 1987 (Act 333) were intended to enhance road safety, strengthen enforcement and modernise service delivery by the Road Transport Department (JPJ).
The amendments also aim to close legal loopholes that could allow certain parties to evade responsibility for offences committed using their vehicles.
