articles.title: No Xi, but Li of China expected in PH-hosted Asean summit - Inquirer.net
articles.summary: No Xi, but Li of China expected in PH-hosted Asean summit  Inquirer.net
articles.full_text:
MANILA, Philippines — China’s warning to rein in Filipino politicians who cross its “red lines” and renewed tensions over the West Philippine Sea are casting a shadow over efforts to stabilize bilateral relations ahead of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit in Manila later this month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is not expected to attend the Asean Summit on Nov. 16 to Nov. 18, but President Marcos is looking forward to welcoming Premier Li Qiang, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Wednesday.
The anticipated visit comes amid continuing diplomatic friction between Manila and Beijing over maritime disputes, political statements and disagreements on joint oil and gas exploration.
Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi discussed the participation of their respective leaders in upcoming regional meetings during a telephone conversation on Nov. 3.
Lazaro conveyed Marcos’ anticipation of Li’s attendance, noting that the Chinese premier had traditionally led Beijing’s delegation to Asean-related meetings in recent years.
READ: Marcos inspects PICC ahead of November Asean Summit
The DFA statement did not confirm whether Xi would attend. The Chinese president has never personally participated in an Asean summit, including the special Asean-China meeting in November 2021, which he joined through video link during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Marcos has expressed hope that Xi would attend the Manila gathering to help conclude the decadeslong negotiations for a Code of Conduct in the South China Sea.
Wang, meanwhile, expressed China’s expectation that Marcos would attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen on Nov. 18 to Nov. 19.
“Both ministers assured each other that their respective leaders would be accorded the proper courtesies and assistance during these meetings,” the DFA said.
The Manila summit is expected to draw leaders of the 11 Asean member states and heads of government from 12 dialogue partners, including President Donald Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
Marcos has also invited Russian President Vladimir Putin, although Moscow has yet to confirm his participation.
The diplomatic exchange, however, was accompanied by a pointed warning from Wang, who urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians he accused of repeatedly attacking and smearing China.
Red lines
In a statement on the telephone conversation, China’s foreign ministry quoted Wang as saying bilateral relations were facing “malicious interference.”
“A small number of politicians” in the Philippines had repeatedly attacked China “out of political prejudice and for their own selfish interests, crossing China’s red lines,” Wang said, without identifying the individuals or specifying the statements that prompted his criticism.
He urged Manila to “strengthen its oversight of the individuals concerned and send a rational and unified message on its China policy.”
The warning came amid a series of diplomatic confrontations, including the Philippine government’s summoning of Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan in October after he made remarks that China could easily win a conflict with the Philippines.
Several Filipino senators subsequently called for Jing’s expulsion, while the Chinese Embassy accused Philippine officials of making provocative statements and undermining bilateral relations.
Beijing also recently accused Manila of putting up obstacles to its participation in the Asean gathering, an allegation rejected by Philippine officials.
Diplomatic reset
The DFA described the Lazaro-Wang conversation as “frank, pragmatic and constructive,” saying it reflected the two countries’ interest in maintaining a stable and predictable relationship based on mutual respect and mutually beneficial cooperation.
Both sides agreed on three principles for managing bilateral ties: maintaining diplomacy and dialogue, avoiding actions and rhetoric that could unnecessarily heighten tensions, and resolving disputes peacefully while responsibly managing differences.
Lazaro stressed that good relations with China served the interests of both countries and the region, and should be sustained through regular high-level exchanges, ministry-to-ministry channels and established bilateral and regional mechanisms.
The discussion also covered maritime concerns, although the DFA said the focus was on restoring relations to an “even keel” and upholding the 1975 Joint Communiqué, which remains the foundation of diplomatic relations and the Philippines’ One China Policy.
The department also welcomed an appeal by Philippine business and sectoral organizations for the stabilization of relations, describing their statement as a constructive contribution to foreign policy discussions.
Teodoro stands firm
But Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. questioned China’s call for prudence on maritime issues, warning that the Philippines could lose the benefits of its maritime resources if it failed to defend its rights in the West Philippine Sea.
Speaking at the 97th founding anniversary of Misamis Occidental in Oroquieta City on Wednesday, Teodoro said the country’s future development would increasingly depend on resources beneath its surrounding waters.
“The resources we need to prosper can no longer be found on land. We must go to the sea,” he said in Filipino.
“That is why we are fighting for our 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone in the West Philippine Sea, and in the even larger Pacific Ocean, so that we may secure the fish and the oil and gas resources found beneath the waters, for the sake of your future,” he added.
Teodoro said other countries could benefit if the Philippines failed to protect its maritime entitlements.
“The West Philippine Sea is a catalyst for development,” he said. “International law has granted that to us. It belongs to us. But if we just sit back and relax, nothing will happen. We have to fight for it.”
He also reiterated his opposition to joint oil and gas exploration with China, disputing the Chinese Embassy’s accusation that he had obstructed negotiations.
Teodoro said former President Rodrigo Duterte terminated the negotiations in June 2022 over constitutional concerns, upon the advice of then Foreign Affairs Secretary Teodoro Locsin Jr.
The Philippines and China signed a memorandum of understanding in November 2018 to establish a framework for possible cooperation in oil and gas exploration, but the talks ended without a final agreement.
“That is illegal,” Teodoro said, citing constitutional restrictions, a Supreme Court ruling and the Philippines’ 2016 arbitral victory.
The Supreme Court declared unconstitutional a 2005 tripartite agreement among the Philippines, China and Vietnam for joint marine seismic surveys. The ruling concerned that earlier agreement, not the separate 2018 Philippine-China framework.
Teodoro also maintained that China had no valid overlapping maritime claim that could justify joint exploration in areas where the Philippines exercises sovereign rights.
“How can we set that aside when it’s the law?” he said when asked whether the two countries could put aside their differences to pursue joint exploration. —With a report from Agence France-Presse

articles.title: [进展] Indonesia Q3 GDP growth at 5.47%, beats expectations - The Business Times
articles.summary: Indonesia Q3 GDP growth at 5.47%, beats expectations  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
Its central bank said its domestic economy remained resilient but could be strengthened further
[JAKARTA] Indonesia’s economy expanded 5.47 per cent in the third quarter from a year earlier, official data showed on Thursday (Nov 5), faster than the 5.18 per cent forecast in a Reuters poll.
Indonesia’s economic growth in the second quarter stood at 5.29 per cent.
South-east Asia’s largest economy has contended with weaker investor sentiment this year amid heightened scrutiny of the government’s fiscal plans and its broader policy directions, as well as lingering downgrade risks on its stock market.
Growth was supported by sectors such as manufacturing, including the processing of palm oil to produce fuel as Indonesia expanded its mandatory biodiesel programme, the statistics bureau said.
The 2026 state budget projects economic growth of 5.4 per cent, although finance minister Suahasil Nazara has said it could slightly exceed that target and reach 5.5 per cent this year.
The target falls within Bank Indonesia’s GDP growth outlook range of 4.9 per cent to 5.7 per cent. At its meeting last month, the central bank said the domestic economy remained resilient but required further strengthening.
President Prabowo Subianto, who took office two years ago, aims to lift economic growth to 8 per cent by 2029. REUTERS

articles.title: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years - BBC
articles.summary: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years  BBCThailand extends activist's jail term to more than 34 years  CNAThailand extends jail term of human rights lawyer to 34 years for offending monarchy  Yahoo News SingaporeArnon and four others jailed for royal defamation  Bangkok PostThai Activist Sentenced to Additional Prison Term For Defaming Monarchy During 2020 Protest  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Cur...
articles.full_text:
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.
The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.
One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.
This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.
On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.
This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.
"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."
The past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.
Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".
Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."
In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions.
"If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."
From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son.
"Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children," one of his letters reads, "The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom."
Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.
Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.
But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.
The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.
That changed on 3 August 2020.
That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.
In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.
In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.
At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.
But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.
One of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.
She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.
A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame.
She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy.
"I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve.
"I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."
In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté.
"It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."
Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.
She joined a movement calling itself Thalu Wang, which translates as "breaking through the palace". Instead of giving speeches, they came up with stunts like holding polls on the street, asking people what they thought of royal motorcades holding up the traffic, or whether they believed the monarchy had too much power.
"We knew the risks, but we thought it would be safer just conducting a poll. It turns out it was not."
She was given two more lèse majesté charges in 2022, and detained before being released on bail. She had to wear an electronic monitor on her ankle and was barred from leaving her home between 4pm and 6am. Her parents were forced to sign a document promising to inform on her. She was facing decades in jail.
Melinn decided she had no choice. With a friend she fled Thailand and eventually got asylum in Canada.
Article 112 is on paper just a law, like any other, passed by the Thai parliament, which can, theoretically, be amended by elected MPs. In fact it has been amended in the past, notably in 1976 when the punishment for breaking it was increased to between three and 15 years in prison.
But today the Constitutional Court has decreed that the law itself, like the institution it protects, is untouchable. The reformist Move Forward party - the successor of Future Forward - was dissolved in 2024, and its leader banned from politics, merely for proposing that the punishments be less harsh. And the courts make it very difficult for those charged under it to defend themselves.
"In many cases, like the one against Arnon Nampa, prosecutors accuse the defendant of lying about the monarchy," says Chaimaneekarakate, the lawyer. "But when we ask the judge to subpoena documents or witnesses who could show the truth of what the defendant says, the judge refuses to do it. When one lawyer protested against the court deciding that the trial would be held in secret, she was warned by the judge to be quiet or face a contempt of court charge."
He says judges sometimes criticise the young activists over their alleged actions even before the trial

articles.title: US midterms: Democrats' victory puts Trump's China diplomacy to the test - CNA
articles.summary: US midterms: Democrats' victory puts Trump's China diplomacy to the test  CNAChina Keeps Faith in Trump as ‘Total Defeat’ Adds New Risks  Bloomberg.comUS midterm shift could squeeze China on AI, bring clarity to bilateral talks  South China Morning PostDemocratic Party's Congressional Control Escalates U.S. Pressure on Taiwan, Semiconductors  조선일보What the US midterms mean for ties with China  Yahoo News Singapore
articles.full_text:
analysis Asia
US midterms: Democrats' victory puts Trump's China diplomacy to the test
Democrats have seized both chambers of Congress in a major blow to US President Donald Trump, shifting the balance of power in Washington as Asia watches for signs of policy change.
SINGAPORE: Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress in the United States midterm elections on Tuesday (Nov 3) - dealing a major blow to President Donald Trump and raising questions about what the political shake-up in Washington could mean for Asia.
Even as the extent of any policy shifts remains uncertain, the new balance of power could complicate Trump’s ability to advance his agenda over the next two years, with potential implications for US-China relations, trade and tariffs, and Washington's security commitments in the Indo-Pacific, say experts.
For Asian economies already grappling with trade uncertainty and rising geopolitical tensions, the key question is where the election results could bring meaningful change - and where US policy is likely to stay the course.
TRADE AND TARIFFS: WHAT CHANGES FOR ASIAN ECONOMIES?
Stephen Olson, visiting senior fellow at ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, a Singapore-based research centre, warned that with the electoral pressure of the midterms behind him, Trump could become less constrained in pursuing an aggressive trade policy, including potentially imposing further tariffs on China and other Asian economies.
“Section 301 tariffs on excess capacity could be forthcoming shortly and new trade actions against key partners could also be opened. That obviously would be bad news, especially in the Indo-Pacific,” Olson said, referring to the provision of US trade law that allows Washington to investigate and take action against foreign countries it believes are engaging in unfair trade practices.
At the same time, the Democrats’ electoral gains could embolden lawmakers from both parties to challenge the president's trade agenda, potentially opening the door to greater congressional scrutiny, he said.
Asian countries, particularly US allies such as South Korea and Japan, will be “hoping that Democrats in Congress will be able to moderate the worst impacts of Trump’s trade policies”, according to Reuters columnist Clyde Russell.
In a commentary published on Wednesday, Russell noted that these countries would welcome a rollback of tariffs and greater consistency in Washington's treatment of its allies.
But not all aspects of Trump's economic agenda are likely to face resistance, Russell said - pointing to Washington’s efforts to develop critical mineral supply chains outside China, including investments in rare earths, tungsten and lithium, as an area where bipartisan support could ensure continuity.
The bigger question is whether Democrats can meaningfully constrain Trump's tariff policies, given the president's considerable executive authority over trade.
Olson said that while Trump would continue to wield broad powers, Congress could push for more exemptions from tariffs on products that directly affect American consumers.
Lawmakers could also seek to reclaim some of the authority over trade policy that Congress has ceded to the executive branch.
“Depending on how badly the Republicans get wiped out, and how badly Trump's aura of political potency gets dented, Congress, including pro-free trade Republicans who have been intimidated into standing down, might be inclined to reassert some degree of Congressional authority on trade,” Olson said.
US-CHINA RIVALRY: CONTINUITY OR CHANGE?
Analysts said the new balance of power in Congress could complicate Trump's efforts to stabilise ties with Beijing, particularly if Democrats push for tougher measures against China.
Adrian Ang, research fellow and coordinator of the United States Programme at the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), a Singapore-based think-tank, said a Democratic-controlled Congress could take a “more hawkish (stance towards) China" than Trump himself.
This could translate into pressure for tougher measures on trade and technology restrictions, as well as renewed scrutiny of a delayed US$14 billion US arms package for Taiwan, Ang added.
China claims Taiwan as its territory and has increased its military presence around the island in recent years. The US maintains close unofficial ties with Taiwan and is its main arms supplier.
“All of those, but especially the last item, will place stress on the new US-China constructive strategic stability based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity agreed to by both presidents, Trump and Xi,” Ang said.
“It will depend on how much pressure Congress can bring to bear on the president and the extent to which the president views his stabilisation of the bilateral relationship as his legacy.”
Chinese policy researcher Li Yaqi said Democrats could raise the political cost of Trump's dealings with Beijing, even if they have limited power to fundamentally change his China policy.
Li pointed to Congress' powers to launch investigations, summon administration officials and influence government spending as potential tools to challenge White House decisions.
Democratic lawmakers could also seek to attach conditions to defence spending legislation to prevent the administration from easing certain sanctions on China, he said.
Drew Thompson, a senior fellow at RSIS, does not expect significant changes to Washington's approach to Taiwan, noting that support for the island has remained consistently strong across both parties.
At the same time, he similarly noted that Democratic lawmakers' emphasis on human rights could put them at odds with Beijing.
“The Democratic Party's ideological support for universal human rights often puts its senators and representatives at odds with China,” Thompson noted.
However, he stressed that the White House would continue to wield the greatest influence over US-China relations, regardless of which party controls Congress.
“While Congress has the power to appropriate, the executive branch is the lead on foreign policy and diplomatic engagement,” he said.
On its part, China has signalled it is keen to maintain stable relations with Washington.
Beijing said it was “willing to continue working” with the US to implement agreements reached between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping - while “properly managing differences and expanding cooperation”.
“The midterm elections are an internal affair of the United States,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a regular press briefing on Wednesday - adding that Beijing remained committed to building a “constructive, strategically stable China-US relationship” based on mutual respect, fairness and reciprocity.
Ang said that the current stability in US-China relations is “the result of a stalemate and mutual vulnerabilities” between the two powers.
Much therefore depends on Trump's willingness to adopt a tougher stance towards China, knowing that Beijing will likely retaliate, he said.
Trump’s upcoming meetings in Asia could offer an early indication of his approach, Ang added.
The president is expected to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila next week before meeting Xi on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.
REGIONAL SECURITY OUTLOOK
Analysts have cautioned against expecting a fundamental change in American foreign policy, including its defence commitments and strategic engagement in the region, simply because Democrats now control Congress.
“The midterm results look dramatic from a US domestic standpoint but for ASEAN, they may moderate but not fundamentally change US policy on trade, use of force, and diplomacy,” Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore (NUS), told CNA.
Unlike a presidential election, the midterms do not change who occupies the White House, with Trump retaining broad powers over foreign policy, military action and tariffs, Chong noted.
Congress could seek to curb some of the president's decisions, but would generally be unable to fundamentally alter his approach, he added.
More substantial intervention would likely require exceptional circumstances, such as impeachment or an issue that commands overwhelming congressional support, both of which are rare.
RSIS’ Ang similarly noted that the president enjoys considerably more freedom in foreign and defence policy than in domestic affairs.
While Congress can exercise oversight and control government spending, these powers may not be sufficient to stop a president determined to pursue a particular foreign policy course, he said.
Ang pointed to the Trump administration's actions during the Iran war in June, when it was prepared to sidestep congressional efforts to invoke the War Powers Act - which seeks to limit the president’s ability to engage US forces in armed conflict without congressional approval.
Without two-thirds majorities in both chambers of Congress, the threshold needed to override a presidential veto, Democrats would struggle to constrain Trump, particularly if Republican lawmakers remained largely united behind him, he added.
Additional reporting by Lee Gim Siong

articles.title: South Korea's EV Export Competitiveness Overtaken by China - 조선일보
articles.summary: South Korea's EV Export Competitiveness Overtaken by China  조선일보
articles.full_text:
South Korea has emerged as the most severely impacted among the world’s top four electric vehicle (EV) exporters—Germany, China, South Korea, and Japan—due to China’s rapid rise. Over the past six years, Germany has maintained its unchallenged lead, and Japan has held steady, while South Korea’s export competitiveness index has fallen below China’s for the first time. In response to the onslaught of Chinese EVs, major markets including Thailand, the EU, Mexico, and Brazil have raised tariff barriers to protect domestic industries. Meanwhile, South Korea has remained defenseless, ceding both domestic and overseas markets, with warnings that its annual EV export revenue could shrink by 2.2 trillion Korean won by 2030.
◇South Korea’s Export Competitiveness Plummets Alone Among Global Top 4
According to the Federation of Korean Industries (FKI)’s report, *Analysis of South Korea’s EV Export Competitiveness and Implications*, based on UN trade statistics, South Korea’s Revealed Comparative Advantage (RCA) index for EVs dropped from 3.02 in 2019 to 1.48 last year—a halving over six years. The index plummeted sharply in the past two years (2.92 in 2023 → 1.48 in 2025). In contrast, China’s RCA surged nearly eightfold, from 0.19 in 2019 to 1.49 last year, overtaking South Korea for the first time.
The RCA measures a country’s export share of a specific product relative to the global average; a value above 1 indicates competitive strength. Among the global top four EV exporters, South Korea’s decline is stark. In 2019, South Korea’s RCA (3.02) was 16 times higher than China’s (0.19) and even exceeded Germany’s (around 2.9). However, South Korea has fallen alone as China rose.
South Korea’s global EV market share has also plummeted. While EVs accounted for 25.0% of global new car sales (up from 2.6% six years ago), China’s EV export share soared from 2.6% to 24.8%, closing in on Germany’s 29%. Meanwhile, South Korea’s share halved from 8.9% to 4.6%.
Amid declining exports, the domestic market has also been breached. According to the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association, Chinese EVs accounted for 38.1% (112,968 units) of the 296,801 newly registered EVs in South Korea from January to September this year. The FKI estimates that if the current trend continues, South Korea could lose 2.2 trillion Korean won (14.7% of last year’s exports) in EV export revenue to Chinese products by 2030.
◇Global Tariff Barriers Rise to 35–50%
Countries are tightening barriers against Chinese EVs. Thailand announced on the 3rd that it will raise the special consumption tax on imported EVs from 10% to 35% starting next January, targeting Chinese vehicles, which accounted for 96% of its EV imports from January to September. The Thai government is also offering tax incentives proportional to local factory investments and domestic component usage to protect its ecosystem.
The EU added countervailing duties of up to 35.3% on Chinese pure EVs in 2024 and launched a safeguard investigation into foreign hybrid vehicles last month. Mexico raised tariffs on non-FTA countries like South Korea and China to 50% this year, while Brazil increased tariffs on imported EVs and hybrids to 35% in July.
In contrast, South Korea’s tariff on Chinese passenger cars remains at a basic rate of 8%, half of the 15% tariff China imposes on South Korean vehicles. Lee Sang-ho, head of the FKI Economic Bureau, urged, “Immediate and substantial policy support, such as introducing a domestic production tax credit, is critical to prevent the collapse of South Korea’s EV production base.”
☞Revealed Comparative Advantage (RCA) Index
The RCA index is calculated by dividing a country’s export share of a specific product by the global export share of the same product. A value above 1 indicates that the country’s export share exceeds the global average, signaling relatively strong competitiveness.

articles.title: PM requests controlling inflation while pursuing double-digit growth - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: PM requests controlling inflation while pursuing double-digit growth  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Hanoi (VNA) – Prime Minister Le Minh Hung on November 4 reaffirmed the Government’s determination to achieve double-digit economic growth while maintaining macroeconomic stability and controlling inflation, stressing that inflation control must be given the highest priority in the final two months of 2026. 
The PM made the statement while chairing the Government’s regular meeting to review socio-economic performance in October and the first 10 months of the year, and discuss key tasks and solutions for the remaining months. 
According to reports presented at the meeting, Vietnam’s economy continued to record positive results across various sectors, with macroeconomic stability maintained and inflation kept under control. The consumer price index (CPI) rose 4.57% in the first 10 months, while state budget revenue reached nearly 2.45 quadrillion VND (95.2 billion USD), equivalent to 96.4% of the annual estimate. 
Traditional growth drivers remained strong. Public investment disbursement reached 720.5 trillion VND, or 75.4% of the assigned plan. Foreign direct investment (FDI) attraction remained a bright spot, with registered capital totalling 54.85 billion USD and disbursed capital reaching 24.08 billion USD. Notably, total export-import turnover exceeded 1 trillion USD for the first time, reaching nearly 1.011 trillion USD. 
Science and technology, innovation and digital transformation continued to be promoted as new growth drivers, while progress on major infrastructure projects was accelerated. Social welfare, cultural development, national defence, security and external relations also received due attention. 
Concluding the meeting, PM Hung acknowledged the achievements while pointing out persistent difficulties and challenges. He noted that public investment disbursement remains low at several ministries, agencies, localities and key projects. The handling of long-standing projects and surplus public buildings and land in many localities have also failed to produce the expected results. 
He called for more concrete measures to boost exports, reduce the trade deficit, stimulate private investment, remove obstacles facing businesses and improve productivity through science, technology and the development of new economic sectors. He also stressed the need to accelerate the development and completion of databases, connect information systems and simplify administrative procedures through the reuse of existing data. 
The Government must also step up efforts to stimulate domestic consumption towards the year-end, while addressing issues related to healthcare, education, culture, employment, social welfare and people's living conditions, he stressed. 
For November and the final two months of the year, the Government leader instructed ministries, sectors and localities to proactively develop action plans to implement resolutions and conclusions of the fourth plenum of the Party Central Committee. Ministries and agencies were also asked to work closely with National Assembly bodies to finalise draft laws and resolutions, ensuring consistency and effective institutionalisation of the Party’s guidelines, and prepare detailed documents for implementation to avoid delays once the legislation takes effect. 
He instructed the steering committee for price management to work immediately with localities where CPI growth over the first 10 months exceeded the national average, particularly major cities, to devise appropriate measures to stabilise prices. Authorities must closely monitor the year-end growth scenario and implement measures to stimulate consumption and tourism, connect supply and demand, promote trade and organise trade fairs during the upcoming holiday and Lunar New Year period. 
Regarding public investment, PM Hung called for reallocating capital from slow-moving projects to those with stronger disbursement capacity, aiming to achieve 100% disbursement of the assigned plan. He also urged stricter control over the number of projects, particularly the construction of administrative offices in provinces and cities, to prioritise resources for essential infrastructure and projects with widespread socio-economic impacts. Major projects must be accelerated, with particular attention paid to site clearance and construction material supplies. The 100-day plan to address bottlenecks in digital transformation must also be completed on schedule. 
On social welfare, the Government leader directed the implementation of the plan based on the conclusions of General Secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam Central Committee and President To Lam regarding support for vulnerable groups. Priorities include accelerating the search for, recovery and identification of fallen soldiers’ remains, meeting the 2026 targets for social housing and rental housing, and ensuring progress in building inter-level boarding schools in border communes. 
The Prime Minister assigned specific tasks to ministries to ensure coordinated implementation. The Ministry of Finance was asked to closely monitor price developments, update inflation scenarios and propose appropriate price management measures, while accelerating reforms in value-added tax and tax administration. 
The State Bank of Vietnam was urged to proactively and flexibly manage the monetary policy to stabilise the value of the Vietnamese currency, interest rates and exchange rates, and create more favourable lending conditions for production, business, priority sectors and small- and medium-sized enterprises. It must also strengthen supervision to ensure the banking system safety. The Ministry of Industry and Trade was tasked with ensuring stable supplies of essential goods, particularly petroleum and electricity, accelerating adjustments to the Power Development Plan VIII and completing the draft decree on petroleum trading in November. It was also instructed to promote exports, control the trade deficit, diversify markets, make effective use of free trade agreements and step up negotiations on a reciprocal trade agreement with the US. 
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Construction must closely monitor prices of building materials, housing and transport services, while coordinating with localities to remove obstacles and accelerate major infrastructure projects. The Ministry of Agriculture and Environment was asked to ensure stable supplies of essential food and agricultural products, balance domestic consumption and exports, and reorganise agricultural supply and distribution networks. 
PM Hung also called for stronger application of strategic technologies, improvements in education and healthcare services, year-end tourism stimulus measures and the development of special policies to attract and retain talented people. 
He assigned the Ministry of National Defence, the Ministry of Public Security and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to strengthen strategic policy research and advice, and accelerate key projects in national defence and security. 
The Prime Minister urged Deputy Prime Ministers and Government members to proactively implement their assigned tasks and contribute directly to the draft National Assembly resolution on the 2027 socio-economic situation, and continue working to ensure that key targets and tasks for the remaining months of 2026 are fulfilled./.

articles.title: Production linked to a "green passport" will allow businesses to go further. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Production linked to a "green passport" will allow businesses to go further.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| Leaders of the Trade Promotion Department at the Vietnam Export Promotion Forum 2026, morning of November 4th. | 
 On the morning of November 4th, the Vietnam Export Promotion Forum 2026, themed "Go Global – Together with Businesses to Reach the World ," was organized by the Trade Promotion Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ).
 The forum aims to implement the Go Global Program, enhancing the internationalization capacity, competitiveness, and ability of Vietnamese businesses to participate more deeply in the global market.
 Vietnamese suppliers are increasingly involved in international trade and supply chains. However, in the context of a rapidly changing global economy , increased competition, constantly restructuring supply chains, and increasingly stringent standards regarding technology, environment, and social responsibility, Vietnamese businesses need to meet many new standards simultaneously. 
 Businesses aiming to expand globally need to start with a foundation of quality, production capacity, and management; access international markets to find customers, learn standards and consumer behavior; and then upgrade their role from mere processing, assembly, and export to mastering technology, branding, and distribution systems. Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Director of the Trade Promotion Department  Go Global represents a fundamental shift in thinking about international economic integration: from primarily exploiting domestic advantages for production, processing, and export, it is gradually moving towards proactively building competitiveness, developing brands, expanding distribution systems, and participating more deeply in international value chains.
 According to this orientation, expanding globally is not just about exporting goods, but also about improving management capabilities, technology, innovation, and gradually participating in higher value-added stages of the global supply chain.
 Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Director of the Trade Promotion Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade), affirmed that Vietnam is facing a new turning point in enhancing its position in the global value chain. This is based on a network of 18 FTAs established after nearly 40 years of reform, with import and export volumes exceeding US$1 trillion by the end of October 2026. 
|  | 
| International trade experts and the business community attend the Export Promotion Forum 2026. | 
 In addition, Vietnam has pioneering businesses: Viettel has invested in 10 markets, leading the market share in 7, with international revenue of approximately $3.3 billion in 2025;FPT has achieved over 35,000 billion VND in IT revenue abroad, with new contracts exceeding $1.5 billion, according to Mr. Phu.
 In the coming period, Vietnam needs to expand its export space and meet the increasingly stringent requirements of the international market regarding quality, green products, and traceability of origin.
 "We need to shift from an approach of 'exporting Vietnamese goods abroad' to 'building a presence of Vietnamese businesses overseas, through brands, offices, factories, warehouses, distribution systems in the host market, and cross-border online sales channels'," Mr. Phu emphasized.
 According to Mr. Nguyen The Thi, Deputy Director of the Bac Ninh Department of Industry and Trade, in the first 10 months of this year, Bac Ninh's exports led the country, estimated at 101.3 billion USD, an increase of nearly 33% compared to the same period last year.
 Despite the large scale of exports, Mr. Thi acknowledged that this does not necessarily translate into a commensurate increase in added value or participation from domestic businesses. Currently, the locality's exports are primarily dependent on foreign companies, with electronics being the key sector.
 In an effort to promote businesses to the global market and increase connections with supply chains, representatives from the Bac Ninh Department of Industry and Trade stated that the locality is accelerating support for businesses to take advantage of FTAs, having issued over 20,000 Certificates of Origin (C/O) to businesses, and focusing on promoting agricultural exports.
 According to Mr. Thi, Bac Ninh will focus on five key tasks in the coming period: continuing to improve the business environment, providing information and warnings about trade barriers and origin fraud to reduce export risks, increasing connections between domestic businesses and FDI businesses, supporting businesses in improving technological levels, and diversifying export markets.
 Sharing his experience of going global, Associate Professor Dr. Su Thanh Long, Director of the International Dairy Project at TH Group , said that the Group's mindset for going global was very clear from the beginning, having decided to apply the highest technical standards in the world. Therefore, the journey of exporting products was quite smooth.
 Another point emphasized by Mr. Long is that the Group's private interests are aligned with the common interests of the nation; the focus is not on maximizing profits but on harmonizing interests with the community and the environment.
 "Up to this point, TH has expanded into many global markets, not just simply exporting, but also transferring technology and scientific expertise. Most recently, Indonesia is paving the way for our businesses to expand there," Mr. Long said.

articles.title: Thailand to clarify 35% excise tax on EV imports for Japanese carmakers - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Thailand to clarify 35% excise tax on EV imports for Japanese carmakers  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas said the government would explain the details of its 35% excise tax on fully built imported electric vehicles (EVs) to foreign carmakers that have invested in manufacturing bases in Thailand.
The briefings follow Cabinet approval of the revised tax structure and will include Japanese manufacturers during an investment roadshow in Japan.
He explained that the measure had been drawn up in response to requests from all carmakers that have invested in Thailand.
It aims to ensure fair competition for investors that establish manufacturing bases and employ Thai workers, demonstrating the government’s commitment to supporting businesses that establish production bases and invest in the country.
The measure will take effect on Friday (January 1, 2027), giving automotive businesses time to adjust and manage existing stock.
“This measure is intended to ensure fairness, not only for Japanese investors but also for carmakers operating in Thailand that have invested in manufacturing bases and employed Thai workers. It is about ensuring fairness for them,” Ekniti said.
Reporters said Ekniti would lead the Thai delegation, known as Team Thailand, on the Japan roadshow from November 18 to 20, 2026.
Joining him will be representatives of the Board of Investment (BOI), the industry minister, the permanent secretary at the Ministry of Finance, the director-general of the Customs Department and representatives of the Joint Standing Committee on Commerce, Industry and Banking (JSCCIB), comprising the chairs of the Federation of Thai Industries (FTI), the Board of Trade of Thailand and the Thai Bankers’ Association.
More than 40 Thai businesspeople will also take part.
The delegation is scheduled to meet Japanese businesses across several industries, including senior executives from six Japanese carmakers with major manufacturing bases in Thailand: Toyota, Honda, Isuzu, Mitsubishi, Mazda and Nissan.
The meetings will be used to present the Thai government’s plans to support the automotive industry and discuss cooperation to improve the capabilities of Thai businesses in the automotive parts supply chain.
The delegation will also hear the companies’ investment plans, recommendations and approaches to supporting the transition to modern automotive technologies, with the aim of building confidence and strengthening long-term investment cooperation.

articles.title: Capital.com Secures MAS License Ahead of Singapore Launch in 2027 - Fintech Singapore
articles.summary: Capital.com Secures MAS License Ahead of Singapore Launch in 2027  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
Capital.com has secured a Capital Markets Services license from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), marking its entry into Southeast Asia.
The license, granted to its local entity Capital Com Securities (Singapore) Pte. Ltd., covers dealing in capital markets products, including securities and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives contracts.
The trading platform plans to begin onboarding clients in Singapore in early 2027.
Founded in 2016, Capital.com holds licenses in jurisdictions including the UK, the EU, the Middle East, Africa and Australia. Singapore is its first regulated market in Southeast Asia.
Capital.com prepares for Singapore launch
Ahead of onboarding, Capital.com is preparing its platform and local services to meet Singapore’s regulatory and operational requirements.
These include identity verification through Singpass MyInfo, full client verification before trading and mandatory two-factor authentication at sign-in.
Once onboarding begins, Singapore clients will have access to market insights and analysis, educational resources, charting tools and risk-management features such as stop-loss orders.
The platform will also provide in-app explanations of financial instruments and risk mechanisms to help users better understand their trading decisions.
“Singapore sets a high bar for how financial services are delivered, and the MAS licensing process examines every part of a firm’s governance, controls and capital,”
said Valentina Rzheutskaya, Executive Director, Capital.com.
“Holding a license here means operating to that standard locally, with supervision of how we onboard clients, communicate risk and safeguard client assets,”
she added.
Former IG Asia CEO to lead Singapore operations
Capital.com has appointed Tony Lim as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Director of its Singapore entity.
Lim has more than 30 years of experience in Singapore’s capital markets, having held roles at the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), Singapore Exchange, DBS Vickers Securities and Saxo Capital Markets.
He most recently served as Chief Executive Officer of IG Asia.
Capital.com has also opened an office at 9 Battery Road in Raffles Place, with local teams covering compliance, operations, client services and marketing.
“Our focus over the coming months is on getting the foundations right, from onboarding and client protections to the education and market insight that help people understand risk before they act,”
said Lim.

articles.title: Thailand reports 470 mpox cases, 3 deaths in first 10 months of 2026 - The Straits Times
articles.summary: Thailand reports 470 mpox cases, 3 deaths in first 10 months of 2026  The Straits Times
articles.full_text:
AI generated
BANGKOK – Thailand recorded 470 mpox cases and three deaths between Jan 1 and Oct 31, prompting its Department of Disease Control to urge people with suspicious symptoms to seek medical attention without delay.
Montien Kanasawadse, director-general of the department, reported the figures on Nov 3, emphasising the importance of early diagnosis, continued disease surveillance and measures to prevent further transmission.
He encouraged anyone who develops unusual rashes, blisters or sores, particularly after possible exposure to the virus, to consult a doctor and provide an accurate account of their symptoms and contact history.
Mpox remains a communicable disease subject to surveillance under Thailand’s Communicable Diseases Act 2015 and the Thai Ministry of Public Health’s 2022 notification on diseases requiring surveillance.
Mpox continues to spread internationally
Montien noted that mpox transmission remains a concern in several regions worldwide.
According to global figures cited by Thailand’s Department of Disease Control, 68,096 confirmed infections and 272 deaths were reported across 107 countries between Jan 1, 2025, and Aug 31.
The department attributed these figures to a World Health Organization (WHO) report published on Sept 14.

It stressed that the international figures cover a different reporting period from Thailand’s 2026 statistics.
Early symptoms may be difficult to recognise
Montien explained that mpox can affect anyone exposed to the virus, making awareness of its symptoms and transmission routes essential.
Early signs commonly include fever, headaches, back pain, muscle aches and swollen lymph nodes.
These may be followed by rashes or lesions on the skin, including the face, body, genitals and around the anus.
Some patients develop only a few lesions, while others may experience pain around the anus.
The skin changes can begin as raised red spots before developing into fluid-filled blisters, followed by pus-filled lesions and scabs. Crusting may begin in the centre of a lesion, and individual spots are often separate rather than clustered together.
However, the department emphasised that symptoms do not always appear in the same order, and patients may not experience every characteristic sign of the infection.
People should therefore seek medical advice if they notice unexplained rashes, blisters or sores, particularly following possible exposure, without waiting for the lesions to spread across their bodies.
Montien also addressed concerns that may prevent patients from requesting medical assistance.
Because lesions can appear in private areas of the body, some people may feel embarrassed or anxious about undergoing an examination.
Montien stressed that illness should not be a source of shame and encouraged patients to discuss their symptoms and exposure history openly with medical professionals.
Healthcare workers, he explained, would provide care with understanding while respecting patients’ privacy and maintaining confidentiality.
PCR testing needed to confirm infection
The Thai Department of Disease Control emphasised that mpox cannot be confirmed by examining a rash or photograph alone.
Its symptoms can resemble those of herpes, chickenpox or other skin infections, making clinical assessment and laboratory testing necessary.
Doctors consider patients’ symptoms and possible exposure history alongside laboratory findings.
The principal method of confirmation is a polymerase chain reaction test, which detects the virus’s genetic material in samples collected from skin lesions.
Routine blood tests cannot confirm mpox infection.
Patients whose initial assessment is inconclusive, or whose tests are negative despite continuing symptoms, should return for further medical evaluation if additional lesions develop or their condition changes.
They should also inform doctors of previous test results and treatment so that further examinations or repeat sampling can be considered when appropriate.
Most patients recover with supportive care
Direk Khampaen, deputy director-general of Thailand’s Department of Disease Control, said most people with mpox recover without requiring specialised treatment.
Medical care generally focuses on managing symptoms, relieving pain, preventing secondary infections in skin lesions and reducing the risk of complications.
However, people with weakened immune systems, pregnant women and young children face a greater risk of severe illness and require closer medical assessment.
Doctors will determine whether additional treatment or admission to hospital is necessary according to each patient’s condition.
Anyone experiencing severe pain, difficulty eating or drinking, lesions affecting the eyes or worsening symptoms should seek immediate medical attention.
Patients urged to avoid close contact
To reduce transmission, the department advised people to avoid direct contact with the skin or lesions of infected individuals.
Close physical contact and sexual activity with anyone showing suspicious symptoms should also be avoided.
Clothing, towels and bedding should not be shared, as contaminated objects can carry infectious material from bodily fluids or lesion scabs.
Those awaiting medical assessment or test results should separate themselves from others, avoid sexual activity and close contact, and keep any lesions covered.
They should also wash their hands regularly with soap or use 70% alcohol-based hand sanitiser and wear a well-fitting face mask.
The department explained that not every confirmed mpox patient needs hospital admission.
Doctors will assess the severity of symptoms, individual health risks and whether the patient can isolate safely at home.
Patients recovering at home should avoid travelling, use separate eating utensils and personal belongings, and clean their clothing and other frequently used items.
They must also follow medical advice and remain isolated until all lesions have healed, scabs have fallen off and new skin has formed. Lesions affecting mucous membranes must also have healed.
Montien reiterated that prompt medical assessment can help patients receive appropriate care while reducing the likelihood of passing the infection to others.
He also called on the public to avoid discrimination and stigma against people with mpox, stressing that respect for privacy is essential to ensuring equal access to healthcare. THE NATION/ASIA NEWS NETOWORK

articles.title: MAS’ Future of Finance Institute Begins Operations with AI Focus - Fintech Singapore
articles.summary: MAS’ Future of Finance Institute Begins Operations with AI Focus  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
The Future of Finance Institute (FFI) has begun operations, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) announced.
First announced in June 2026, the institute will initially focus on AI adoption in financial services through three programmes covering knowledge sharing, AI deployment and risk management.
FFI aims to support the adoption of emerging financial technologies by bringing together financial institutions, technology companies and researchers.
Its three programmes, PathFin.ai, BuildFin.ai and SafeFin.ai, will focus on sharing practical experience, developing tools and standards for AI deployment, and strengthening risk management practices, particularly for agentic AI.
PathFin.ai to support AI knowledge sharing
FFI will establish a Knowledge Hub under PathFin.ai to help financial institutions identify, evaluate and adopt AI solutions that meet their needs.
The institute will also create Communities of Practice involving professionals from banking, insurance, capital markets, financial advisory and payments.
Participants will share experiences and discuss common challenges in AI adoption through industry exchanges, webinars and learning journeys.
BuildFin.ai to develop AI tools and standards
Under BuildFin.ai, FFI will collaborate with financial institutions, technology companies and researchers to develop guidance, industry standards and shared tools for deploying AI, including agentic AI.
The programme will build on the Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) framework, which MAS developed with industry partners.
FFI will focus on developing practical safeguards and tools to support the safe use of AI agents in financial services.
SafeFin.ai to strengthen AI risk management
SafeFin.ai will bring financial institutions together to develop practical resources for implementing MAS’ Guidelines on AI Risk Management.
It will also enhance the MindForge AI Risk Management Toolkit to further address AI use case risk assessments, testing and assurance, and risks involving third-party AI.
MAS appoints interim CEO
MAS has appointed Alan Lim as FFI’s interim Chief Executive Officer. He will continue serving as Head, Financial Infrastructure and AI Office at MAS while overseeing the institute’s strategy and operations.
“FFI is a public-private platform for MAS, financial institutions, technology firms and the research community to pool expertise and collaborate in fast-moving technology areas such as AI. It will seek to anchor key capabilities in Singapore and connect the ecosystem to accelerate innovation and support safe adoption of new technologies,”
said Chia Der Jiun, Managing Director, MAS.
FFI plans to progressively expand its work beyond AI into other areas of financial innovation, including tokenisation.

articles.title: These Are the 10 Best Passports in the World for Visa-free Travel—and No. 1 Lets You Visit 163 Countries With Ease - Yahoo Lifestyle Singapore
articles.summary: These Are the 10 Best Passports in the World for Visa-free Travel—and No. 1 Lets You Visit 163 Countries With Ease  Yahoo Lifestyle SingaporeHow Are Passports Ranked ? Key Criteria Explained  Sarkaritel.com
articles.full_text:
Securing a visa before a foreign trip can be a time-consuming experience, sometimes requiring costly fees, complicated applications, or weeks-long waits. But if you have a United Arab Emirates passport, you can travel to 128 countries visa-free and obtain visas on arrival in 35 more, making it the best passport for visa-free travel in the world, according to a study by Passport Reports.
The online platform considers data on passport strength and global mobility to rank the destinations that "ordinary passport holders can enter and under what conditions," according to its methodology.
The United Arab Emirates topped the list with an overall mobility score of 173 out of 200, giving its passport holders easy access to 163 countries, as well as 10 more by an electronic travel authorization (ETA) form. Emiratis only need to apply for a visa in advance for 25 countries (including the U.S.), the fewest of any state in the study. According to Passport Reports, the United Arab Emirates' score has been rising since 2020, when it was ranked No. 28. The following year, it jumped to the top spot and has held that position for five consecutive years.
Singapore took the number two spot, with a passport mobility score of 164. While holders of Singaporean passports can travel to one more country than those in the United Arab Emirates (129), the number of countries that require a visa on arrival is significantly less, 24. Singaporeans need an ETA for 11 countries, while 34 more require advance visas. Singapore climbed 18 spots in 2025, from No. 18 to No. 2, maintaining its runner-up position this year as well.
Japan follows Singapore at No. 3, up eight spots from 2025. Its citizens don't need visas for 114 countries and can receive visas on arrival in 36 more. Japan's overall mobility score is 162. This is Japan's highest ranking; it has been on a steady rise since 2021, when it ranked No. 24. Japanese passport holders need an ETA for the U.S., U.K., and Canada, but can travel visa-free in the European Union. Malaysia (No. 4) and South Korea (No. 5) round out the top five passports for visa-free global travel.
The United States ranks significantly lower, at No. 28, with a mobility score of 153. American citizens can travel to 111 countries without a visa, but need an ETA for 10 and receive their visa on arrival in 32. U.S. passport holders need to apply for a visa to visit 45 countries. The United States has had a rough run since 2022, when it achieved its highest ranking at No. 12. Since then, American passports have been in decline, with the exception of 2025, when they climbed just one spot from 27 to 26, but then fell two spots this year.
Despite Asian countries occupying the first five spots, European passports dominate the top 10, with 11 countries sharing spots six through 10.
Below are the top 10 best passports for visa-free travel:
- United Arab Emirates
- Singapore
- Japan
- Malaysia
- South Korea
- Luxembourg
- Spain
- Switzerland
- Belgium, France
- Denmark, Finland, Sweden, Germany, Italy, Netherlands
