articles.summary: Việt Nam targets high-value investment to move up global value chain  vietnamnews.vn
articles.full_text:
| Deputy Finance Minister Lê Tấn Cận speaks at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit 2026 in HCM City on November 3. — Photo courtesy of the organiser | 
HCM CITY — Việt Nam is seeking to attract high-quality foreign investment in strategic technologies, research and development, and green and digital transformation, while strengthening links between foreign investors and domestic businesses, Deputy Finance Minister Lê Tấn Cận has said.
Addressing more than 250 business leaders, policymakers, and investors at the inaugural Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit in HCM City on November 3, he outlined Việt Nam's ambition to become a regional hub for innovation, advanced technology, and international finance as the country pursues double-digit economic growth and high-income status by 2045.
He said despite global economic and geopolitical uncertainties, Việt Nam had demonstrated resilience and maintained strong economic growth, with GDP expanding by 7-8 per cent in recent years on the back of manufacturing, services, and exports.
GDP grew by 9.01 per cent in the first nine months of 2026, providing a foundation for the country to pursue its target of double-digit annual growth during 2026-30, he said.
Việt Nam also continued to attract foreign direct investment, particularly in high-tech industries, semiconductors, and green energy, he said.
He emphasised the government's shift from attracting foreign investment primarily for manufacturing towards building an innovation ecosystem with stronger links between multinational companies and domestic enterprises.
"Việt Nam prioritises investors with foundational and core technologies, modern management capabilities, and commitments to technology transfer, green transformation, and digital transformation."
He outlined five priorities for cooperation with international investors: joint research and development in AI, semiconductors, biotechnology, and clean energy; investment in strategic sectors such as high technology, digital infrastructure, and modern logistics; stronger links between foreign investors and domestic businesses to build resilient value chains; development of skilled human resources and knowledge ecosystems; and cooperation in developing Việt Nam's international financial centres.
He underlined the government's commitment to strengthening the private sector, improving infrastructure and providing a stable and transparent investment environment, encouraging international companies to regard Việt Nam as a long-term partner in innovation and higher-value economic activities.
"We want foreign businesses and investors to see Việt Nam not only as a manufacturing location or consumer market, but also as a partner in research, technology innovation, product development and expansion into regional and global markets."
| Nguyễn Lộc Hà, Standing Vice Chairman of the HCM City People's Committee, speaks about the city's economic potential following its merger with Bình Dương and Bà Rịa-Vũng Tàu. — Photo courtesy of the organiser | 
Nguyễn Lộc Hà, Standing Vice Chairman of the HCM City People's Committee, highlighted the expanded city's economic significance following its merger with the former Bình Dương and Bà Rịa-Vũng Tàu provinces in July 2025.
With a population of more than 14 million and accounting for approximately 23.5 per cent of national GDP, HCM City is positioning itself as an internationally competitive centre for finance, technology, innovation, and trade, he said.
The city attracted more than US$19 billion worth of FDI in the first nine months of 2026, four times the figure recorded in the same period last year and accounting for more than 30 per cent of the national total.
Major projects included the Cần Giờ international transshipment port, with investment of more than $4.9 billion, and an AI Factory data centre project worth approximately $2.1 billion.
Beyond attracting large-scale projects, the city wanted to strengthen cooperation between international investors and domestic enterprises in manufacturing, research, and services to enable both export to regional markets and selling at home.
Priority areas include automation, AI, energy management, workforce training, an international financial centre, free trade zones, and logistics infrastructure.
Hà said the city hoped summit connections would lead to concrete cooperation plans and long-term investment projects.
Andrew Staples, Fortune's editorial director for Asia and co-chair of the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit, said Việt Nam's rapid economic growth is among the reasons his magazine chose HCM City to host the summit.
| Panelists at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit 2026 in HCM City on November 3. — Photo courtesy of the organiser | 
The region's 500 largest companies generated combined revenues of $1.9 trillion, up 3.4 per cent year on year. Việt Nam's 72 companies on the list recorded collective revenue growth of 10.5 per cent, three times the regional average, Staples pointed out.
Held with the theme “New Horizons, Enduring Growth,” the summit brings together leaders from banking, energy, manufacturing, technology, infrastructure, and other major industries to examine Southeast Asia's competitiveness and the rise of regional multinationals.
The programme features discussions on artificial intelligence, energy, regional connectivity, international finance, and the development of globally competitive businesses.
The programme also included the Fortune Most Powerful Women Asia Leaders Breakfast, the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Awards Ceremony, and the unveiling of Fortune's Best Companies to Work For in Southeast Asia list.
According to speakers, looking towards 2027, Southeast Asia is expected to maintain its growth momentum, supported by supply chain diversification, new investment, technology-driven exports and rising domestic consumption.
However, slowing global growth, US-China trade and technology tensions and energy market volatility remain key risks, they said.
Ted Osius, former US ambassador to Việt Nam, said global economic growth is forecast at arouond 2.7 per cent, possibly rising to 2.8 per cent in 2027, while Asia is expected to expand by 4.9 per cent.
He said Việt Nam is well positioned to benefit from supply chain shifts, supported by innovation-friendly policies, infrastructure development, and a young workforce increasingly familiar with AI.
As global supply chains are reconfigured, Southeast Asia, particularly Việt Nam, is attracting investment in electronics, semiconductors, electric vehicles, data centres, and advanced manufacturing.
But speakers stressed that attracting factories is only part of the challenge, and countries also need to use investment to strengthen domestic capabilities, develop competitive local businesses, and promote innovation.
Salil Chari, FedEx's president for Asia-Pacific, said Southeast Asia is becoming increasingly important in global trade networks. Trade between Việt Nam and Singapore and Malaysia had tripled, while Vietnamese businesses are seeking better integration of technology systems, including data centres, he added.
Thammasak Sethaudom, president and CEO of Siam Cement Group (SCG), highlighted growing competition from China's excess production capacity, which is bringing more competitively priced products into regional markets.
He said SCG is restructuring by consolidating smaller factories, expanding larger production facilities, and investing in automation to improve product quality and precision.
The company is also adopting a Southeast Asia-wide business strategy rather than focusing on individual national markets, he said.
Liher Urbizu, president and managing director of SAP Southeast Asia, said ASEAN was increasingly moving from being a technology user to becoming a technology creator, with substantial investments flowing into innovation centres across the bloc.
Speakers agreed that regional integration, automation, AI adoption, and long-term investment in domestic capabilities would be crucial for Southeast Asia to move up global value chains and remain competitive amid geopolitical uncertainty and changing trade patterns.— VNS

articles.title: Thailand to Raise Imported EV Taxes to 35% in Push to protect Local Production - Thailand Business News
articles.summary: Thailand to Raise Imported EV Taxes to 35% in Push to protect Local Production  Thailand Business News
articles.full_text:
BANGKOK — In a major policy intervention aimed at safeguarding domestic vehicle production and encouraging localized industrial investment, the Thai cabinet has approved substantial excise tax increases on imported battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and range-extended electric vehicles (REEVs), effective January 2027.
According to Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas, the excise tax rate on fully imported BEVs will rise sharply from 10% to 35%. Similarly, the tariff on imported REEVs will jump from 15% to 35%. The regulatory overhaul follows urgent warnings from domestic automotive industry groups, which cautioned that local manufacturers faced a severe competitive crisis due to an influx of low-cost Chinese imports under previous tax structures.
The strategic shift underscores the government’s determination to reinforce Thailand’s position as Southeast Asia’s primary automotive manufacturing and export hub—a market historically dominated by traditional Japanese original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) such as Toyota Motor, but increasingly shaped by global EV leaders like BYD.
Key Takeaways
- Significant Excise Tax Structure Shift: Excise taxes on fully imported BEVs and REEVs will increase to 35% starting in January, closing the price gap between foreign-built vehicles and locally assembled models.
- Protecting $4.5+ Billion in Capital Investments: The policy safeguards existing investments, supporting the Board of Investment’s (BOI) cumulative approval of $4.59 billion across 189 projects within the country’s EV ecosystem as of August 2026.
- Rapid Electrification Dynamics: Alternative powertrain vehicles—including BEVs, hybrids, and plug-in hybrids—accounted for 55% of all new car registrations in Thailand during the first seven months of 2026, surpassing internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles for the first time in history.
Market Implications and Economic Landscape
The updated tax policy signals a pivotal transition in Thailand’s EV roadmap from initial market penetration to localized industrialization. Early government incentives—such as direct price subsidies and lowered import tariffs—successfully catalyzed rapid consumer adoption. However, this surge in demand primarily benefited foreign assembly lines, putting immediate pressure on local supply chains and automotive component manufacturers.
By raising the barrier on completely built-up (CBU) imports, the Thai government is forcing foreign automakers to transition rapidly from importing finished vehicles to localized assembly (CKD operations). Global brands including BYD and Great Wall Motor, which have already committed substantial capital to local production facilities, stand to benefit relative to brands relying exclusively on cross-border shipments.
Chinese firms BYD and Great Wall Motor have invested in Thailand’s electric vehicle ecosystem. These investments are part of a larger wave of activity that has attracted over $4 billion into the sector.
BYD operates an electric vehicle manufacturing plant in Rayong, which began producing vehicles in 2024 and has an annual capacity of 150,000 units. Additionally, cumulative investment approvals for the electric vehicle ecosystem in Thailand reached $4.59 billion across 189 projects as of August 2026. The rise of these Chinese manufacturers has significantly increased their market share in the country, even as the government introduces new tax measures to encourage local production and protect existing supply chains.
For the local business landscape, this policy pivot offers critical support to domestic auto parts suppliers and protects employment within the manufacturing sector. As EVs now represent the majority of new vehicle registrations in the country, forcing localized production guarantees that supply chain value, technological transfer, and high-skilled labor opportunities remain within the domestic economy.

articles.title: Vietnam eyes opportunities amid supply chain shifts in Southeast Asia - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Vietnam eyes opportunities amid supply chain shifts in Southeast Asia  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Ho Chi Minh City (VNA) – Vietnam has a prime opportunity to attract investment in high-tech industries, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, data centres, and logistics, while enhancing its role in global value chains as Southeast Asia becomes an increasingly significant destination for international investment.
The issue was discussed by business leaders, experts, and international corporate representatives at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit, organised by Fortune magazine in Ho Chi Minh City on November 3.
Supply chains shift towards Southeast Asia 
Geopolitical tensions, trade protectionism, tariff changes and technological competition are prompting global businesses to adjust production, sourcing and investment strategies, diversify manufacturing locations and strengthen supply chain resilience. 
Thomas Knudsen, Executive Chairman of Toll Group, noted that supply chains are gradually shifting from traditional manufacturing hubs to Southeast Asia. He expects the trend of moving production from China to ASEAN to continue, supported by stronger regional connectivity and infrastructure development, as well as rising investment demands.
Building resilient supply chains requires flexible transport options, transit warehousing and better cross-border connectivity, he said, noting that the region's dynamism, expanding real-time payment systems and free trade agreements offer significant advantages.
However, to fully capitalise on its advantages, the region needs to strengthen its connectivity with global markets and establish effective links between the public and private sectors.
James Nesbitt, Managing Director and Head of Global Subsidiaries for Singapore and ASEAN at Standard Chartered, said businesses are diversifying suppliers and customer markets, increasing inventories and adjusting production methods to minimise supply chain disruptions, while security and political factors are increasingly influencing investment decisions and production organisation.
According to Thammasak Sethaudom, President and CEO of SCG, competition from excess manufacturing capacity in China is spreading across the region. Businesses need to expand production, leverage free trade agreements, cut costs and increase added value. He said automation could improve precision, product quality and resource efficiency, allowing companies to focus more on design, research and development.
Vietnam ready to welcome new waves of investment
To realise this goal, the country is focusing on building a new-generation investment ecosystem that connects foreign-invested enterprises with domestic businesses, while developing logistics, data and clean energy infrastructure and a high-quality workforce.
It aims to attract foreign investors as partners in technology research, innovation and product development, rather than merely producers for the domestic market. Priority areas include semiconductors, electronics, sustainable value chains and high-quality workforce training.
Nguyen Loc Ha, Standing Vice Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee, highlighted the city's strengths in finance, trade, services, industry, high-tech industrial parks and the Cai Mep – Thi Vai deep-water port, saying that these create favourable conditions for connecting production chains and development of logistics, trade and financial services.
In the first nine months of 2026, the city's GRDP grew 9.06%, while registered foreign investment exceeded 19 billion USD, four times the figure recorded in the same period last year and accounting for over 30% of the national total.
Ha said the southern metropolis seeks stronger links between investors and local businesses, suppliers, and partners in automation, AI, energy management and workforce training. It is also developing an international financial centre, free trade zones and logistics infrastructure.
Businesses stressed that opportunities from global supply chain shifts lie not only in attracting investment but also in converting it into technology, knowledge, production capacity and domestic added value, helping Vietnam boost competitiveness and strengthen its role in regional and global production and trade networks./.

articles.title: Enhancing investment efficiency through green transformation. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Enhancing investment efficiency through green transformation.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Green transformation becomes a competitive advantage.
 The target of achieving an average GDP growth rate of 10% or more per year during the 2026-2030 period requires the Vietnamese economy to make a shift in productivity, investment efficiency, and value-added creation capacity, instead of primarily relying on expanding input factors. In this process, sustainable development is not only an environmental requirement but is also directly linked to innovating the growth model, improving the quality of capital flows, and strengthening the competitiveness of businesses.
 The pressure for transformation becomes even more apparent as the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) enters its official implementation phase from January 2026, along with increasingly stringent environmental, social, and governance (ESG) requirements from international buyers. Meeting green standards is gradually becoming a condition for businesses to maintain orders, access markets, and participate in global supply chains.
 Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang emphasized the need to enhance endogenous capacity in human resources, technology, and management to capitalize on opportunities arising from the shift in global investment flows and supply chains. According to the Deputy Prime Minister, the selection of investment destinations is now based not only on cost advantages but increasingly prioritizes safety, adaptability, and long-term strategic linkages. Notably, digital transformation and green transformation are intertwined, reshaping production methods, market standards, and competitive advantages among countries. Along with the development of artificial intelligence, automation, and ESG standards, these changes require Vietnam to shift from exploiting traditional advantages to improving productivity, innovating technology, and enhancing value-added capabilities. 
|  | 
| Illustrative image created by AI | 
 From a business perspective, Thue Quist Thomasen, Chairman of NordCham Vietnam, believes that Vietnam not only needs to attract more foreign direct investment (FDI) but, more importantly, needs to improve the quality of capital flows, linking long-term investment with the development of domestic supplier capabilities and improving energy efficiency and emission control.
 The effectiveness of green transition needs to be reflected in substantive changes in production practices, rather than just commitments or ESG reports. Information disclosure does not equate to decarbonization; a well-prepared sustainability report does not automatically reduce the cost per unit of product or help a business win more orders.
 From an investment perspective, the requirement is not only to attract projects that meet green standards but also to assess their ability to generate long-term economic value. Energy-saving solutions, optimized raw materials, and technological improvements can help businesses reduce operating costs, increase production efficiency, and thereby improve investment effectiveness and competitiveness.
 International experience shows that economic growth and emission reduction are not necessarily two opposing goals. According to the Swedish Ambassador to Vietnam, Johan Ndisi, between 1990 and 2022, the Swedish economy grew by approximately 79% while greenhouse gas emissions decreased by more than 50%, linked to investment in innovation and clean technologies.
 In Vietnam, several Nordic businesses have applied green solutions in production and business, from electrifying seaports and using heat pump systems to improving the efficiency of industrial equipment. These solutions demonstrate that green transformation can create economic benefits through technological improvements, reduced operating costs, and increased productivity. “Green transformation is not the price to pay for competitiveness, but rather a driving force for competitiveness,” emphasized Johan Ndisi.
 Improving the quality of growth through efficient resource utilization.
 To achieve double-digit growth, the requirement is not only to increase the scale of investment but also to improve the efficiency of resource allocation and utilization. In a context where growth potential based on input factors is increasingly pressured, the quality of capital flows, labor productivity, and technological innovation capabilities will determine the sustainability of growth. This is also the basis for green transformation to become a driving force for economic development, rather than merely focusing on emission reduction.
 However, the green transition also presents businesses with the challenge of balancing initial investment costs with long-term economic benefits. Investments in energy-efficient equipment, process improvements, or the use of environmentally friendly materials only truly drive growth when they contribute to increased productivity, reduced operating costs, and enhanced product value. This requires businesses to evaluate the effectiveness of investments throughout the entire project lifecycle, rather than focusing solely on immediate costs or compliance requirements.
 Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, stated that , in the context of unpredictable geopolitical, trade, energy, technology, and climate risks, productivity, adaptability, resilience, and the capacity to create new value will increasingly determine the position of businesses and the economy. Traditional growth drivers such as capital expansion, labor, and production scale remain important, but Vietnam can hardly continue to rely solely on these factors. According to him, the question is no longer whether or not to transform, but how quickly and deeply to transform so that each investment in green, digital, and innovative technologies truly generates productivity, competitiveness, and new value.
 From this perspective, experts believe that improving the effectiveness of green investment depends not only on the technological innovation capabilities of each enterprise but also on the quality of the business environment and access to resources. Improving policy mechanisms, developing human resources, promoting innovation, and expanding green finance tools will contribute to reducing transition costs while encouraging projects that can create added value and long-term economic efficiency.
 In a strategy for double-digit growth, green transformation should be viewed as a driver of improving investment quality, rather than simply a requirement to comply with environmental standards. When investments contribute to improved productivity, resource conservation, and enhanced competitiveness, the benefits of green transformation will not only affect individual businesses but will also lay the foundation for sustainable economic growth.

articles.title: Vietnam's trade surplus accelerates in October - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam's trade surplus accelerates in October  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam's trade surplus widened sharply to $7.31 billion in October, significantly higher than the previous month's level. Two consecutive months of trade surpluses helped narrow the cumulative trade deficit in the first 10 months to $12.07 billion, bolstering expectations that the full-year 2026 deficit could fall below $10 billion.
A turning point for the trade balance
According to the National Statistics Office's report on the socioeconomic situation in October and the first 10 months of 2026, Vietnam's total merchandise trade was preliminarily estimated at $122.03 billion in October, up 3.7% from the previous month and 47.4% year-on-year.
Exports reached $64.67 billion, up 8.7% month-on-month and 51.4% year-on-year, while imports stood at $57.36 billion, down 1.4% from September but still up 43.1% from a year earlier.
The gap between exports and imports resulted in a merchandise trade surplus of $7.31 billion in October, significantly higher than the $1.3 billion recorded in September. This marked Vietnam's second consecutive month of trade surplus, indicating an improvement in the trade balance after several months of deficit.
In the first 10 months, total merchandise trade reached $1,010.55 billion, up 32.3% year-on-year. This was the first time Vietnam's trade turnover had exceeded the $1 trillion mark.
Exports totalled $499.24 billion, up 27.5%, while imports reached $511.31 billion, up 37.4%. As imports grew faster than exports, Vietnam still recorded a merchandise trade deficit of $12.07 billion, compared with a surplus of $19.49 billion in the same period last year.
The surpluses in September and, particularly, the sharp increase in October have therefore helped narrow the cumulative trade deficit considerably. However, this cannot yet be taken as evidence of a sustained reversal in the trade deficit trend, as import growth in the first 10 months remained nearly 10 percentage points higher than export growth.
Trade turnover exceeding $1 trillion reflects a strong expansion in international trade, but also highlights continued high demand for imports serving production, business activities and investment. As a result, the trade balance in the final two months of the year will depend not only on whether export momentum can be sustained but also on the composition and pace of import growth.
A test for the final two months of the year
At the Ministry of Industry and Trade's regular press briefing for the third quarter of 2026, Trinh Thu Hien, deputy director of the Import-Export Department, said the year-end peak export season provided grounds to expect the trade deficit in the final months and for the whole of 2026 to fall below $10 billion.
The forecast was made when the trade deficit in the first nine months remained close to $20 billion. The subsequent surpluses in two consecutive months, particularly October's $7.31 billion surplus, have strengthened the basis for that expectation.
However, for the full-year trade deficit to fall below $10 billion, Vietnam would need to record a net trade surplus of more than $2.07 billion in the final two months, based on the cumulative deficit of $12.07 billion after 10 months.
One favorable factor is the continued strong growth in exports. In October alone, export turnover rose 51.4% year-on-year, while the 10-month figure increased 27.5%. If orders and deliveries remain strong during the year-end peak season, exports will continue to play an important role in narrowing the trade deficit.
On the other hand, import pressures warrant continued monitoring. Import turnover rose 37.4% in the first 10 months, considerably faster than export growth. Although imports fell 1.4% month-on-month in October, they were still up 43.1% year-on-year. This indicates that pressure on the trade balance has not yet fully eased.
However, the trade deficit should not be assessed solely in terms of the size of the surplus or deficit, Nguyen Tuan Viet, CEO of Vietgo, a trade consulting company, told The Investor. He said a trade deficit over a given period could reflect the accumulation of domestic capacity if imports were used for investment, production-line upgrades and technological development.
According to Viet, it is important to distinguish between imports serving production, investment and technology upgrades and those that fail to generate commensurate added value.
"If we want to move fast, we need to import technology and gain access to and apply the world's most advanced technologies," he said.
When translated into new production capabilities, imported resources can lay the foundation for improving product quality and the competitiveness of domestic businesses.
This perspective suggests that improving the trade balance is not simply a matter of reducing imports to achieve a surplus. More important is improving the efficiency of imports, developing domestic production capacity and enabling Vietnamese businesses to participate more deeply in supply chains. These are also prerequisites for export growth to generate greater added value for the economy.
October's sharp increase in the trade surplus has brought Vietnam closer to its goal of keeping the full-year trade deficit below $10 billion, but the final two months will remain a crucial test. Alongside sustaining export momentum, the challenge will be to ensure that imports serving production and technological innovation translate into genuine competitiveness rather than simply expanding trade turnover.

articles.title: From ‘Made in Vietnam’ to ‘Trusted in Vietnam’: Why source-level inspection is becoming a new trade advantage - Theinvestor
articles.summary: From ‘Made in Vietnam’ to ‘Trusted in Vietnam’: Why source-level inspection is becoming a new trade advantage  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam is now one of the world’s 15 largest trading economies, with import-export turnover passing $930 billion in 2025. Yet scale alone no longer secures a place in global supply chains.
As buyers rewire their sourcing, they are putting harder questions to every supplier. Can you prove the product meets the standard? Can you prove how it was made? And can you prove it before the goods leave the factory gate?
For Vietnamese exporters, the answers increasingly decide who keeps an order and who loses it. The label “Made in Vietnam” says only where goods were produced. What buyers now want to know is whether the product, and the process behind it, can be trusted.
Where shipments fail
Failures in international trade rarely come from a single mistake. More often they stem from a chain of blind spots. A buyer may not know whether its counterparty is a genuine manufacturer or a trading intermediary, or whether the plant has the machinery and workforce for a large order.
Samples may deviate from agreed specifications, or quality may slip when production moves from sampling to mass output. Days before departure, a miscounted container, a wrong packaging specification or a labeling error can undo an entire contract.
The consequences tend to surface at the destination port, where they are most expensive to fix. A rejected consignment brings contractual penalties and the cost of reverse logistics or destruction. Most damaging of all, it can mean removal from a buyer’s approved vendor list.
The remedy is independent evidence of conformity gathered at each stage of production rather than at the end. Inspection at source turns quality control from a reactive check into a series of decision gates: factory audits, sample matching, during production (DUPRO) checks and pre-shipment Inspection (PSI). Each gate closes off a risk before cargo crosses the border.
A case in point
Consider a global fashion group producing millions of garments at factories in Nam Dinh and Dong Nai for the U.S. and EU markets. It had to respect strict limits on hazardous chemicals and demanding Acceptable Quality Limit (AQL) standards, while meeting delivery dates that could not slip. The buyer appointed Vinacontrol, Vietnam’s pioneering conformity assessment organization, as its independent inspection partner stationed on site.
Inspectors checked sample conformity, technical parameters, visual quality and color fastness, and drew random samples for chemical and physical testing in laboratories accredited to ISO/IEC 17025.
At the DUPRO stage, they found a color fastness non-conformity. The factory reprocessed the batch before mass production began, averting estimated losses of several hundred thousand dollars that would have followed had finished goods been rejected or destroyed at the destination port.
Not only for the large
Global brands can afford resident inspectors. Smaller exporters, which make up the bulk of Vietnamese suppliers, often see such arrangements as out of reach. The arithmetic suggests otherwise. The fee for a staged inspection is typically a fraction of the cost of a single rejected container, before counting the lost relationship with the buyer.
A practical path is incremental. A smaller manufacturer can begin with a factory assessment and pre-shipment inspection on its highest-risk orders, then add in-production checks as volumes and buyer expectations grow. Depending on the scope and complexity of the assignment, a quality inspection may cost from several dozen to several hundred US dollars; for larger export orders, that can amount to less than 1% of the contract value, while giving suppliers a chance to catch non-conformities before the goods leave the factory.
Beyond quality: ESG and digital traceability
Buyers no longer ask only whether a product is safe and well made. They want evidence on labor conditions, environmental performance and the origin of raw materials. Source inspection increasingly covers these questions alongside product quality.
Digitalization is accelerating the shift. Electronic inspection reports, QR-code traceability and data shared with buyers in near real time are replacing paper certificates that arrive after the fact. Exporters able to supply such records on demand will be better placed as digital product passports and similar requirements spread.
A national asset
Vietnam’s trade agreements, including the EVFTA and the CPTPP, offer preferential market access, but only to goods that satisfy destination-market standards. Domestic capacity to test, inspect and certify therefore becomes a strategic asset rather than a back-office function.
Vinacontrol, for instance, operates more than 40 branches and international-standard laboratories across major industrial hubs, allowing manufacturers to obtain recognized evidence without sending samples abroad. Its experts also act as technical partners, advising on market entry, operational discipline and continuous quality improvement.
The larger prize is reputational. If “Made in Vietnam” describes geography, “Trusted in Vietnam” describes a track record that can be verified. Building it would help the country move beyond contract manufacturing toward higher-margin segments of the value chain.
What exporters can do now
1. Assess factories early. Confirm that partners are genuine manufacturers with the capacity to deliver, before orders are placed.
2. Inspect in stages. Use sample matching, DUPRO and PSI as decision gates, not as formalities.
3. Keep the paper trail. Retain test reports and inspection records, since they are the main defense in a technical dispute.
4. Track the rules. Monitor application dates and requirements in each destination market, and agree on documentation with buyers in advance.
In an environment where trust is demanded in writing, inspection at source is shifting from a compliance cost to a competitive engine. Exporters that can show their work, independently and in time, will be the ones that keep their place in the world’s supply chains.
More information on Vinacontrol’s inspection solutions is available on the company’s website.

articles.title: Vietnam's trade turnover tops $1 trillion for first time - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Vietnam's trade turnover tops $1 trillion for first time  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
Vietnam's total trade turnover exceeded $1 trillion for the first time in the first 10 months of 2026, driven by strong demand for electronics and manufactured goods, official data showed on Tuesday.
Exports and imports reached a combined $1,010.6 billion between January and October, up 32.3% year-on-year, according to the National Statistics Office under the Finance Ministry.
Exports rose 27.5% to $499.2 billion, while imports increased 37.4% to $511.3 billion. Shipments of computers and electronic components surged 71% to $149.4 billion, making them a major driver of export growth. Exports of machinery and equipment increased 30.4% to $63.3 billion.
Foreign-invested companies accounted for 81.2% of exports, worth $405.3 billion, highlighting the country's reliance on overseas manufacturers.
Meanwhile, imports of production materials and equipment made up 94.1% of total imports.
China remained Vietnam's largest import source, with shipments worth $212.5 billion. Vietnam recorded trade surpluses of $140.1 billion with the United States and $40.8 billion with the European Union.
The latest figures come as Vietnam seeks to strengthen its manufacturing base and diversify export markets amid growing uncertainty over global trade and supply chains.

articles.title: The real estate market under the impact of macroeconomic growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The real estate market under the impact of macroeconomic growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The sustained positive macroeconomic growth is creating further impetus for the recovery and development of the real estate market. Notably, in the third quarter of 2026, the national economy achieved a growth rate of 9.95%, creating an important foundation to strengthen market confidence, improve demand, and unlock investment flows.
Economic growth provides a foundation for the market.
According to the General Statistics Office, GDP in the third quarter of 2026 increased by 9.95% compared to the same period last year, higher than the 8.15% increase in the first quarter and the 8.81% increase in the second quarter. For the first nine months of 2026, GDP increased by 9.01%. It is assessed that the economic growth in the third quarter of 2026 is not only an indicator of the recovery of economic activities, but also contributes to creating a more favorable environment for investment, business, and consumption decisions. In particular, given the difficulties experienced by the real estate market, the improvement in the macroeconomic situation will provide an important foundation for gradually restoring liquidity and boosting transaction activities.
Along with stable macroeconomic growth, investment and asset accumulation continue to accelerate. Specifically in the third quarter of 2026, asset accumulation increased by 21.39%, and final consumption increased by 8.96% compared to the same period last year. These figures reflect the improvement in demand and investment activity in the economy. Foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows also contribute to strengthening market prospects. According to data from the Ministry of Finance , in the first nine months of 2026, total registered FDI in Vietnam reached US$50.4 billion, an increase of 76.4% compared to the same period last year, with implemented capital reaching US$21.1 billion, an increase of 12.1%. This is a crucial resource driving demand for the development of industrial, logistics, office, and residential real estate in localities with production and business activities and attracting foreign experts.
In particular, in the first nine months of 2026, the disbursement rate of public investment capital reached approximately 64% of the plan (about VND 644,000 billion). The boost in public investment not only directly stimulates economic growth but also has a ripple effect on the real estate market, giving real estate businesses more opportunities to access resources, implement projects, and fulfill financial obligations, strengthening the confidence of people and investors when deciding to buy a house.
However, from the perspective of financial expert Nguyen Quang Huy, the positive impact of macroeconomic factors on real estate is not uniform or immediate. High GDP growth is a necessary but insufficient condition to guarantee a comprehensive market recovery. The ability to absorb products also depends on price levels, lending interest rates, people's income, appropriate supply, and the financial health of businesses. This is also why the current market shows a clear differentiation between segments, regions, and product groups.
You may also like
The market is recovering selectively.
According to a report by the Ministry of Construction , in the third quarter of 2026, the whole country recorded approximately 92,000 successful real estate transactions, equivalent to 92% compared to the previous quarter. The inventory in 27 out of 34 localities was reported at around 51,950 houses and land plots. These figures show that transaction activity remains sustained, but absorption has not yet truly broken through.
Regarding this issue, financial expert Nguyen Quang Huy believes that the market is entering a recovery phase with higher demands for supply quality and investment efficiency. After a period of rapid growth, homebuyers and investors are becoming increasingly cautious in choosing products. Factors such as project legality, developer reputation, construction progress, construction quality, exploitation potential, and cash flow generation potential are receiving more attention. Conversely, products with selling prices far exceeding their usability value, heavily dependent on expected price increases, or lacking exploitation potential will face difficulties.
“Although the macroeconomic environment is providing positive momentum, the housing market still faces the challenge of balancing supply and demand. Housing demand in major cities is very high, but access to housing for a segment of the population remains limited due to high prices relative to income. If supply continues to be concentrated in the high-end segment, lacking affordable products, the improvement in the economy may not necessarily translate into corresponding purchasing power in the apartment market,” Mr. Huy analyzed.
According to Dr. Tran Xuan Luong, a real estate market research expert, the current period demands a change in the development strategy of businesses. Restructuring investment portfolios and focusing resources on projects with complete legal documentation, practical implementation potential, and products that meet market demand will help businesses enhance their resilience to market fluctuations.
You may also like
At the same time, efforts to remove legal obstacles for projects need to be further accelerated. This is a crucial solution to unblock supply, free up land resources, and limit prolonged project delays that cause waste. When eligible projects are implemented, the market will have more products, buyers will have more choices, and businesses will have the opportunity to improve cash flow and reinvest.
Furthermore, Dr. Tran Xuan Luong believes that controlling capital flows into the real estate sector is also a matter of particular concern at present. Credit should be directed towards feasible projects that meet actual needs and have the potential to create value for the economy, thus contributing to ensuring the safety of the financial system. The State needs to have mechanisms to encourage credit institutions to develop home loan products that suit the financial capabilities of the people, especially young people and those with middle incomes.
“The development of the real estate market needs to be more closely linked to socio-economic development strategies, urban planning, and infrastructure investment. The formation of satellite urban areas, new economic centers, industrial zones, and development corridors will open up opportunities for the market, while contributing to the redistribution of population, labor, and investment resources. This is also an opportunity for real estate to shift from a growth model heavily based on land value to a development model based on construction quality, amenities, exploitation potential, and added value,” Dr. Tran Xuan Luong observed.

articles.title: Carlsberg underscores long-term investment at Nordic-Vietnam Business Summit - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Carlsberg underscores long-term investment at Nordic-Vietnam Business Summit  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
At the Nordic-Vietnam Business Summit 2026, Carlsberg Vietnam highlighted how sustained investment, resource-efficient production and local capability development can turn stronger bilateral ties into lasting business and economic value.
As Vietnam deepens economic cooperation with the Nordic countries, the focus is increasingly shifting towards the broader contribution of international investment to the country's development. Beyond expanding production capacity, long-term investment can generate lasting value by improving productivity, transferring expertise and strengthening local business capabilities.
These priorities were central to discussions at the Nordic-Vietnam Business Summit 2026, held in Ho Chi Minh City on October 29, where Carlsberg Vietnam participated as a strategic partner. Organized by NordCham Vietnam and its partners as part of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026, the summit examined how stronger international ties can foster investment, technology cooperation and sustainable growth.
Representing Carlsberg Vietnam, Peter Wachenschwanz, senior director of Integrated Supply Chain, joined representatives from APM Terminals and Phuc Sinh Corporation in a leadership dialogue titled “Turning Momentum into Action for the Next Chapter of Nordic–Vietnam Cooperation.”
As a long-term Danish investor, Carlsberg shared its perspective on how sustained investment in operational efficiency, sustainability and local capabilities can strengthen its business while contributing to Vietnam’s sustainable growth.
Building on the momentum of the state visit
The summit followed the state visit to Denmark by Vietnam’s Party General Secretary and President To Lam from October 19 to 21, which marked the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations and the elevation of bilateral ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
Shared priorities in investment, technology and the green transition are providing a stronger foundation for businesses to pursue projects that deliver long-term value.
For Carlsberg, the visit was an opportunity to reaffirm Vietnam’s importance as one of the group’s key growth markets. Group CEO Jacob Aarup-Andersen took part in high-level discussions with Vietnam’s senior leadership and presented Letters of Intent to the chairmen of the People’s Committees of Hue and Danang, setting out the group’s investment and development intentions for 2026-2031.
These include approximately $65 million in intended investment at Phu Bai Brewery in Hue city, focused on modernizing production, advancing digital and green transformation, improving resource efficiency, and strengthening quality, food safety and supply-chain capabilities.
In Danang, the company’s intentions encompass commercial development, digital transformation, operational modernization and more efficient, sustainable logistics, alongside environmental and community initiatives. Subject to relevant approvals, these plans would build on Carlsberg’s established presence in central Vietnam and strengthen its manufacturing and commercial capabilities in the region.
Peter Wachenschwanz, senior director of Integrated Supply Chain at Carlsberg Vietnam, said during the discussion: “Long-term investment creates lasting value when technology, people and partnerships develop together. For Carlsberg Vietnam, the next phase is about building on our expanded capacity to operate more efficiently and sustainably. Combining our global experience with Vietnamese expertise helps us strengthen our business while contributing to Vietnam’s long-term competitiveness.”
Putting Nordic-Vietnam cooperation into practice
Carlsberg Vietnam’s Phu Bai Brewery illustrates how sustained investment can drive production growth while improving operational efficiency.
The nearly $90 million expansion, inaugurated in August 2025, increased the brewery’s annual capacity by more than 50%, making Phu Bai the largest beer production facility in Carlsberg Asia and reinforcing Vietnam’s role in the group’s regional operations.
Alongside the capacity increase, the new brewing line uses approximately 20% less water and 15% less energy than its predecessor. A rooftop solar project is expected to meet up to 10% of the brewery’s electricity needs, supporting its transition to renewable energy.
Real-time performance dashboards enable teams to monitor production-line efficiency and maintain consistent quality. Meanwhile, a fully electric forklift fleet and AI-enabled cameras contribute to cleaner and safer operations.
Creating value beyond the brewery
The discussion also highlighted how the benefits of investment can extend across domestic supply chains. Wachenschwanz emphasized the importance of looking beyond the brewery gates and working with local suppliers and logistics partners to improve efficiency, quality and sustainability.
For Nordic-Vietnam cooperation, these partnerships provide a practical way to combine international technology and operational experience with Vietnamese business capabilities. Knowledge sharing, technical cooperation and skills development can help local partners meet evolving requirements and participate more effectively in global supply chains.
Predictable policies, clear implementation requirements and effective coordination between businesses and authorities are essential to realizing these opportunities. Such conditions help companies turn investment intentions into viable projects and coordinate improvements across manufacturing, energy and logistics.
After more than three decades in Vietnam, Carlsberg aims to build on its established manufacturing presence and long-standing local partnerships through continued investment in its operations, people and partnerships. This approach aligns the group’s growth ambitions with Vietnam’s development goals and brings its purpose of brewing for a better today and tomorrow to life.

articles.title: Leading Trade Economist Professor Davin Chor Appointed MAS Term Professor at NUS - Monetary Authority of Singapore
articles.summary: Leading Trade Economist Professor Davin Chor Appointed MAS Term Professor at NUS  Monetary Authority of Singapore
articles.full_text:
Singapore, 5 November 2026… The National University of Singapore (NUS) and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) have jointly appointed Professor Davin Chor as the MAS Term Professor in Economics and Finance from 5 to 11 November 2026. Professor Chor will be hosted by the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy (LKYSPP) at NUS and the Economic Policy Group of MAS during the term of the Professorship. 
2	Professor Chor is the Michael G. Fisch 1983 Professor and Globalisation Chair at the Tuck School of Business, Dartmouth College, and Research Associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER). A Singaporean economist, he received his PhD in Economics from Harvard University. He is widely recognised as a leading scholar in international trade and political economy and currently serves as Associate Editor of the Journal of International Economics. 
3	Professor Chor's work focuses on international trade and political economy. His recent research examines the economic and political effects of US-China tariffs and the reallocation of US supply chain trade. Notably, a paper he co-authored, examining the shift in direct US sourcing from China towards other countries was presented at the 2023 Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium. He has published in leading journals including Econometrica, and the Journal of International Economics and co-authored the chapter on global value chains in the Handbook of International Economics.
4	Professor Joseph Liow, Dean of the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, said, “Professor Davin Chor is widely recognised for his groundbreaking contributions to the study of global value chains and international trade. His research has provided the field with foundational tools and insights that have transformed how scholars and policymakers understand the dynamics of global production and the forces shaping today’s shifting trade landscape. We are delighted to welcome him to LKYSPP, where his insights will enrich our faculty’s research and our students’ understanding of these critical issues.”
5	Mr Edward Robinson, Deputy Managing Director (Economic Policy) and Chief Economist, MAS, said, “Professor Chor’s research has advanced our understanding of how global production networks shape trade and economic activity. His expertise is especially valuable as trade tensions and geopolitical developments prompt firms to reassess their supply chains. As an open economy deeply integrated into global supply chains, Singapore stands to benefit from his insights into the risks and opportunities of shifts to the global trading system. It is our great privilege to welcome him as the 26th MAS Term Professor.” 
6	Professor Chor will deliver a public lecture at NUS on 6 November 2026 titled, "US-China Trade at a Crossroads: Reflections on the Outlook for China’s Growth”. In his lecture, he will offer a glimpse at how China has been doubling down on exports as a growth engine, even though this may ultimately not be a sustainable strategy. In addition, Professor Chor will engage in dialogue sessions with NUS faculty members to discuss his latest research findings. 
7	Professor Chor will also give a talk at MAS and engage senior policymakers and economists on issues in international trade, global supply chains and the impact of globalisation.
About the MAS Term Professorship in Economics and Finance
First established in 2009, the MAS Term Professorship in Economics and Finance is awarded to distinguished scholars, who are appointed as Visiting Professors at the Department of Economics at the NUS Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences, the NUS Business School, or the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy. It aims to strengthen Singapore’s financial and economics research infrastructure and contribute to a vibrant research community and culture at local universities. Since its inception, the MAS Term Professorship in Economics and Finance has been awarded to 26 distinguished scholars over the last 17 years.
*****
About National University of Singapore (NUS)
The National University of Singapore (NUS) is Singapore’s flagship university, which offers a global approach to education, research and entrepreneurship, with a focus on Asian perspectives and expertise. We have 15 colleges, faculties and schools across three campuses in Singapore, with more than 40,000 students from 100 countries enriching our vibrant and diverse campus community. We have also established more than 20 NUS Overseas Colleges entrepreneurial hubs around the world.
Our multidisciplinary and real-world approach to education, research and entrepreneurship enables us to work closely with industry, governments and academia to address crucial and complex issues relevant to Asia and the world. Researchers in our faculties, research centres of excellence, corporate labs and more than 30 university-level research institutes focus on themes that include energy; environmental and urban sustainability; treatment and prevention of diseases; active ageing; advanced materials; risk management and resilience of financial systems; Asian studies; and Smart Nation capabilities such as artificial intelligence, data science, operations research and cybersecurity.
For more information on NUS, please visit nus.edu.sg .
About Monetary Authority of Singapore
As Singapore’s central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) promotes sustained, non-inflationary economic growth through appropriate monetary policy formulation and close macroeconomic surveillance of emerging trends and potential vulnerabilities. It manages Singapore's exchange rate, foreign reserves and liquidity in the banking sector. MAS is also an integrated supervisor overseeing all financial institutions in Singapore — banks, insurers, capital market intermediaries, financial advisors, and financial market infrastructures. Being an integrated supervisor allows MAS to adopt a consistent and progressive regulatory and supervisory approach and framework, thereby ensuring a level playing field across all market segments, sectors and activities. With its mandate to foster a sound and progressive financial services sector in Singapore, MAS also helps shape Singapore’s financial industry by promoting a strong corporate governance framework and close adherence to international accounting standards. In addition, it spearheads retail investor education. MAS ensures that Singapore’s financial industry remains vibrant, dynamic and competitive by working closely with other government agencies and financial institutions to develop and promote Singapore as a regional and international financial centre.
For more information, please visit www.mas.gov.sg .

articles.title: From tiny bowls to banana leaves: the food ideas Tony Lim leaves behind - Free Malaysia Today
articles.summary: From tiny bowls to banana leaves: the food ideas Tony Lim leaves behind  Free Malaysia TodayBoat Noodle, BananaBro founder Tony Lim passes away  The StarBananaBro and Boat Noodle founder Tony Lim dies at 47, Lifestyle News  AsiaOne.com'We will miss your smile': Boat Noodle founder Tony Lim dies at 47  NST OnlineLogistics Chaser To Cash King: How Late BananaBro Founder Cracked Malaysia’s Cross-Cultural Food Code  TRP | The Rakyat Post
articles.full_text:
His death was announced on Monday, prompting tributes to an entrepreneur who had a knack for spotting an established food tradition and finding a fresh way to present it.
Here are four things worth knowing about the ideas that shaped the businesses he left behind.
1. Small bowls can create large appetite
Lim launched Boat Noodle in Malaysia in 2014 after being inspired by the small bowls of noodles he had eaten in Thailand. The father of two told Vulcan Post that boat noodles was one of the foods he most enjoyed in Bangkok, where his wife is from.
The first outlet was a tiny space in Empire Damansara in Selangor – but it did not stay quiet for long. Diners queued for the noodles and began stacking their empty bowls into increasingly ambitious towers for photographs.
Lim later recalled that one of the early outlets sold as many as 8,000 bowls in a single day, and that the bowl-stacking craze had given the fledgling business a considerable boost.
There was a practical Malaysian consideration to his concept as well: Lim said traditional versions in Thailand can contain animal blood in the broth, so his Malaysian outlets instead offer a halal version.
2. Going bananas, bro
Four years later, Lim turned his attention from Thai noodles to banana leaf rice.
According to an early profile, the idea grew out of a cycling trip around Malaysia with two friends. A banana leaf rice meal in mainland Penang made such an impression that they persuaded the proprietor of that eatery to move to KL and become head chef of the new venture.
The first BananaBro outlet opened at Berjaya Times Square in 2018. Lim later told media that the aim was to offer a consistent menu in a bright, comfortable environment while keeping the food quick and affordable.
Then came one of the more wonderfully ridiculous chapters in the business’s history: an April Fool’s joke advertising a banana-leaf-shaped blanket proved so popular online that the blanket was actually produced!
The gag drew 1.3 million views and more than 11,000 interactions, and personalised versions were eventually sent to fans. The “Banana Leaf Blankie” even went on to win at the 2024 Kancil Awards.
3. Food was not his original profession
Lim was trained as an automotive engineer and worked in his family’s logistics and transportation business before moving into food and beverage.
His first taste of the F&B business came in 2012, when he helped his sister set up a Chatime franchise in Cambodia. A few years later came the boat noodles and banana leaf rice – hardly the most obvious career path for someone with his original background.
In a 2019 interview with Astro Awani, Lim described himself “not as a chef trying to become a businessman, but as a businessman trying to become a chef”.
4. Malaysians love their boats and banana leaves
On the surface, tiny bowls of Thai noodles and a sprawling banana leaf meal have almost nothing in common. Yet Lim approached both in much the same way: take a favourite form of dining, preserve what makes the food recognisable, then rethink the experience around it.
The formula clearly connected with Malaysians. By the time of his passing, there were 49 Boat Noodle outlets and more than 40 BananaBro branches across the country.
The banana leaf biz alone had passed 30 outlets by 2023 and recorded RM70 million in revenue that year, according to BFM.
While Lim’s culinary career has sadly been cut short, it demonstrated something warm and familiar about Malaysia’s food culture. Dishes travel, traditions evolve – and sometimes an entrepreneur’s contribution is simply to see old ideas through fresh eyes.

The Indonesian citizens were initially offered jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but when arriving in Russia, were told to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, undergo training and potentially be deployed to conflict zones.
JAKARTA: Indonesian authorities have uncovered a human trafficking syndicate involving 58 citizens who were allegedly recruited to work as mercenaries in Russia.
Thirteen people have been named as suspects, including two Russians and a Ukrainian citizen, the National Police Criminal Investigation Department (Bareskrim Polri) said on Monday (Nov 2).
Nurul Azizah, director of Bareskrim Polri's directorate of crimes against women and children and human trafficking, said at a press conference that the perpetrators used social media, job portals and messaging apps to lure victims with promises of lucrative overseas employment, state news agency Antara reported.
“We are coordinating through the Indonesian National Police’s International Relations Division and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Everything is still under further review,” Nurul said in response to CNA's queries on Tuesday.
The victims were initially offered jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after going through the recruitment process and being dispatched to Russia, they would be directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, undergo training and potentially be deployed to conflict zones.
“It is true that they did not directly offer jobs as mercenaries, but rather as logistics workers,” Nurul told reporters in Jakarta on Monday, as quoted by Kompas.
The victims were promised signing bonuses of up to US$35,000 and monthly salaries of around US$3,000.
Rita Wulandari Wibowo, director of Women and Child Protection at Metro Jaya Regional Police, said that recruiters also promised some victims child allowances of more than 3 million rupiah along with other benefits, Kompas reported.
“But in reality, none of these promises were fulfilled; the actual values were significantly lower, with some victims yet to receive any payments to this day,” Rita said on Monday.
The 58 individuals were identified after five police reports were made. Bareskrim Polri, together with the West Jakarta Metropolitan Police, Metro Jaya Regional Police and the Bogor Police, are investigating.
In a case investigated by the Bogor Police, victims were temporarily housed at a facility in Sukamantri Village in Bogor, with two suspects, identified by the initials FIK and STH, responsible for overseeing the victims’ living arrangements while they awaited departure.
Another suspect identified as MBH served as the financier throughout this process, covering recruitment expenses, lodging fees, medical check-ups, daily food costs and travelling arrangements, Kompas reported.
Additional reporting by Kiki Siregar

articles.title: Post midterm elections, Asia faces a more constrained but no less unpredictable Trump - The Straits Times
articles.summary: Post midterm elections, Asia faces a more constrained but no less unpredictable Trump  The Straits TimesTrump’s defeat in the midterms will reshape Asean and East Asia — Phar Kim Beng  Newswav
articles.full_text:
News analysis
Post midterm elections, Asia faces a more constrained but no less unpredictable Trump
AI generated
COLUMBIA, SOUTH CAROLINA – If there’s a trillion-dollar question hanging like haze in the skies over the United States and Asia, it’s probably related to President Donald Trump’s post-midterm avatar.
Will he just focus on his golf courses and the White House ballroom remodelling projects since he is now officially a lame duck?
Or will he march down the legacy road, take even more aggressive actions to carve out his name in history?
And, just as likely, get buried under a barrage of Democratic-initiated investigations and lawsuits?
Or will it just be business as usual?
The answers will come soon enough.
Trump will convene a meeting of the world’s largest economies, by virtue of the US hosting the G-20 leaders’ summit on Dec 14 to 15.
Before this, he is scheduled to visit Manila, from Nov 16 to 18, for the annual ASEAN summit. Immediately afterwards is the two-day Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping for their third meeting this year, the second in China.
Which Trump will show up? A president more willing to strike deals or more keen to establish that he remains in charge?
After the Nov 3 midterm elections, which ended the rule of the unified Republican government, the Democrats are taking control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate when the new Congress convenes in January.
The newly empowered opposition is expected to challenge the administration’s priorities, obstruct legislation and launch investigations of the Trump administration on various fronts, from the legality and justification of military strikes in Iran to the Trump family’s foreign business dealings.
Joseph Chinyong Liow, the dean and professor in East Asian Affairs at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, expects a long spell of unpredictability.
“I would be very surprised if President Trump takes a reconciliatory turn in his politics,” Liow said. “More likely he will double down to assert his presidential authority over both chambers,” he added.
For Asia’s export-driven economies, the central concern circles around Trump’s sweeping, volatile tariff regime enacted within months of his inauguration even as the US threatens even more tariffs under some ongoing investigations.
The midterm defeat will not give way to a rollback of Trump’s signature economic policy, although some Democratic leaders had vowed to repeal tariffs on goods from Canada, among the US’ largest trade partners.
But the President could simply veto any bid to restrict or repeal his tariff powers. Overriding the veto would require two-thirds support in both chambers, in other words, substantial Republican backing.
Democratic lawmakers can also be expected to bear down on Trump’s handling of the eight-month-old Iran war, in part to address the higher petrol and diesel prices that riled up voters. Heavily reliant on Middle Eastern energy imports, Asia is closely watching for signals on post-midterm oil prices.
Bob McNally, president of the Rapidan Energy Group, a leading energy market and geopolitical risk research firm, said he was not expecting a decline in oil prices in the short run.
“The elections themselves should not have a big impact on oil prices, which will be driven mainly by perceived and actual interplay of diplomacy and military escalation between the US and Iran,” he said.
Oil had slumped before the election in hopes of a diplomatic deal. But McNally said he had not revised the odds favouring military escalation in the coming weeks.
Over a longer timeframe, oil prices could go higher if the Democrats dismantle policies under Trump’s energy dominance agenda, said an oil industry source. Those efforts opened access to vast federal lands, accelerated drilling approvals and removed environmental oversight.
Also scrutinised will be the windfall gains, in excess of US$130 billion (S$166 billion), which oil majors made after the Iran war.
New restrictions are also likely on the growth of data centres to address voter backlash against rising utility costs, noise pollution and distrust of the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence. These will impact production at Asian tech companies, mainly in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, that supply the critical hardware that powers America’s AI buildout.
Greater oversight of AI, likely in the form of new probes by congressional committees against AI giants, will add compliance hurdles for Asian developers. But it could also stimulate Asia’s own sovereign AI push.
Analysts also expect the heat to turn up on pharmaceutical companies, including in Asia, that have made drug-pricing deals with the Trump administration.
China or Asia did not show up as a major issue in the exit polls of voters, said US economist Stephen Roach, the former chairman of Morgan Stanley Asia.
But he expected the Democratic leadership in the US Congress to take a firm stance on China.
“I would look to the China policy of the Biden administration as a template – creating a source of tension with Trump’s endorsement of ‘constructive strategic stability’,” said Roach. The phrase, adopted in May to describe the new framing of the US-China relationship to manage their rivalry, could come under attack.
The Biden administration enacted some of the most restrictive conditions on exports of advanced semiconductors and chipmaking equipment to China while also raising tariffs on strategic industries like China-made electric vehicles.
But the fundamentals of the US-China relationship will remain largely on the current trajectory, argued Han Shen Lin, the Shanghai-based China managing director for The Asia Group, a strategic advisory.
“The Republican setback tempers Trump’s negotiating leverage and constrains his room for manoeuvre, but Washington’s strategic concerns over China are firmly bipartisan,” Lin said.
“Policy recalibrations: yes. Fundamental change: no.”
Tariffs may become more negotiable but technology restrictions – particularly around semiconductors and AI – are too rooted in national security and unlikely to ease significantly, he said.
Still, the next two years in US-Asia interactions will hit different.
Beijing may see some political opportunity, said Lin, but it won’t mistake electoral turbulence for American decline.
“While Xi can approach Shenzhen from a position of even greater confidence, he’ll likely seek greater predictability and leverage rather than a grand bargain,” he said.
“At the G-20, I expect China to project stability and portray Washington as increasingly unpredictable,” he added.
Frederick Kempe, president of the Atlantic Council, said things could also take a dangerous turn. Xi might wager there is “no better time than the next two years to seize regional opportunities,” he said.
“Xi may increase his military probes around Taiwan, responding to a president who has shown a willingness to provide compromises,” Kempe said in an analysis, referring to Trump’s decision to delay weapon deliveries to Taiwan.
Asia will also plan for the post-Trump scenario.
“China and South-east Asia will still deal with the President as president and not underestimate him,” Liow said.
“But one eye must surely be on what might unfold after two years.”
