articles.title: EU Envoy: Thailand Can be Europe’s Platform in Southeast Asia as FTA Talks Advance - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: EU Envoy: Thailand Can be Europe’s Platform in Southeast Asia as FTA Talks Advance  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Luisa Ragher tells The Standard forum a trade deal, green investment and skills could help Thailand climb the value chain and attract European capital.
The European Union has pitched itself as a “trusted and long-term partner” for Thailand’s economic transformation, with its ambassador saying a free trade agreement (FTA) now under negotiation could anchor deeper investment, technology transfer and a shift towards a greener, higher-value economy.
Luisa Ragher, the EU’s ambassador to Thailand, delivered a keynote on “Thailand–EU FTA: Trade, Green Transition & Growth” at the opening of “Economic Forum 2026: Reinvent Thailand”, hosted by The Standard.
“Thailand is not just a market for European companies. It can be a platform for European investment in Southeast Asia,” she said, describing the country as a potential regional production base.
Ragher said the world was becoming more fragmented and more strategically contested, with geopolitics reshaping trade and supply chains, while artificial intelligence and the energy transition transform production.
At a time of rising protectionism, she said, the EU remains committed to open, rules-based markets and has the world’s largest portfolio of trade agreements, including deals with Singapore, Vietnam and Indonesia. Negotiations continue with Thailand and Malaysia.
She stressed that the relationship is already substantial. EU–Thailand trade in goods reached about 44 billion euro in 2025, with services trade of about 14 billion euro. European investment stock in Thailand stands at about 40 billion euro, making Europeans the third-largest source of foreign investment.
EU-invested companies support about 22,000 direct jobs, plus many more indirect ones, and European visitors contribute almost 6 billion to the economy.
The EU, she added, invested more than 400 billion euro in research and development in 2024.
Ragher said the FTA should not be viewed narrowly. “FTAs are often reduced to tariffs and market access. They are important, but the agreement we are negotiating is much more,” she said.
The deal covers access to markets for goods, services, investment and public procurement, along with fairer and more transparent rules and commitments on sustainability, including labour rights, environmental protection and climate resilience.
A study commissioned by the EU found it could raise Thailand’s GDP by 1.25% and exports by 2.8%. The greater prize, she said, lies beyond immediate trade gains.
It is the chance to move up the value chain through more advanced technology, higher skills, more productive businesses and more resilient supply chains.
The agreement could also support Thailand’s twin ambitions of joining the OECD and becoming a high-income, innovation-driven economy by 2037.
The ambassador said Thailand must shift from growth driven by capital and labour to growth driven by productivity, innovation and competition. Labour productivity grew 2.3% a year between 2015 and 2025, down from 4.8% in the previous period.
She outlined three conditions for success: Let businesses grow, invest and compete, while allowing new entrants to challenge established players.
Provide clear, predictable regulation, implemented consistently. Ensure investment, domestic or foreign, benefits the wider economy through stronger links between investors, companies, universities and workers, so that knowledge, technology and skills spread.
“Investors have choices,” Ragher warned, noting that they weigh institutional quality, workforce skills, regulatory transparency and ease of operating across borders.
Accumulated FDI inflows into Thailand between 2015 and 2023 equalled about 11% of annual GDP, a figure she said compared unfavourably with some regional peers.
That was no reason for pessimism, she added, pointing to the strong interest shown in applications to the Board of Investment. But applications are not investment, she said, and the task now is to turn interest into productive projects, skills, jobs and technology transfer.
Demographics add urgency. People aged 65 and over made up 15.4% of Thailand’s population in 2024, so future growth will depend increasingly on raising output per worker.
“Investing in people is therefore as important as investing in infrastructure,” she said.
On the green transition, Ragher said competitiveness in manufacturing increasingly depends not only on what is produced but on energy efficiency, renewable energy, low-carbon logistics and sustainable agriculture, as investors and regulators raise expectations on emissions.
European firms can contribute technology and investment expertise, she said, while Thailand offers a strong industrial base, renewable energy potential and a strategic position in regional supply chains.
The EU is working with Thailand on projects, including support for an immigration system improvement scheme, and is exploring cooperation on energy connectivity, renewable energy uptake and sustainable aviation.
“Our green transition should not be seen as a constraint on competitiveness. It is an opportunity to attract investment, develop new industries and be a first mover,” she said.
Ragher closed with three priorities, which she said echoed those set out earlier by the World Bank:
Move up the value chain and invest in people, across agriculture, tourism, advanced manufacturing, digital services and clean energy, with closer links between education and the economy.
Strengthen the investment climate by opening services and investment, making public procurement more transparent and accessible, and ensuring predictable rules, effective digital government and fair competition.
Use openness, including the FTA, to accelerate transformation and build competitive advantage.
“It is about building an economy that creates better opportunities, higher-value jobs and more sustainable prosperity for the next generation,” she concluded.

articles.title: Rena Lee’s historic election to world’s top court a milestone for Singapore, say observers - The Straits Times
articles.summary: Rena Lee’s historic election to world’s top court a milestone for Singapore, say observers  The Straits TimesSee more headlines and perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
AI generated
SINGAPORE – The election of Singaporean Rena Lee to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) is a significant milestone for Singapore, which has consistently championed a rules-based international order as a small state, said observers.
At a time when multilateral institutions face mounting pressures, her election underscores Singapore’s commitment to defending the rule of law and strengthening its governing bodies, they added.
They said it also reaffirms Singapore’s support for the UN’s principal judicial organ, which plays a critical role in resolving disputes between states and safeguarding the interests and sovereignty of all countries.
Lee is the first Singaporean and only the second person from South-east Asia to join the bench of the world’s top court.
Senior Minister and Minister for Home Affairs K. Shanmugam said it was a significant achievement: “Her election reflects both her personal standing and the respect Singapore has internationally through our longstanding commitment to international law and a rules-based international order.”
Simon Chesterman, David Marshall Professor of Law at the National University of Singapore (NUS), said international law is fundamental to Singapore’s security and prosperity in a world where power is distributed very unevenly.
The significance of Lee’s election for Singapore is that one of its most distinguished jurists will help uphold an institution on which small states depend, he said, noting at the same time that she will not be there as Singapore’s representative or advocate, and has to exercise independent and impartial judgment.

“International law cannot eliminate power politics, but it provides a framework for constraining power and resolving disputes peacefully,” said Chesterman.
“At a time when that framework is being challenged, we need distinguished and independent jurists to uphold it more than ever.”
Lee being on the bench of the world court, based in The Hague in the Netherlands, also signals Singapore’s commitment to international law and to respecting the decisions of the court, said former ambassador Tommy Koh.
The election, held at the United Nations headquarters in New York City on Nov 3, featured 10 candidates vying for five seats.
To be elected as judge, a candidate had to obtain an absolute majority of votes in both the UN General Assembly and UN Security Council, which held simultaneous meetings to vote.
Former deputy prime minister and law minister S. Jayakumar, who appeared before the ICJ to argue Singapore’s case on Pedra Branca in 2007, described the election as a tight contest.
That Lee had been elected in the first round of polling, securing the highest number of votes – 151 out of 191 – in the General Assembly and joint highest of 13 out of 15 in the Security Council, shows the high regard the international community has for her as well as Singapore, he said.
With Lee being from Singapore and South-east Asia, she will also bring greater diversity of legal perspectives to the ICJ bench, said Koh, who chairs the International Advisory Panel of the Centre for International Law at NUS.
As the world court, the ICJ must be representative of the different regions, legal traditions and political systems, he said.
While the court does not have a formal requirement for the geographical distribution of the seats, Article 9 of its statute states that electors should ensure “representation of the main forms of civilization and of the principal legal systems of the world” on its bench as a whole.
The last South-east Asian to serve on the ICJ bench was Judge Cesar Bengzon of the Philippines, whose term ended in 1976, more than five decades ago.
Lee’s election is also a boost for greater gender diversity, as the top court has only had seven permanent female judges in its 80-year history, compared with 110 male judges.
Lee’s nine-year term will start on Feb 6, 2027, and last until 2036.
Observers said Lee’s election is also a powerful vote of confidence in her standing as an international lawyer.
In her three decades as an international law practitioner, she has served as a government legal adviser, diplomat and international negotiator. She has expertise over a wide range of international law matters, including the law of the sea, climate change and environmental law, among others.
She is best known for her role in successfully steering complex, high-stakes negotiations that culminated in the adoption of the landmark High Seas Treaty, during her tenure as president of the UN Intergovernmental Conference on Marine Biodiversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) from 2018 to 2023.
Known as the BBNJ agreement, the treaty establishes a legally binding framework to protect marine life and regulate commercial activities in international waters.
Lee also holds positions in the Permanent Court of Arbitration and the Panel of Conciliators of the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes.
She was appointed Singapore’s Ambassador for International Law in 2023, and was Ambassador for Oceans and Law of the Sea Issues before that. She was also elected as a member of the Legal and Technical Commission of the International Seabed Authority, which acts as an advisory body on the exploration and exploitation of the international seabed.
Koh, who had helped campaign for Lee, said she was greatly admired by those who worked with her on the BBNJ negotiations, and that the successful adoption of the treaty was due in large part to her inspiring leadership at the conference.
Chesterman said Lee brings a combination of legal expertise and practical experience to the role.
“Her leadership of the negotiations that produced the historic high seas biodiversity treaty demonstrated not just a mastery of international law, but an ability to bridge differences between countries with very different interests,” he said.
In a LinkedIn post after the election, Lee said the journey to the ICJ has been one of the most meaningful of her career.
“I met representatives from all over the world and heard their experiences, concerns and hopes for international law and the multilateral order. Each conversation taught me something and I will carry these lessons with me to the court,” she said.
“I do not take the responsibility vested in me lightly… I will serve with impartiality, integrity and independence, in upholding and applying international law.”

articles.title: How Vietnam became an FTA success story - Fibre2Fashion
articles.summary: How Vietnam became an FTA success story  Fibre2Fashion
articles.full_text:
By dismantling tariff barriers, widening access to overseas markets, and institutionalising transparent trade rules, FTAs create the certainty businesses require to venture confidently beyond domestic borders.
At a time when supply chains are being reconfigured with relentless speed, geopolitical rivalries are intensifying, and industrial competition has become unforgiving, the role of FTAs has fundamentally transformed. What were once viewed primarily as policy mechanisms have evolved into indispensable engines of economic positioning and growth.
For export-driven economies, these agreements increasingly determine whether a country can attract investment, sustain industrial momentum, and remain integrated within global commerce.
Yet the existence of an agreement alone does not guarantee much. Many nations struggle to convert signed treaties into measurable trade gains, often finding implementation fragmented and benefits uneven. A select few, however, have managed to transform FTAs into tangible economic leverage, and Vietnam stands out as one of the finest examples.
Over the last decade and a half, Vietnam has methodically reshaped its identity within global trade. Rather than treating FTAs as symbolic political achievements, the country embedded them at the core of its economic blueprint. That strategic orientation accelerated the rise of a manufacturing ecosystem deeply intertwined with global demand, enabling Vietnam to evolve into a major export powerhouse.
Today, Vietnam ranks among the world’s most comprehensively connected free trade agreement (FTA) economies, participating in roughly 19 bilateral and multilateral trade agreements spanning close to 60 economies. Its portfolio encompasses major trade frameworks such as the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), the European Union–Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), as well as bilateral agreements with key markets including the United Kingdom-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (UKVFTA), the Vietnam-Israel Free Trade Agreement (VIFTA), and the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) with the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
Collectively, these agreements have granted Vietnam preferential access to some of the world’s largest and most lucrative consumer markets.
The consequences of this expanded market access have been transformative. Vietnam now enjoys deeply rooted trade linkages with the European Union (EU), the United Kingdom (UK), Japan, Canada, Australia, China, South Korea (Republic of Korea), and member economies of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), firmly embedding the country within the most influential global trade corridors.
Few industries illustrate this shift more vividly than textiles and apparel. According to some estimates, Vietnam’s garment exports have surged from approximately $13 billion some 15 years ago to nearly $45 billion today, with projections indicating continued growth in the years ahead.
This is not merely incremental growth; it represents a structural transformation propelled by sustained market access and a steady export-oriented strategy.
A critical driver behind this success has been Vietnam’s disciplined and highly coordinated approach to negotiating and administering trade agreements. Its FTA framework operates through a centralised system supported by substantial technical expertise, allowing the country to move efficiently from negotiation to implementation and, ultimately, to commercial execution.
The benefits are visible across multiple export destinations, including Japan, the European Union, the United Kingdom, and South Korea, where well-established agreements continue to reinforce export stability and investment inflows.
Vietnam’s experience demonstrates that FTAs are not simply legal trade instruments confined to policy circles. When pursued with strategic intent, they become catalysts for industrial expansion and economic transformation.
For export-driven economies, especially those reliant on apparel manufacturing and exports, the implications are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: competitiveness is no longer determined solely by low labour costs or production scale. It is equally shaped by how effectively a country integrates itself into global trade networks, and Vietnam offers a fitting example of what can be achieved when such integration is pursued with long-term strategic vision.

articles.full_text:
Investment in Vietnamese climate technology startups fell 52% in 2025, largely reflecting the absence of a major funding round that had inflated the previous year's figures, said a new report.
Last year, Vietnam recorded $49.86 million in climate tech investment across 33 deals, down from 60 deals totaling $104.2 million in 2024, according to the Vietnam Climate Tech Ecosystem report co-compiled by New Energy Nexus Vietnam, SNV Vietnam, World University Service of Canada (WUSC), and RMIT University Vietnam.
Researchers attributed the sharp decline to an exceptional $70 million Series A investment in Techcoop in 2024. Excluding that transaction, the funding decline was more moderate, with investment falling 19% to $27.86 million from $34.2 million.
Energy transition attracted the largest amount of capital in 2025, securing $26.71 million, up 72% from the previous year, the report shows. It was also the only segment to attract funding through all three channels: equity investment, debt financing and grants.
The report also found that Vietnam introduced 29 policies related to climate and innovation in 2025.
Tran Phuong Thao, country director of New Energy Nexus Vietnam, said investors remained willing to provide capital to Vietnamese climate tech startups, while founders continued to face strong demand for funding.
However, the report highlighted a gap in financing for companies seeking to scale up. No deals were closed in the $350,000-to-$1 million range in 2025, compared with four in 2024.
The composition of funding also shifted significantly. Equity investment declined sharply, while debt financing surged from $3 million to $20 million. The trend points to the need for more diverse financing pathways to help startups move beyond the incubation stage and become eligible for larger investments.
Beyond access to capital, climate tech startups also face a shortage of skilled workers, according to the findings. Some 73% of surveyed companies ranked specialized technical and professional skills among their three most urgent recruitment needs, while 50% identified these positions as the hardest to fill.
Lindsay Umalla, head of energy at SNV Vietnam, said capital was entering the sector faster than the workforce could adapt. To accelerate growth, startups need to recruit more experienced, multidisciplinary talent, she said.
The wider ecosystem should also strengthen links between training, recruitment and financing to develop a core workforce capable of supporting the industry's expansion, the expert recommended.

articles.title: Philippines’ digital economy projected to reach $42 billion in 2026 as AI use deepens - ET CIO SEA
articles.summary: Philippines’ digital economy projected to reach $42 billion in 2026 as AI use deepens  ET CIO SEA
articles.full_text:
The Philippines’ digital economy is on course to reach about $42 billion in gross merchandise value (GMV) in 2026, as artificial intelligence (AI) shifts from novelty to a routine part of how consumers shop, study and work. The 2026 e-Conomy SEA study projects 15 per cent growth this year from $36 billion in 2025, with the market potentially reaching $157 billion by 2035. GMV, the study’s yardstick, measures the value of transactions across the digital sectors it covers.
AI is already shaping the start of the buying process: about a third of consumer journeys in the country now begin with an AI tool. The headline growth rate sits below the 17 per cent projected for Southeast Asia as a whole, where the digital economy is forecast to reach $368 billion this year. The Philippines nonetheless leads the region in digital payments growth and ties Vietnam in digital insurance, pointing to financial services as a particular strength.
Broad adoption, uneven depth
What AI is used for
Where growth is concentratedE-commerce remains the largest segment, with GMV growing 15 per cent to $28 billion. Online media is the fastest-growing, up 26 per cent to $6 billion and accelerating from 23 per cent a year earlier. Online travel is projected to expand 14 per cent to $3 billion, compared with 9 per cent last year, while mobility and food services are growing more slowly, at 2 per cent, to $4 billion.
Payments and financial services lead
Digital lending is expected to reach $7 billion in outstanding loan balances, up 17 per cent from $6 billion in 2025, and could climb to $31 billion by 2035. Digital insurance is growing 16 per cent to $110 million, measured by annual premium equivalent and gross written premiums.Policy backdrop and outlookNational AI Center for Research and Innovation, National Privacy Commission frameworks and the Internet Transactions Act as supports for digital development. Prep Palacios, Google’s country manager for the Philippines, said stronger user confidence and wider local use cases will depend on continued policy support and cooperation across the ecosystem.
The key test, the study suggests, is whether widespread access and rising trust translate into deeper use among both consumers and enterprises. With consumer applications still dominating, enterprise adoption will be an area to watch, particularly as the country seeks to sustain growth amid geopolitical and macroeconomic pressures.

articles.title: More than 20 banks simultaneously reduced lending interest rates. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: More than 20 banks simultaneously reduced lending interest rates.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Dan Tri Newspaper) - A representative from the State Bank of Vietnam stated that more than 20 banks have implemented preferential credit programs, while interest rates on new loans have decreased by 0.2-0.5% per year.
At the regular government press conference in October, organized by the Government Office on November 4th, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Pham Thanh Ha stated that commercial banks have adjusted down the listed deposit interest rates by 0.5% per year for terms of 6 months or more.
This is the initial result after the State Bank of Vietnam implemented measures to reduce market interest rates, in the context of increased capital demand from the economy to serve growth targets.
According to the Deputy Governor, interest rates in the domestic market have been under considerable pressure recently. The economy's demand for capital has increased significantly, while the global economic situation has been complex, leading many central banks to adjust interest rates upwards.
In response to this situation, the State Bank of Vietnam has implemented a comprehensive set of solutions to reduce market interest rates.
Notably, in October, the State Bank of Vietnam directed credit institutions to focus all resources, reduce costs, share profits, and aggressively implement solutions to lower interest rates.
As directed, credit institutions are implementing a 0.5% annual reduction in listed deposit interest rates and new deposit interest rates for terms of 6 months or more. Simultaneously, lending interest rates for production, business, and priority sectors are being reduced by 1.5-2% per year.
You may also like
After a short period of implementation, the policy has yielded initial results. Specifically, regarding listed deposit interest rates, commercial banks have adjusted them down by 0.5% per year for terms of 6 months or more, as directed by the State Bank of Vietnam.
Specifically, state-owned commercial banks and commercial banks with 100% foreign capital generally saw a decrease of 0.5% per year. Joint-stock commercial banks generally saw a decrease of 0.5-0.7% per year.
According to Deputy Governor Pham Thanh Ha, based on actual deposit interest rates, data from the end of October shows that the average interest rate on newly generated deposits has decreased by approximately 0.4% per year compared to mid-October.
On the lending side, the average interest rate on new loans in the latter part of October also decreased by about 0.2-0.5% per year compared to the middle of the month.
Notably, more than 20 banks have announced preferential credit programs for the manufacturing, business, and priority sectors, with interest rate reductions of 1.5-2% per year.
Besides requiring interest rate reductions, the State Bank of Vietnam continues to implement solutions to support liquidity and capital for credit institutions. The State Bank of Vietnam continues to coordinate the use of monetary policy tools such as open market operations, refinancing, and short-term foreign exchange-VND swaps.
Specifically, on November 3rd, the State Bank of Vietnam announced the implementation of a 6-month foreign currency-VND swap operation for credit institutions.
This solution aims to provide relatively long-term VND funding to credit institutions, helping the banking system have more abundant VND capital. This, in turn, contributes to lowering interest rates and supporting the achievement of high growth targets.
Regarding future operational direction, the Deputy Governor stated that the State Bank of Vietnam will continue to closely monitor global and domestic economic developments, and flexibly manage monetary policy to contribute to controlling inflation, stabilizing the macroeconomy, and supporting sustainable economic growth.
You may also like
Regarding the foreign exchange market, the agency continues to closely monitor domestic and international developments, managing the exchange rate flexibly in accordance with market conditions. Exchange rate management will be coordinated with monetary policy tools to stabilize the foreign exchange market, contributing to macroeconomic stability, controlling inflation, and supporting growth.
Regarding credit, the State Bank of Vietnam will implement management solutions appropriate to macroeconomic developments and the economy's capacity to absorb capital. The goal is to contribute to promoting growth, controlling inflation, and ensuring the safety of the banking system's operations...
Regarding interest rate management, the State Bank of Vietnam continues to direct credit institutions to aggressively implement solutions to reduce interest rates.
Speaking further at the press conference, Minister and Head of the Government Office Doan Xuan Phong said that reducing interest rates is one of the important issues recently concluded by the Prime Minister and has received public attention.
The Minister requested that the State Bank of Vietnam, following the directives issued, continue to rigorously inspect and urge commercial banks to ensure that interest rate reductions are implemented genuinely and not merely formally. The requirement to reduce deposit interest rates by 0.5% per year and lending interest rates by 1.5-2% per year needs to be closely monitored.

articles.title: Supachai Unveils Five Key Strategies to Position Thailand as Regional Economic Powerhouse - kaohoon international
articles.summary: Supachai Unveils Five Key Strategies to Position Thailand as Regional Economic Powerhouse  kaohoon international
articles.full_text:
Suphachai Chearavanont, Chairman and Executive Chairman of Arise Ventures Group and Senior Vice Chairman of CP Group, has urged Thailand to accelerate economic restructuring and build a stronger investment ecosystem to improve its global competitiveness and expand its role in international supply chains, targeting annual GDP growth of 4–5%.
Speaking at THE STANDARD ECONOMIC FORUM 2026, Suphachai said the global economy was entering a new world order shaped by five major forces: geopolitical fragmentation, the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies, the transition to clean energy, the expansion of the digital economy and digital currencies, and the growing influence of the Global South, including BRICS, India, and ASEAN.
He said Thailand’s strategic location at the heart of Southeast Asia offers an opportunity to become a regional economic hub, supported by five key development priorities.
The first is a New Economy Hub, attracting investment in data centers, semiconductors, cloud technology, AI, robotics, and electric vehicles while upgrading existing industries, particularly automotive manufacturing. Thailand should also help local SMEs integrate into emerging supply chains.
The second is a Technology and Innovation Hub, with greater investment in research and development. Thailand currently spends approximately 0.9% of GDP on R&D, compared with 2.8% in China. Suphachai called for foreign companies to establish research centers and collaborate with Thai universities, alongside tax incentives and matching funds to strengthen the startup ecosystem.
The third is a Human Capital Hub, focusing on AI skills development and technology entrepreneurship through university startups and research laboratories. Thailand has approximately 2 million university students and 500,000 graduates annually, providing a potential talent base for the next generation of technology businesses.
The fourth is a Food Security and Healthcare Hub, leveraging Thailand’s agricultural and healthcare strengths in food technology, biotechnology, smart farming, and wellness tourism. The global wellness tourism market is valued at around US$1 trillion and is projected to reach US$1.4 trillion by 2030.
The fifth is a Trade, Logistics and Financial Hub, using Thailand’s geographic position to connect China, ASEAN, and the Indian Ocean. Suphachai also proposed cooperation with Hong Kong, Singapore, and Nasdaq to attract technology companies and startups to raise capital through Thailand’s financial market.
He emphasized that foreign direct investment (FDI) is essential to achieving the 4–5% growth target. Vietnam attracted approximately US$30 billion in investment last year, compared with Thailand’s US$9 billion. To attract more capital and technology, Thailand needs geopolitical neutrality, political stability, consistent economic policies over the next four to 10 years, and stronger public-sector governance and transparency.
Suphachai also called for greater use of AI in public administration, the development of a cashless economy, and investment in cybersecurity and AI defense. He further highlighted regional infrastructure development, cross-border energy cooperation, and the potential use of Thailand’s approximately US$300 billion in international reserves to support infrastructure and new-economy investment, subject to relevant legal and risk-management requirements.
He concluded that Thailand’s ability to capitalize on the AI transition will depend on policy continuity, investment in technology and human capital, and an ecosystem capable of attracting global investment.

articles.title: To reflect practical conditions - Vietnam Economic Times
articles.summary: To reflect practical conditions  Vietnam Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Alongside the influx of FDI, the number of foreigners working and living in Vietnam has continued to rise. Vietnam’s 2026 Economic Census found that the country had 29,786 FDI enterprises as of the end of 2025, while a report reviewing the implementation of Decree No. 219/2025/ND-CP showed that 162,858 foreign workers from approximately 110 countries and territories were employed in Vietnam as of the end of last year. Technical workers accounted for the largest group, at 85,951, followed by 44,342 specialists, 22,416 managers, and 10,149 executive directors. These figures point to substantial demand for housing among foreigners living in Vietnam.
To reflect changing conditions and the country’s development priorities, as well as to institutionalize new policies and orientations set by the Party and the government, the draft revised Law on Housing proposes several amendments, including changes to the rules governing homeownership in Vietnam by foreign organizations and individuals.
Policy adjustments
Vietnam first piloted a policy allowing foreigners to own homes in 2008 under Resolution No. 19/2008/QH12. The right was subsequently formalized under the Law on Housing 2014, which took effect on July 1, 2015, and was retained in the Law on Housing 2023, which expanded eligibility and eased conditions for foreign homeownership in Vietnam.
Since the Law on Housing 2023 took effect on August 1, 2024, the number of homes owned by foreign nationals in Vietnam has risen sharply compared to previous years. According to a report from the Vietnam Association of Realtors (VARS), only slightly more than 3,000 foreigners purchased homes in Vietnam between 2015 and the end of the third quarter of 2023. Most were apartments in commercial housing projects, concentrated in major cities and provinces.
However, the Ministry of Construction (MoC)’s Report No. 356/BC-BXD, dated September 9, 2026, stated that ownership certificates were issued for approximately 6,188 homes nationwide purchased by foreign organizations and individuals.
Foreign buyers tend to favor projects with integrated planning and comprehensive amenities. This trend suggests that the homeownership policy under the Law on Housing 2023 has been implemented effectively, encouraging foreign organizations and individuals to invest in residential property in Vietnam and providing housing for those living in the country. It has also helped absorb some of the market’s high-end housing supply, supported real estate market development, improved infrastructure and urban environments, and stimulated economic growth and local employment.
After more than two years of implementation, several provisions of the Law on Housing 2023 have revealed shortcomings and inconsistencies.
Regarding housing for foreigners, some stakeholders have raised concerns that the Law on Housing 2023 and the Land Law 2024 do not recognize foreign individuals as land users and do not specify how ownership certificates should be issued when a homeowner does not hold land-use rights over the underlying plot. Current legislation also lacks provisions governing land-use rights when homes are sold to foreign organizations or individuals and when foreign owners subsequently resell them to Vietnamese buyers.
This raises several practical questions. If a home is sold to a foreign buyer without transferring land-use rights, who retains those rights? If a foreign owner without land-use rights resells the property to a Vietnamese buyer who is entitled to such rights, how should the transfer contract be handled, and how should related issues be resolved? At recent meetings, several National Assembly (NA) deputies called for a review of these provisions to ensure consistency with relevant rules under the Civil Code and the Law on Management and Use of Public Property, particularly those concerning assets established as collectively owned by the people and the handling of such assets.
Redefining foreign homeownership
Vietnam is entering a new stage of development, with ambitious targets and stricter legal requirements. As a result, certain provisions of the Law on Housing, including those governing homeownership by foreign nationals, need to be revised to reflect practical conditions and the development orientations of the Party and government. The proposed changes also aim to address existing shortcomings, improve consistency across the legal system, establish a more transparent and secure regulatory environment with lower compliance costs, improve the investment and business climate, and simplify administrative procedures.
Deputy Minister of Construction Nguyen Van Sinh said the draft had been revised to incorporate several changes. These include removing provisions on accommodation for specialists and workers outside industrial parks and in dormitories; excluding foreign workers from the group eligible to rent social housing; adjusting the rules on foreign ownership of landed houses; and revising provisions on the rights and obligations of foreign owners, as well as the handling of residential property when the ownership period expires.
The MoC had initially proposed adding rules on accommodation for these groups following feedback from several agencies. The draft had included definitions, eligibility criteria, construction investment procedures, and operational management requirements under Clause 8, Article 2, and Articles 50 and 51.
However, the NA Standing Committee and the Committee on Legal and Judicial Affairs called for careful consideration before including this type of accommodation in the draft law. They argued that the boundary between social welfare policy and commercial real estate activity remained unclear, creating a risk that the policy could be exploited or transformed into commercial property projects, potentially affecting policies on accommodation in industrial parks and social housing. The Ministry of Public Security (MPS) also proposed removing the relevant provisions.
On the proposal to remove foreign workers from the group eligible to rent social housing, the MoC noted that Resolution No. 201/2025/QH15 allows businesses, State agencies, political organizations, socio-political organizations, and public service units to rent social housing for their own officials, civil servants, public employees, and workers, including foreign workers. The Ministry had proposed incorporating this provision into the revised law.
However, after reviewing feedback from the MPS, the MoC proposed excluding foreign workers. The police argued that foreign workers employed by businesses are largely specialists, managers, and highly-skilled technical staff whose incomes are relatively high, making them ineligible for preferential social housing policies. They also noted that separate policies already provide accommodation for workers in industrial parks.
The draft also removes the right of foreign organizations and individuals to own landed houses. Under the Law on Housing 2023, foreign owners may hold up to 250 villas or adjoining houses in an area with a population equivalent to that of a ward. If the draft is approved and takes effect, foreign organizations and individuals would no longer be allowed to own landed houses in residential projects, including villas and adjoining houses, and would be limited to apartments in housing development projects.
Another proposal in the draft allows the government to determine the foreign ownership quota for apartments, replacing the current law’s explicit 30 per cent cap. Under existing rules, the Ministry of National Defense and the MPS are responsible for identifying areas where national defense and security must be safeguarded. Local authorities then use this information to determine and publicly announce which projects may be purchased by foreign buyers.
NA deputies have argued that this is a sensitive issue involving national defense, security, and the rights and obligations of foreign nationals in Vietnam. They called for consultations with competent authorities and consideration of whether the ownership cap should remain explicitly stated in the law.
Foreign ownership
Speaking during a group discussion on October 22, Mr. Nguyen Thanh Tam, NA Deputy from Ho Chi Minh City, said allowing foreign organizations and individuals to legally own homes could help attract investment. However, ownership limits also affect population management, territorial administration, and national defense and security, particularly in border areas, along coastlines, on islands, and near critical infrastructure.
He said a higher foreign ownership rate should not automatically be considered a security risk, but any adjustment must be evidence-based and subject to clear oversight mechanisms. Mr. Tam therefore proposed retaining the 30 per cent cap in the law while authorizing the government to regulate how the quota is calculated, how apartment numbers are managed, how buildings with multiple sections or projects with several buildings are treated, and how subsequent transactions are monitored.
Regarding foreign ownership of residential property in Vietnam, the Ho Chi Minh City Real Estate Association has proposed amending Clause 1 and Points a and b of Clause 2, Article 9, of the draft Law on Real Estate Business, to allow the following.
- Domestic organizations and individuals, overseas Vietnamese who are Vietnamese citizens, and foreign-invested economic organizations may purchase, lease, or acquire housing through lease-purchase or installment payment arrangements in accordance with housing laws. They may also purchase, lease, or acquire through lease-purchase or installment payment arrangements tourist apartments, resort villas, office-apartments, adjoining commercial houses, construction works, and floor space in buildings designed for office, tourism, or accommodation purposes.

articles.full_text:

JAKARTA – Former Indonesian president Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono has called for a return to “civilised politics” following the arrest of three police generals accused of wiretapping President Prabowo Subianto.
“How has our country ended up like this? How can our politics be so wild? It seems that in the pursuit of political power, all methods have been justified, regardless of whether they are right or wrong, moral or immoral,” Yudhoyono wrote in a post on his official X account on Nov 4.
“As a citizen who deeply loves this nation, much like any other Indonesian, I appeal to President Prabowo to revive civilised politics.”
Yudhoyono’s comments come after the National Police named the three generals as suspects in an alleged scheme to illegally wiretap Prabowo and several other government officials and civil society leaders.
One of the suspects, Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had served as National Police chief from 2021 to 2026, and was recently appointed Presidential Chief of Staff.
The scandal has rocked Indonesian politics, with questions raised about the extent of the wiretapping and the motives behind it.
Coordinating Minister for Legal Affairs Yusril Ihza Mahendra said on Nov 3 that there was so far no indication that the suspects had intended to overthrow the government, but that further investigation was needed.

Yudhoyono himself had been a victim of an alleged wiretapping attempt by Australian intelligence agencies, leaked documents published by The Guardian in 2013 showed.
The revelation led to strained relations between the two countries, with Indonesia going so far as to recall its ambassador, though Australia never directly admitted to the attempt.
Then Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott refused to apologise or comment on the matter at the time, saying in Australia’s Parliament: “I don't believe Australia should be expected to apologise for reasonable intelligence-gathering activities.”
With 44 seats, Yudhoyono's Democratic Party is the seventh-largest party in Indonesia’s Parliament and is part of Prabowo's governing coalition.
His son, Agus Harimurti Yudhoyono, is also part of Prabowo’s Cabinet, serving as Coordinating Minister of Infrastructure and Regional Development. However, the senior Yudhoyono has largely remained outside politics since Agus took over the party chairmanship in 2020.

articles.title: Thailand Unveils ‘STI DEE’ Blueprint as Finance Ministry Becomes Prototype for National Reform - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Thailand Unveils ‘STI DEE’ Blueprint as Finance Ministry Becomes Prototype for National Reform  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
The Deputy PM says the ministry will publish five years of procurement data on Monday (November 9), hold the 70% debt ceiling and use BOI incentives to lift Thai skills and wages.
Thailand’s Finance Ministry will become the first test case of the government’s “Reinvent Thailand” agenda, with a sweeping overhaul built on transparency, digital services and efficiency, Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas said on Wednesday (Novermber 4).
Speaking in a panel discussion at the opening of “Economic Forum 2026: Reinvent Thailand”, hosted by The Standard, Dr Ekniti said the ministry would be a “prototype” for reform. Its strategy, named “STI DEE”, will be formally unveiled on Monday, he said, although he previewed its main elements on stage.
The first element is stability, covering fiscal strength, the energy transition and investment. The second, “DEE”, stands for disclosure, ease and efficiency.
Disclosure is the most radical. The ministry will open its procurement data from the Comptroller General’s Department, going back five years, so that the public and lawmakers can scrutinise it.
“I will open the wounds,” he said, so that problems can be seen and solved together.
He noted that last year’s budget data was released in machine-readable form, which MPs from both government and opposition have used for AI-driven analysis.
He intends to brief parliament on the approach on Thursday (November 5). “Ease” means using digital tools to make dealings with the state simpler. “Efficiency and effectiveness” means the public sector should drop what it does not need to do and leave to private firms what they can do better.
Dr Ekniti was unequivocal that fiscal discipline remains the foundation of his policy, describing it as the team’s “back line” in a football analogy. The deficit, which was projected at 4.4% of GDP, closed the fiscal year ended September at 3.4%, a result he said had won global praise.
All three major credit rating agencies have moved their outlooks on Thailand from negative to stable. The benefits reach households and businesses, he argued.
He said the ten-year government borrowing cost in Thailand is about 2%, against close to 5% in the United States, nearly 8% in Indonesia, roughly 4% in Malaysia and 2.3% in Singapore, on the figures he quoted that morning. Public debt is about 67–68% of GDP, he said, and he wants it to fall.
He ruled out lifting the public debt ceiling, which stays at 70% of GDP, compared with global norms of 90–100%. He rejected the idea of using the 200 billion baht emergency loan decree simply to spend it.
“If it is not all used, that is fine,” he said, stressing efficiency and effectiveness.
On revenue, he said collection had exceeded targets, helped by digital systems. The government had aimed to cut the deficit below 3% within three years and was close to achieving it. He defended the cabinet’s proposed rise in excise tax on cars, particularly imported ones, as an action meant to achieve several aims at once.
It would ensure fairness for foreign investors who employ Thais and build local supply chains, he said, and raise revenue. Investors had pleaded with him, he said, as imports flooded in.
The global minimum tax, set at 15% under international rules, was already generating about tens of billions of baht in additional corporate income, he added.
He said the government had held back on some tax measures, including one affecting air travel, because high oil prices from the Middle East conflict had already pushed up fares.
Tourism and jobs, he judged, were worth more than the revenue, and the measure would wait for the right moment. He also aims to bring people outside the tax system into it so that those who pay do not resent neighbours who do not.
As chairman of the Board of Investment (BOI), Dr Ekniti said he had changed the agency’s targets. It now measures actual investment rather than applications, plus jobs created and skills developed. Since the start of the year, BOI-backed projects had generated about 120,000 jobs.
Actual investment grew about 27% in the third quarter, he said, and a recent round of projects was worth around 600,000 million baht. He tells investors to build a “skill bridge”, asking how many Thais they will hire and train.
One top-two global firm in optical data transfer is expanding in Saraburi and Ayutthaya, employing 30,000 people, with research ties to Thammasat University and Suranaree University of Technology in Nakhon Ratchasima.
Thailand, he said, is in the global spotlight after hosting the IMF–World Bank meetings, as a neutral trading nation in a fragmented world. The country must catch the “high-speed train” passing through it.
Seven private-sector-led industries will announce key performance indicators on Monday (November 9): modern agriculture, food processing, smart electronics, electric vehicles, wellness and others.
Old sectors will be upgraded rather than abandoned, he said, with tourism shifting from “sickness” to wellness.
The 200 billion baht loan decree, he said, targets three areas: electricity, transport fuels and skills. About 70 billion baht has been approved, including 50 billion for household solar, with subsidies and the right to sell power back, and the rest for smart meters and grid upgrades.
Around 100 billion more is planned for transport, including E20 petrol, B20 diesel and locally built pickup trucks. For people, about six million Thais aged 20–60 earn under 100,000 baht a year and will be retrained with the education and labour ministries.
By 2030, he said, Thailand should post GDP growth above 3%, lift investment from 22% to 30% of GDP, and climb from 26th to the top 20 in competitiveness within three to four years. Growth must spread beyond the wealthy, he said, addressing the K-shaped recovery. This might be Thailand’s “last chance”, he added.

articles.title: Director at unit of Indonesia richest family's bank makes Forbes Asia's Power Businesswomen list - VnExpress International
articles.summary: Director at unit of Indonesia richest family's bank makes Forbes Asia's Power Businesswomen list  VnExpress International
articles.full_text:
Formerly known as Bank Royal, which BCA acquired in 2019 in a push into digital banking, BCA Digital launched its blu mobile banking app in 2021 and became profitable in 2023 under Budiati’s leadership, according to the list, which spotlights 20 trailblazing women business leaders in Asia.
The digital lender has since expanded substantially, with net profit more than quadrupling to Rp213.4 billion (US$11.8 million), loans rising by 85% to Rp8.6 trillion and deposits jumping 59% to Rp14.3 trillion.
It is now the country’s sixth-largest digital bank with a client base of 3.1 million as of December 2025, according to Forbes.
| Lanny Budiati, president director of BCA Digital. Photo from the company's annual report | 
BCA Digital has recorded growth despite a sluggish domestic economy and stiff competition from rivals such as SeaBank, owned by Singapore billionaire Forrest Li's Sea, and Bank Jago, backed by ride-hailing and payments giant Gojek.
Younger Indonesians, particularly Gen Zers and millennials, have been key to the digital lender’s expansion as it positions itself as a mobile-first banking experience tailored to their financial needs.
Budiati said last July, when blu first surpassed 3 million users, that these segments made up more than 90% of the platform's user base.
"We believe the next decade of banking will be defined by trust, access, and personal relevance," Lanny told Asian Business Review. "Blu is here to accompany young Indonesians through each phase of their financial growth—not just as a bank, but as a partner for life."
Before heading BCA Digital, Lanny had started as a management trainee at BCA in 1991 and spent a few years at other lenders in Indonesia before rejoining in 2001 and taking on roles including BCA’s regional head of West Java.
BCA, Indonesia’s largest bank by market capitalization, is more than half owned by the Hartonos, the richest family in the country, through their holding company Dwimuria Investama Andalan, according to Bloomberg.
Billionaire Robert Budi Hartono became the bank’s sole controlling shareholder earlier this year after his brother Michael Bambang Hartono passed away. Robert is also Indonesia’s richest individual, with an estimated net worth of US$11.9 billion as of Nov. 4.

articles.title: Indonesia urges OIC states to deepen digital economy ties - ET CIO SEA
articles.summary: Indonesia urges OIC states to deepen digital economy ties  ET CIO SEA
articles.full_text:
Indonesia has called on member states of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) to strengthen cooperation in the digital economy through artificial intelligence (AI), youth entrepreneurship and broader market access.
“The challenge is how to maximize the potential of young people so that they do not merely become technology users but can also create innovations, develop businesses, and generate added value for the economy,” she said in a statement.
Roro said Indonesia has significant digital economy potential, with a population of more than 281 million, including 62.39 million millennials and 57.64 million Generation Z members. She added that improving skills, particularly in digital trade and entrepreneurship, is essential to boosting productivity and competitiveness.
To help local businesses reach global markets, the Ministry of Trade has introduced four initiatives: the InaExport platform, the Campuspreneur programme, digital-based export training, and the promotion of electronic trade documents, including electronic Certificates of Origin (e-SKA). InaExport is a free platform that connects exporters with prospective international buyers and provides information on market potential, export destinations, tariffs and market access requirements.
Roro also encouraged OIC members to share experiences in developing their digital economies. She said the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) and cross-border payment connectivity through Indonesia’s Quick Response Code Indonesian Standard (QRIS) could serve as references for strengthening digital trade among countries.
Why the digital economy matters for the OIC
The appeal comes at a time when many OIC economies are trying to accelerate digital inclusion, expand online commerce and build the infrastructure needed to support new businesses. The grouping spans Asia, the Middle East, Africa and parts of Europe, and its members range from advanced technology hubs to markets still working on basic connectivity. That diversity makes cooperation both more complicated and more valuable.
Indonesia’s call reflects a broader view that digital tools are no longer optional for economic resilience. Countries that can digitise trade, improve logistics and enable secure online transactions are better placed to absorb shocks and attract investment, which is especially relevant for governments seeking to diversify beyond commodities. As major economies compete to shape the rules of digital trade, data governance and AI, a more unified OIC approach could also give members greater leverage in international forums.
What deeper cooperation could look like
Still, the push from Indonesia suggests the digital economy is moving higher on the OIC agenda. If member states can turn the call into specific programmes, the bloc could build a more connected market for digital services, talent and innovation. For economies looking to widen their growth base, that would be more than a technology story. It would be a competitiveness strategy.

articles.title: Northern Vietnam, Eastern Europe: The Unusual Origin Of Vietnam’s Billionaire Class - Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Northern Vietnam, Eastern Europe: The Unusual Origin Of Vietnam’s Billionaire Class - Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
By Le Hong Hiep
Key Takeaways:
- As of 31 October 2026, Pham Nhat Vuong leads Vietnam’s eight Forbes billionaires, all ethnic Kinh from the North and mostly first-generation founders shaped by Soviet-bloc study and trade, in sharp contrast to the ethnic-Chinese dominance among the top fortunes in Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand.
- Post-1975 nationalisation and the Sino-Vietnamese rupture dismantled the pre-1975 Hoa commercial networks, allowing a cohort of returnees to accumulate capital abroad and later align closely with the state under To Lam, securing major infrastructure and industrial projects.
- The configuration reduces foreign influence and supports national-champion diplomacy, yet risks “red crony capitalism,” limited succession planning and continued heavy concentration in real estate and finance rather than technology.
As of 31 October 2026, Forbes’ real-time billionaire tracker put the fortune of Pham Nhat Vuong, founder and chairman of Vingroup, Vietnam’s largest private conglomerate, at roughly US$27.7 billion. This placed him around 93rd globally and second in Southeast Asia, behind Indonesia’s Prajogo Pangestu.[1] Vuong’s wealth has increased significantly over the past year, propelled by the runaway share performance of his conglomerate’s property, retail and electric-vehicle arms. He now sits at the top of a list of eight Vietnamese US-dollar billionaires recognised by Forbes, the largest such cohort in the country’s history.
What is less often remarked upon, but arguably more revealing, is who these eight billionaires are not. All are ethnic Vietnamese, or Kinh. All hail from northern Vietnam,[2] and most share a formative period of studying, trading or doing business in the former Soviet Union and Eastern Europe before returning to Vietnam to build their business empires. Strikingly, not a single one is an ethnic Chinese, or Hoa, entrepreneur, despite Vietnam having long had a sizeable Chinese-descended business community.
This is a distinctly Vietnamese pattern. In Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand, a substantial share of the wealthiest individuals are ethnic Chinese entrepreneurs or members of Chinese-origin business dynasties that have accumulated wealth over several generations. This article therefore raises two questions: why are the social and ethnic origins of Vietnam’s billionaire class so different from those of its neighbours, and what does this difference imply for Vietnam’s economic development, socio-economic structure and foreign policy?
The article begins by comparing Vietnam’s billionaire class with those of Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand, using data available at the end of October 2026. It then explains the divergence by tracing it to the post-1975 socialist transformation of the economy, the weakening of the ethnic Chinese business community, and the subsequent rise of a distinctive cohort of entrepreneurs shaped by their experiences in the former Soviet bloc. It concludes by examining the economic, political and foreign-policy implications of this configuration, as well as how Vietnam’s billionaire class may evolve in the years ahead.
Comparing Vietnam’s Billionaire Class with Its Neighbours
The tables below draw on Forbes data to compare Vietnam’s billionaires with a representative sample of the wealthiest individuals/families in Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand.
For Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines, Table 2 lists each country’s top eight billionaires or billionaire families by net worth, mirroring the size of Vietnam’s own Forbes cohort in Table 1 to make the comparison as direct as possible.
The contrast is unmistakable. Vietnam’s Forbes-recognised billionaires are all ethnic Vietnamese. Across Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand, 26 of the top 32 entries (81 per cent) trace to Chinese immigrant families. The pattern holds in each country. In Indonesia, five largest fortunes—Pangestu, Low, the Hartono brothers, and Salim—rank ahead of Pribumi data-centre magnate Otto Toto Sugiri and Indian-origin industrialist Sri Prakash Lohia. Malaysia’s top eight are all of Chinese descent except for last-ranked Bumiputera tycoon Syed Mokhtar AlBukhary.
The Philippines’ Ang, Tan and four Sy siblings remain fixtures, alongside two non-Chinese fortunes—Enrique Razon’s ports empire and Manuel Villar’s property conglomerate, now ranked first and fourth. Meanwhile, four branches of Thailand’s Chearavanont/CP Group dynasty, plus the Sirivadhanabhakdi, Prasarttong-Osoth and Sathientham families, occupy seven of its top eight places, leaving energy tycoon Sarath Ratanavadi as the sole non-Chinese entrant.
Unlike many of their peers in the four neighbouring countries, whose family fortunes were built over several generations, Vietnam’s billionaires are almost all first-generation founders who accumulated their wealth from the 1990s onward. Seven of them, with the exception of Hoa Phat Group’s Tran Dinh Long, also share a distinctive biographical background rooted in a particular historical legacy: Vietnam’s socialist-era ties with the Soviet bloc.
Why Is Vietnam’s Billionaire Class Different?
Historical Legacies: The Weakening of the Ethnic Chinese Business Community after 1975
Before 1975, ethnic Chinese entrepreneurs occupied a commanding position in the South Vietnamese economy, with a strong presence in trade, finance, rice distribution and light manufacturing.[3] After reunification, the socialist transformation of private capitalist industry and commerce launched in the late 1970s nationalised or collectivised much of this commercial base. Ethnic Chinese traders were disproportionately affected because they were heavily concentrated in precisely the sectors targeted by the campaign.[4]
The timing compounded the disruption. As Sino-Vietnamese relations deteriorated over Cambodia, border disputes and Vietnam’s growing alignment with the Soviet Union, culminating in the brief but bloody border war of 1979, Vietnam’s ethnic Chinese community became increasingly subject to political suspicion and discriminatory treatment. By several accounts, the authorities also encouraged or facilitated their departure. Roughly 450,000 ethnic Chinese reportedly left or were expelled across the northern border between 1978 and 1979 alone, with the exodus continuing into the 1980s.[5]
The result was a major rupture in the commercial networks, accumulated capital, and intergenerational structures that had sustained Hoa’s entrepreneurial strength. This had no close parallel in Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia or the Philippines, where Chinese-origin business networks retained much greater continuity, allowing capital, commercial knowledge and family enterprises to compound across generations.
A substantial ethnic Chinese population remains in Vietnam and continues to play an important role in business, particularly in and around Ho Chi Minh City. Yet, partly because of the historical disruptions described above, and partly because of the way opportunities have been distributed in Vietnam’s post-Doi Moi political economy, Chinese-Vietnamese entrepreneurs appear to have developed in less proximity to the state; this has proved important to the rise of some ethnic Vietnamese business groups. In sectors such as real estate, infrastructure and finance, access to land, credit, licences and state-linked projects has often been crucial to rapid expansion.
The most consequential recent example is also instructive because of how it ended. Truong My Lan, the daughter of a Chinese-Vietnamese trader who reportedly began by selling cosmetics at Ho Chi Minh City’s Ben Thanh Market, built a sprawling real estate and financial empire through Van Thinh Phat Group and reportedly cultivated relationships with numerous former city officials.[6] Her empire collapsed in 2022–24 in what prosecutors described as Vietnam’s largest-ever fraud case, centred on her de facto control of Saigon Commercial Bank.
Other prominent Chinese-Vietnamese entrepreneurs, such as Dang Van Thanh of Thanh Thanh Cong, the Tran Kim Thanh–Tran Le Nguyen brothers behind Kinh Do Group, Ly Ngoc Minh of Minh Long ceramics, and Co Gia Tho of Thien Long stationery, have built substantial and, in some cases, multi-generational businesses. Yet none has reached the scale, political visibility or state-adjacent reach of Vietnam’s current dollar billionaires.
The Rise of the “Eastern European” Generation
Vietnam’s private sector began to accelerate from the 1990s, and a striking number of the entrepreneurs who rode that wave had previously studied, lived or traded in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. Many had gone there on scholarships. The Soviet-era scholarship system generally favoured academically strong students with politically acceptable backgrounds, including children of government officials and state employees. After the collapse of communism in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, a number of these Vietnamese students stayed on and went into business, often in trading and fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG). These ventures allowed them to accumulate the initial capital that later financed their expansion in Vietnam.
Vingroup founder Pham Nhat Vuong is the paradigmatic example. After graduating from the Moscow Geological Prospecting Institute, he moved to Kharkiv, Ukraine, where he built the Mivina instant-noodle brand through Technocom before selling the business to Nestlé in 2009,[7] reportedly for US$150 million. That capital, together with the commercial experience gained in Ukraine’s turbulent post-Soviet economy, helped provide the foundation for Vingroup, now Vietnam’s largest private conglomerate.
Vuong was not alone. His wife, Pham Thu Huong, and his sister-in-law, Pham Thuy Hang, were also shareholders in Technocom in Ukraine during the 1990s. His early business partner, Le Viet Lam, co-founded Technocom with him before returning to Vietnam to establ

articles.title: Vietnam real estate developers roll out unconventional incentives to sell homes - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam real estate developers roll out unconventional incentives to sell homes  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Mounting bond repayment pressures and weakening market liquidity are driving Vietnamese real estate developers to introduce increasingly flexible financing schemes, including instalment plans resembling consumer purchases, as they seek to boost sales and ease cash flow constraints.
Vietnam's real estate market is undergoing a significant correction, with financial fundamentals, cash flow management and legal transparency emerging as critical measures of survival for property developers.
Reports from credit rating agencies such as VIS Rating and market research firms show that corporate bond maturities remain high, putting considerable pressure on the balance sheets of many developers.
Figures show that an estimated VND75-93 trillion ($3.61 billion) in corporate bonds will mature in the final quarter of the year alone. The real estate sector accounts for the largest share, with about VND46.9 trillion, or nearly half of the market's total repayment obligations.
Looking at the broader picture, total bond maturities are estimated at around VND276 trillion ($10.72 billion), of which the real estate sector makes up VND156 trillion, equivalent to about 57%.
The temporary mismatch between short-term funding raised through capital markets and the long investment recovery periods of large-scale projects and urban developments has created a difficult liquidity challenge for developers.
As bank lending is tightly controlled to safeguard system stability, alternative funding channels have narrowed considerably. Developers can no longer rely on the previous model of issuing new bonds to refinance old debt at relatively low funding costs.
Furthermore, coupon rates on newly issued real estate bonds remain elevated at 12.5-13% per year, adding to financial burdens and eroding profit margins.
Unconventional sales and financing schemes
These market shifts have fundamentally changed how developers operate. Rather than waiting for market sentiment to improve or offering incremental discounts with limited impact, developers are forced to explore every possible way to move inventory, including monthly instalment plans similar to those used for purchasing smartphones or motorbikes, in an effort to lower barriers to homeownership.
To unlock cash flow and reduce unsold inventory, a number of developers have proactively introduced flexible financing models.
Vinhomes, for example, has launched its "Buy a Vinhomes home without worrying about interest rates" program, offering preferential mortgage rates of just 3% per year for 18 months or capping interest rates at a maximum of 9% per year for five years.
Masterise Homes, meanwhile, is offering early-payment discounts of 15-17%, combined with financial protection that caps interest rates at 7.5% per year for 24 months.
Similarly, An Gia Group is offering buyers at its The Gio Riverside project in Ho Chi Minh City a 100% exemption from VAT, alongside direct discounts of up to 13.3%.
For the affordable housing segment targeting genuine homebuyers, Phu Dong Group requires an initial equity contribution of just 10-20%, combined with an extended payment schedule starting at only 0.5% per month.
More unusually, the market has seen several unconventional offers. The developer of AVA Center in HCMC is offering a "zero-dong home purchase" program.
Under the scheme, buyers pay an initial registration fee of VND30 million ($1,165) and make no payment at the first instalment when signing the sale and purchase agreement.
Their own payments are then spread over an extended period, at just 1% per month from instalments two through 16, covering a total of 450 days.
During the initial phase, banks finance 55% of the apartment's value, with disbursement beginning from the second instalment.
Upon handover, at the 17th instalment, buyers pay a further 15%, while banks disburse another 10%. The final 5%, payable upon issuance of the ownership certificate, is also covered by the bank.
Under this structure, buyers contribute 30% of the property value through payments made according to the agreed schedule, while banks finance the remaining 70%.
The developer also offers additional financial support, including a principal repayment grace period of up to 36 months and full interest subsidies during the first two years.
Another example is OBC Holdings, which has recently introduced a VND60 billion ($2.33 million) financial support package for the first 300 buyers at its A&K Tower project in HCMC under a "three-zero home purchase" program.
Buyers are required to pay an initial VND50 million ($1,942) and make no further payments until apartment handover. The package also includes a zero-interest-rate subsidy, a 24-month principal repayment grace period and discounts of up to 13%, providing another financing option for homebuyers.
Buyers urged to exercise caution
Commenting on the market, Vo Hong Thang, director of consulting & project development at DKRA Group, said overall demand for apartments had fallen sharply, largely due to buyers adopting a wait-and-see approach as interest rates remained high and credit was tightly controlled.
At present, most developers are stepping up incentives, including discounts for payments made according to construction schedules and extended principal repayment grace periods, to improve liquidity, he stated.
However, he noted financial experts caution that the growing range of flexible promotional schemes requires homebuyers to remain vigilant.
Financial expert Huynh Trung Minh said preferential mortgage rates during the initial period could ease upfront financial pressure but also carry risks when loans switch to market-based floating rates.
Buyers should therefore carefully assess the entire life cycle of their loans, including the duration of interest-rate support, adjustment margins and total repayment costs, he advised.
Echoing this view, real estate expert Le Quoc Kien noted that the costs of most fixed-rate programs and principal repayment grace periods are effectively incorporated into property selling prices.
Once the support period ends, buyers may find themselves in a vulnerable position if they have not properly assessed the property's underlying value, he said.
From a personal risk management perspective, Nguyen Hoang, deputy director of Eagle Academy, recommended that buyers develop long-term financial plans and maintain a safe level of equity.
Monthly principal and interest payments, he said, should not exceed approximately 40% of total household income to provide a financial cushion against potential market fluctuations.
Experts also emphasized that for developers, the only sustainable way to retain customers is to focus resources on accelerating construction, completing infrastructure and resolving legal procedures so that actual properties can be handed over and genuine cash flow generated from real value.
For homebuyers, taking advantage of preferential financing packages offered by developers can present an opportunity to secure a home. However, buyers should carefully investigate the developer's financial capacity, the project's legal status and actual construction progress.
They should also ensure they have a stable monthly income sufficient to meet banks' lending requirements and service their debt once promotional periods expire.
In addition, buyers should carefully review the terms and conditions in both sale-purchase agreements and bank loan contracts, paying particular attention to late-payment penalties, actual disbursement conditions tied to construction progress and any additional costs.
